The Schrödinger equation's high-dimensional bound state problem can be transformed into a nonlinear eigenvalue issue via a finite basis method. However, finding approximate solutions to this issue can be very challenging due to its nonlinearity and the intricate relationships between its input and output parameters. One of the primary difficulties in tackling this problem lies in exploring the nearly 20-tuple input parameter space that influences its solutions. One approach to addressing this challenge involves the utilization of two-layer neural networks based on two-dimensional Gaussian radial basis functions. However, it's been discovered that a well-generalized two-layer Gaussian RBF neural network often fails when applied to high-dimensional Schrödinger equation problem. This paper presents counterexamples to show why a well-generalized two-layer Gaussian RBF neural network frequently falls short in such scenarios. Additionally, a modified two-layer Gaussian RBF neural network is proposed by incorporating an additional 'ridge penalty' term, and it's been proven that this modified network is effective in tackling the challenging high-dimensional Schrödinger equation problem. Numerical simulations confirm that this modified network delivers superior results. One of the new network's key benefits lies in its ability to explore the intricate relationships between its input and output parameters more effectively, thereby significantly reducing the search space size associated with this problem. Several numerical results illustrating the new network's performance and benefits are presented. These results suggest that this modified network generalizes more effectively and achieves more robust outcomes when applied to high-dimensional Schrödinger equation problem. One of the new network's key performance and stability comparison results against the regular two-layer Gaussian RBF neural network also provided. One of the primary reasons for this research lies in its relevance to a wide range of high-dimensional extension problems that can be reduced to nonlinear eigenvalue issues via a finite basis method. By understanding the generalization properties of two-layer neural networks, we can better design and train them to deliver superior results in various applications, such as the challenging high-dimensional Schrödinger equation problem under consideration. Artificial intelligence techniques like artificial neural networks have greatly advanced our understanding of neural systems by mirroring nature's designs. By studying and training these algorithms on biological data, we can learn important insights into the functioning of natural neural systems. Researchers have been applying these algorithms to growing brains to predict their future development and to design intelligent machines based on these models. In a recent study, we employed an advanced neural network – the Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) – to analyze temporal information from the C. Elegans wasp, an animal researched extensively due to its large, mapped nervous system. By studying local neural activity in the C. Elegans and predicting its future based on this information, we demonstrated the feasibility of using RNNs on this animal. This achievement marks the first time an AI algorithm of this type has been applied to C. Elegans and showcases the integration of cutting-edge AI techniques with the study of biological nervous systems. Our study opens up new possibilities in utilizing RNNs to analyze and understand biological systems. It also sets the stage for employing AI algorithms on developing brains, predicting and modeling the intricate functioning of natural neural systems. Further research could involve employing AI-based models to design and assess interventions, predicting and mitigating negative outcomes such as brain damage due to toxins or accidents. Ultimately, we could use these algorithms in a reverse direction – taking in biological data and transforming it into insights that guide AI-based designs.

This paper introduces a new framework for text representation that leverages recall as a fundamental memory operation to incorporate declarative knowledge. Our approach innovates upon traditional knowledge graph embedding methodologies by incorporating a recall layer in the embedding architecture. The recall layer uses the query to selectively retrieve relevant memory vectors, facilitating the embedding of challenging words during training. Empirically, we demonstrate that this recall-based framework outperforms baseline embeddings in multiple downstream tasks, such as text classification, link prediction, and word similarity, ultimately showcasing its superiority in textual representation. To support and reproduce our findings, we provide a comprehensive, publicly accessible repository. Accurate nuclear weights of various isotopes are crucial for understanding numerous astrophysical phenomena, particularly the creation of actinide elements in cosmic "r-process" events. To determine the effect of new r-process observations on the type of supernova involved, nuclear weight must be estimated based on recently proposed supernova models. To facilitate this process, researchers have created a machine learning network capable of quickly calculating nuclear weights under real-time astrophysical conditions, allowing for rapid simulations of r-process events and their comparison with observed element abundances. When applied to the latest r-process observations, this model supports the notion that all observed actinide elements are formed in neutron-star mergers, and that mergers of various binary combinations and merger types with various types of massive stars cannot produce the observed abundances at the level required. Moreover, the model reveals that merging with neutron-star black hole pairs produces the highest levels of the heaviest isotopes and greatest differences in element ratios, suggesting that binary mergers of neutron stars should be the primary focus of investigation. To ensure the accuracy of isotope separation in this process, the researchers have also developed a weight estimation process for individual isotopes. This study has established a large, general nuclear weights database (over 5000 nuclei) that can be accessed for free at  https://github.com/alaniza/dense_nu_weights. The code for the neural network is also available at this site, enabling researchers to rapidly calculate nuclear weights under a wide range of astrophysical conditions (10^10-10^22) and to predict future investigations of r-process elements by name (e.g. 256Ca, 310U etc.) for a broad range of element precursors (10^1-10^6). Applying this technology to the investigation of r-process elements rapidly produces element abundance tables in under a second. By combining these results with the predicted yields of various types of supernovae, researchers have created a tool for investigating supernovae that can be used for the investigation of individual supernovae and their elements. Applying this technology to the investigation of neutron star mergers, the researchers have found a merger of neutron stars with massive O-red supergiants as the most probable cause for the production of the heaviest r-process elements and for their precise correlation with the metallicity of nearby stars. The transfer learning technique has become prominent in the field of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) for leveraging domain-specific knowledge. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are particularly beneficial in areas like chemistry and drug development, where understanding molecular structures can be crucial. Since creating high-quality, graph-based datasets is expensive and time-consuming, it's often more cost-effective to train GNNs on one dataset and then apply them to similar domains. However, it's still unclear how effectively GNNs can transfer knowledge across various domains, which domains are more suitable for transfer learning, and whether incorporating domain information into GNNs enhances performance. In this paper, we experimented on the Graph Classification benchmark, comparing the results of training with real data versus synthetic data generated by ZEMG. The introduction of domain information into GNNs through Mixing Graph Neural Networks (MixGNN) yielded a notable boost in performance. Additionally, we found that GNNs can successfully transfer knowledge across related domains, specifically those sharing the same central node. Notably, the enhancements caused by incorporating domain information increased significantly with the network's depth. Therefore, it's recommended that GNNs be designed as multi-layered networks to take full advantage of incorporating domain information. Moreover, using synthetic data such as generated by ZEMG did not lead to overfitting and actually improved the model's generalization to new domains. This suggests that employing synthetic data and pre-training domain-specific GNNs can effectively facilitate transfer learning. Finally, it's been observed that certain domains are more suitable for transfer learning than others, with the centrality of a domain being a determining factor. Centrality was found to be a valuable characterizer for understanding the effectiveness of transfer learning. The code used will be publicly available at: https://github.com/alexk0n/papers-MixGNN.SystemService.

Online education has become increasingly prominent due to its convenience and reach. However, students are still looking for a more personalized learning experience. A suggestions system is proposed in this study to address this need, using a dual feature distribution model that takes into account students' interests and their perceived abilities. The effectiveness of the suggested material is evaluated through a relevant scoring system. Preliminary tests conducted on 1081 actual student suggestions provided by an expert tutor reveal that the proposed approach is superior to a one-dimensional model that only considers students' interests. When compared to a multi-feature model that incorporates multiple factors including interests and academic abilities, the dual feature distribution model outperforms it by achieving a 10.7% higher accuracy rate. Furthermore, the proposed approach has been successfully demonstrated on a learning platform for Chinese language skills. An additional contribution of this study is the development of two quantitative metrics that assess the quality of a suggestions system. The performance of the proposed approach is also compared to a holistic scoring method that aggregates reviews from multiple experts. The results show that the proposed system outperforms the holistic method by achieving a 25.2% higher accuracy rate. Lastly but most importantly, this study showcases that a well-designed suggestions system can indeed provide valuable suggestions. Specifically, the proposed approach has been successfully tested on a 2000 user population in 2020. The study's findings provide a responsive framework for generating personalized learning suggestions and assessing their effectiveness using a variety of factors. The proposed approach has also been implemented on a technological level, utilizing a TensorFlow library. The proposed learning has the potential to enhance both the relevance and accuracy of the suggested material for each individual student. An in-depth evaluation of the proposed approach was conducted through multiple comparison methods, including leaving a portion of the samples untouched and repeating the analysis multiple times. The results indicate that the proposed approach consistently performs better than the two comparison models. To achieve a one-pass solution for the set disjointness problem on streams with elements from {0,1}, we can use the linear sketch technique. Generally, linear sketches for this problem involve utilizing vectors, matrices, or graphs to create set representations that remain relatively small despite growing input sizes. Typically, this property relies on exploiting the discrete linear system defined by the sets, where the presence of a 1 in the output vector indicates membership in a given set. However, this approach poses a challenge when dealing with empty sets, as it necessitates distinguishing between the actual discrete linear system and the trivial one that includes all possible linear combinations.  In contrast, we can overcome this difficulty by instead defining the discrete linear system as the union of the actual sets and the singleton sets, where each singleton set contains a single, uniquely labeled element. This reformulation allows us to accurately determine the disjointness of all empty sets in the stream through a pre-processing step that simply outputs 0. For the significant cases where there are non-empty sets, we can use the linear system created at the end of the first pass to compute a disjointness oracle with minimal space usage and allow for subsequent queries. In particular, we can achieve a space-efficient sketch by taking O(k) rows from a specially-constructed matrix A and then taking linearly-dependent O(k) columns from the output vector, where these matrix and vector combinations remain constant despite growing input sizes. In contrast to the typical linear sketches, we can simplify the approach by removing the need to address the trivial discrete linear system and instead directly rely on exploiting the union of the actual sets and the singleton sets, where the presence of a 0 in the output vector indicates membership in the family of singleton sets. In order to achieve this, we can use the Refutation Sketch from the Not-so-Elementary Techniques for Sketching linear decision lists and then taking the transpose of the output vector. This allows us to accurately determine the disjointness of all empty sets in the stream and we can output a space-efficient determination of disjointness. In fact, we can make the above sketch two pass efficient by simply storing the singleton sets in the sketch in the first pass. In terms of communication complexity, we can achieve a determinant oracle for matrices with k rows with O(k) rows and linearly-dependent O(k) columns. Speech enhancement technologies seek to improve speech quality by removing unwanted distortion, with many existing systems focusing on pre-recorded speech datasets that have inherent flaws. In contrast, our research explores the idea of utilizing real-time speech recognition directly from audio inputs to instantly improve speech quality without the limitations of pre-defined datasets. Our study involved examining the effectiveness of this approach in challenging healthcare settings where breathing sounds from multiple patients overlap. The results showed that our immediate speech recognition system excelled over traditional deep learning methods in maintaining high accuracy with reduced distortion, even in complex dual-patient scenarios. The key to our success lies in leveraging the advanced error correction capabilities of modern speech recognition tools. This discovery has the potential to lead to a wide range of applications in various complex audio environments. The source code for our immediate speech enhancement solution can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/huypm/DesnoisingSpeechWithSpeechToText. Additionally, our research was supported by a COVID-19 grant from the National Science Foundation, award number IES-2045162. The data for this project can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/huypm/BreathingWithBreathing. The instrumentations for the immediate speech enhancement are shown below.

Figure 1: The flowchart illustrating the concept of immediate speech enhancement.

The figure demonstrates how this approach enhances speech in two patient scenarios by integrating real-time speech recognition into the audio processing pipeline. The key steps in our solution are as follows. First, the breathing sounds from two patients are loaded into the audio processing system. The system then uses a speech detection module to identify spoken words from the audio inputs. The detected words are subsequently sent to a speech recognition module, which leverages advanced neural networks to accurately transcribe the speech. The transcription is then used to inform the audio processing module, which utilizes the spoken words to interpret the audio context. The result is an enhanced audio signal free from distortions caused by the overlapping speech. In our study, we evaluated the effectiveness of our immediate speech enhancement solution using a patient mix dataset that simulated a challenging healthcare environment. The results showed that our approach exceeded the performance of traditional deep learning systems in maintaining high accuracy with reduced distortion. The accuracy of our solution was found to be 90.52% as compared to 87.42% for the state-of-the-art deep learning system. A rational function p/q is considered bicritical if it has exactly two critical points, each with a degree of 1. The sequence of iterates obtained by raising such a function to successive powers is studied, along with the motion of the critical points in the complex plane. Research reveals that for bicritical functions with certain properties, the group of symmetries that arises from the transformation can be easily determined. Moreover, there are infinite cases in which this symmetry group consists of just two elements, as well as others in which it has much more complexity, consisting of 12, 24, or even 6 elements. The authors are also able to find rational functions with large symmetry groups and a value of 2, 3, 4, 6, or 12 for the degree of the preimages of the critical points. Notably, there are no bicritical functions that exhibit a symmetry of 8 by having all images converge; however, such functions with a different type of convergence are constructed. The research on these symmetry groups has led the authors to ask whether all bicritical functions with a symmetry of 6 can be rational, a question that remains unanswered. The full list of possible symmetry groups has been gathered through an analysis that involves iterating the function, studying its action on the complex plane, and employing tools from geometric topology. The possible symmetry groups consist of 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 elements and the authors are able to confirm nearly all of these possibilities with minimal exceptions. The possible symmetry groups were found by considering which elements of the symplectic group can be approximated by iterations of bicritical functions. The authors are also able to demonstrate that if a symmetry of 8 is realized through a combination of all images converging to fixed points, then it must be a diagonal matrix; otherwise, it belongs to a particular subgroup. The tools from geometric topology have also allowed the authors to prove that bicritical functions with a symmetry of 8 can be rational, a fact that remains inconsistent with the case where all images converge. Notably, the authors are also able to construct an infinite family of rational functions with a symmetry of 8 that does not belong to this particular subgroup, leaving only one case that remains unsolved - whether bicritical functions with a symmetry of 8 can be rational. The remaining paper is dedicated to describing these symmetry groups and drawing a connection to the problem of classifying all bicritical rational functions under a particular constraint

Research demonstrates that neural networks can be modified temporarily, allowing them to perform new tasks without affecting their underlying architecture. Our paper introduces the concept of delta lenses, which are filters that temporarily alter specific neurons or groups of neurons when applied. Multiple delta lenses can be combined to create a universal method for updating any compatible network, enabling the adaptation of expert networks to new, unlabeled tasks. To develop delta lenses, we propose a new supervision approach. We then present practical applications, such as using delta lenses as a regulatory mechanism for neural network growth or creating a method of "learning by doing" based on reinforcement learning. Additionally, we showcase a simple, universal delta lens designed to facilitate the transfer of knowledge between networks with similar architectures. Our findings are illustrated using a fully connected network as a model system and reinforced by experiments using training data featuring self-playing video games. Overall, the research demonstrates that temporary modifications to neural networks can facilitate a range of applications, including transferable learning, training without labels, and reinforcement learning. Our work establishes a new framework for understanding neural network learning and provides a approach for creating delta lenses. We anticipate that the principles discovered may lead to breakthroughs in machine learning algorithms in general. We investigate two types of events, multigroup and multiplicity, recorded by the Horizon-10T (H10T) facility, and attempt to provide an explanation for their origins. These occurrences are analogous to events that take place when particles interact with each other in various ways and a target material. We calculate the expected counts for these events using established interaction rates and statistical probability models applicable to such interactions. The calculated values are then compared with the actual recorded counts. Our analysis suggests that the observed events may be a combination of distinct group and multiplicity phenomena. We provide a theoretical framework to help better understand these events, and in doing so, we place the observed phenomena within the context of the standard model of particle physics, classifying them as spontaneous processes that result in the simultaneous creation of a certain particle pair, and offering a simplified model to describe the observed spatial and temporal correlations between them. The similarity between the proposed simplified model and an existing model suggests that the observed events may not be a clear indication of new physics beyond existing particle interactions. However, we acknowledge that the observed spatial and temporal correlations between the events could serve as a unique signature to help identify unconventional quantum mechanics models, including those related to the concept of axion-like particles. Finally, we reflect on the prospect of using the recorded data to further refine existing interaction rate models, and express hope that the observed events may ultimately contribute valuable insights that could help bridge the gap between astroparticle and particle physics research. The central element of this architecture serves as a base unit for detecting images, similar to how individual photoreceptors function as a sensory unit for detecting light patterns. The surrounding elements, on the other hand, contribute towards enhancing the overall stability of the network against interference from external inputs. By strategically placing a competition mechanism among these supporting sensors, we are able to achieve a level of image segmentation precision that surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. The supporting sensors are also found to be adept at detecting distant, high-level features within image data. By combining the output from central and peripheral sensors, we are able to attain a level of classification accuracy that is comparable to existing top-tier methods on the entire scope of ImageNet 22M dataset variants, in addition to exhibiting a significant resilience against various forms of network perturbation analysis such as adversarial attacks, pruning, and other such scenarios. Representations learned by deep neural networks capture signal variability within a class, but also include image-specific details that are unique to each example's surroundings and non-relevant to the class as a whole. For instance, in the class of "dolphins," these representations might include variable aspects like the animal's flipper size, making them less relevant for learning the class. To overcome this limitation, we've developed a framework that produces prototypes specifically at the class-level, using entropy regularization to prevent the model from focusing on individual examples' nuances. By minimizing entropy during fine-tuning, our prototype learning framework produces representations that can be easily manipulated by Bayesian neural networks, resulting in accurate and interpretable classification even with extremely few sample labels. Evaluations on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate our approach' exceptional 1-shot, 5-shot, and 10-shot generalization capabilities. Furthermore, the framework also allows users to predict the likelihood of class-specific attributes based on an attribute-specific margin adjustment. The code for our framework is available at https://github.com/asharakeh/cproto. Additionally, our reports on the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 can be found at https://research.google.com/pubs/DL4SHEET. In particular, the third reference shows our framework's extension, which can predict the likelihood of class-specific attributes without any additional training. The code and reports for this refinement are available at https://github.com/asharakeh/extended-DL4SHEET. Both the original and the extended frameworks demonstrate solid 1-shot, 5-shot, and 10-shot generalization capabilities to datasets with many classes (i.e., more than 10 classes) and on various tasks, such as object classification, image retrieval, and more. Moreover, the framework's predictions can be made at the same speed as training the model, which takes hours depending on the size of the dataset and the model's complexity. The well-known identity $a^2+b^2+c^2=1^{2^{3}}-2^{3}\cdot 1$ in the field of two elements, established by P. Erdős, demonstrates a set of three elements whose sums equal all integers up to $3\cdot 2^{2^{3}}-1$. 
In this study, we investigate the encompassing numbers of rings. Encompassing numbers of rings are more complicated since they cannot be confined to finite sets through basic mathematical operations. 
Our primary goal in this research is to confirm that certain finite rings, particularly the rings of $2\times 2$ matrices over the field of two elements, possess encompassing numbers as subsets of $2^{3}\cdot 1$ and establish a method to study such issues in larger rings. 
Additionally, a challenge is proposed in this research to determine whether there exists a finite ring, especially any noncommutative finite ring, that has an encompassing number as a subset. 
The proposed problem of determining the smallest possible encompassing number for finite rings might offer a significant area of research for mathematicians.

map of interconnected brain regions. This study uses a sophisticated approach
to systematically record the functional links between 196 distinct brain areas
as recorded through 52 different technologies in a vast database of over 1.3
billions measurements. By developing a new method to evaluate functional links,

center and involve external sensory inputs. In contrast, areas with fewer
interconnections are often specialized and located in the default mode network.

united by shared patterns of activity and functionality. Our study provides a
thorough mapping of functional brain networks, reveals trends in their
structure, and offers insights into the underlying mechanisms governing human
cognition. This work also provides access to a data repository containing the

These findings may also be applicable to similar methods used to analyze final particle interactions within the Large Hadon Collider experiments. To improve the performance of continuous reinforcement learning using off-policy methods, we propose a new, efficient experience replay strategy that accelerates the convergence of these algorithms. The proposed algorithm, variance reduction experience replay (V-ER), leverages a correlation matrix to identify and prioritize episodes with low variance in the state-action values, thereby optimizing experience replay. V-ER integrates seamlessly with advanced off-policy algorithms and is easy to configure, as it doesn't require tuning. Our empirical evaluations demonstrate that V-ER outperforms standard experience replay approaches and leads to significant improvements in the return metric for three challenging domains. Furthermore, V-ER enables a substantial reduction in the required number of steps to achieve a high return in each episode. The findings of our study support the efficacy of V-ER across multiple parameter settings and confirm its ability to enhance the overall sample efficiency of off-policy methods. In this study, the superbosonization equation is contrasted with the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation to establish their equivalence. These formalizations hold the potential to simplify proofs for free energy representations, particularly in regards to Gaussian models and their application in supersymmetric field theories. Moreover, they may offer a more direct and straightforward method of proof compared to existing strategies. As a demonstration of their utility, the free energy for a Gaussian model is formally represented using both superbosonization and Hubbard-Stratonovich transformations. Notably, the free energy derived via superbosonization maintains a symmetric form across all field types, whereas the derivation via Hubbard-Stratonovich yields an asymmetric expression depending on whether fields are bosonic or fermionic. This distinct form of the free energy derived via superbosonization suggests its potential for further interpretation and understanding. Specifically, it seems that the superfermionic pair susceptibility, resulting from the fermionic field's self-action, may be negative in certain scenarios, which could potentially contribute to a quantum phase transition. As an application, the pairing instability in a model involving a $Z_N$ symmetric vector boson is investigated. This model can be interpreted as a simplified representation of a $U(1)$ symmetric vector boson model, specifically when $N=2$. Within this model, it has been shown that the pair of a $Z_N$ charged boson and an $Z_N$ neutral fermion can mediate a superfermionic pair superbosonization coupling, leading to a pairing instability. Moreover, it has been demonstrated that the superfermionic pair superbosonization coupling has the potential to stabilize the condensation of $U(1)$ charged complex scalons in a $N=2$ component supersymmetric field theory. As an example of its utility, the pairing instability has been investigated near a zero-temperature critical point in a $N=2$ component supersymmetric field theory where fermions and bosons are not mutually local. Future predictions in time-series data like time-of-day temperature forecasts are reliant on understanding the underlying spatial and motion patterns. However, existing forecasting models neglect these patterns, relying solely on past time-series data. This study investigates how to extract motion details from spatial-temporal data to boost predictive capabilities. We introduce a novel method using recurrent neural networks that isolates and models motion dynamics in a static image sequence. The proposed approach expands on an earlier model by incorporating motion features and variable intervals. To test these methods, we created the MoD dataset, comprising images depicting vehicles driving in different directions. We found that our proposed methods not only identified the inherent motion dynamics but also the direction of the vehicles. Furthermore, we evaluated the impact of our approaches on spatial-temporal forecasting, using the predicted motion direction to inform spatial prediction accuracy. Ultimately, our research reveals that detailed motion analysis can enhance spatiotemporal forecasting. The MoD dataset and proposed methods are available at https://github.com/daniellbarker/ModRNN. We contend that integrating motion details into forecasting models, as demonstrated in this study, can improve their overall performance. However, we also acknowledge that using motion features in forecasting may compromise the model's portability to domains with considerable changes in spatial distribution, as illustrated in the additional experiment presented in this paper. Specifically, we found that using motion-aided models leads to overestimation in leaving the training dataset out. Consequently, while detailed motion analysis offers future promise in time-series forecasting, it is crucial to conduct further research into its extended applications. The additional experiment is detailed in Section 6.3. To summarize, the main contributions of our study are fourfold. Firstly, we developed a method to extract motion details from static image sequences. Secondly, we discovered that our approach identified the direction of the vehicles in the test dataset. Thirdly, we found that incorporating motion features leads to enhanced spatiotemporal forecasting performance and accuracy. Lastly, we identified that using motion-aided models may result in decreased QED values when testing on datasets with substantial spatial changes. In summary, our research provides insights into the benefits of detailed motion analysis for spatiotemporal forecasting and forecasting, as well as some potential drawbacks. This research focuses on implementing inter-procedural data flow analysis between a Rust and JavaScript program, leveraging their shared use of JavaScript's TypedArray. Our tool, Josephine, achieves data tracking and ensures compatibility by translating Rust's data types into JavaScript types applicable to TypedArray. In the case of Rust's generics, we perform type inference to determine the specific type and then apply the same mapping as for typed arrays. Additionally, we have developed a proof assistant's language to examine the soundness of Josephine's analysis, demonstrating its capacity to identify common data flow problems in real-world scenarios, such as use-after-free errors. With a future integration of static typing, Josephine could provide comprehensive protection against the misuse of data, ultimately enabling a safer environment for cross-language development. Our research indicates that the combination of advanced typing systems in Rust and JavaScript has the potential to significantly reduce the likelihood of errors when interacting across these languages.

An extension of this research's outcomes was submitted to Rust Conference 2021 as "Type Inference for Cross Language Data Flow Analysis" and presented at the conference.

By relying on experimental measurements of fracture strength and a vast existing database, particularly from multiple studies examining fracture strength along different axes of single-crystal silicon samples, a link between strength and fractality is established. This relationship is found to follow a distinct pattern when strengths are considered in relation to the area of interest, exhibiting a power-law dependence for values less than 1 and linear behavior for values greater than 1. This unique property is attributed to the elastic point failure theory, which posits that fractures occur when local stresses exceed the material's strength coefficient. This concept is found to harmoniously integrate both types of strengths, contributing groundbreaking insights into the inherent properties of crystalline materials. This understanding may ultimately lead to the design of more efficient and low-dispersion structures in these materials. We introduce a random point, denoted as x_{*}, within the strip, and generate a collection of imaginary discrete loops surrounding this point. Both the point x_{*} and the loop collection are found to be equivalent to a particle distribution on a one-dimensional log-scale whose density becomes infinitely large at x_{*}. We establish a duality in the loop configuration when the width of the strip exceeds 2h, and propose that the vector of field values at the lattice points converges to a point process with the Bessel point process, first introduced by Schiebold, as its law. This point process possesses the property where its two-point correlation function is zero, and is referred to as skew-Bessel. In the field of computational biology, the shaping power of cellular forces is recognized for its influence on the development and health of multicellular organisms. However, the in-depth analysis of cell shapes from a mechanical perspective requires highly precise and computationally demanding techniques. These methods primarily excel in the realm of simulations but have not been effectively applied to the creation of generative models for biological cell shapes. This study proposes a novel approach centered around implicit neural representations that enables the development of flexible and accurate generative models capable of modeling complex cell shapes. Our results demonstrate that our model outperforms existing methods by capturing more details of a cell shape dataset. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of our approach by using it to create artificial cell shape examples that reveal hitherto unknown patterns in the data. Specifically, we show that artificial cell shape examples match real cell shapes in terms of morphology while exhibiting contrasting spatial arrangements of cells and nuclei. These findings reveal novel correlations between structural features in the data that were not previously observed. The proposed method and corresponding code are available for public use. An additional code is provided for creating artificial cell shape examples with desired properties. This work explores the present state of document accessibility, focusing especially on making documents accessible to 'print-challenged' individuals. We'll delve into the two primary technologies used for accessing printed documents: e-readers/scan-and-evaluate systems, which have been well-studied and widely available, and 3D-printed documents, which have garnered less attention but are becoming increasingly important due to their unique benefits. We'll also discuss the challenges and potential solutions associated with 3D printing, including accessibility, and investigate the feasibility of using 3D printing for accessing documents. We'll examine various use cases and outline strategies for addressing the major hurdle of cost, considering both individual and institutional perspectives. Finally, we'll share our team's experiences and insights from an ongoing project that aims to expand accessibility to document printing. Our research hopes to contribute to a greater understanding of this topic and spark meaningful discussions within the community. By identifying the requirements and limitations of document accessibility, especially for 'print-challenged' individuals, we can work towards addressing the primary obstacle – 3D print cost. We'll explore economic models, such as 3D printing as a subscription service, with a focus on developing strategies. Additionally, we'll reflect on how the pandemic has accelerated the need for document accessibility, and how the 'print-changed' generation is transforming the understanding of accessibility. We'll share compelling use cases from 'print-changed' individuals and explore how the 'zoom generation' is shifting the paradigm of accessibility. Importing document formats is already a significant issue, but we'll also look at how the 'print-changed' population is impacted by border control and migration. Importing countries face significant challenges in providing print materials, and we'll examine the accessibility of e-books and print books within the EU and the US, especially for 'print-challenged' individuals. We'll explore the role of technology and the digital divide in creating a new generation of 'print-changed' individuals. Although the term 'print-changed' is not yet widely established, we'll argue that it effectively captures 'print-challenged' individuals' unique characteristics. We'll also find that 'print-changed' individuals are not limited to low-income individuals but can come from a broad spectrum of income levels. Ultimately, we'll reflect on how 'print-changed' individuals' unique characteristics and societal influence can contribute to advancing the 3D printing and document accessibility movement. While BERT excels at understanding phrases, its predictive framework has a limitation: it cannot regress beyond the context's boundary. XLNet, on the other hand, can not only understand phrases but also regress beyond the context's boundary, thereby significantly improving its comprehension. Our research demonstrates that this enhanced pretraining approach yields substantial improvements. Specifically, in the area of natural language understanding, XLNet models outperform BERT models by up to 10% in many cases. Moreover, in the area of natural language inference, XLNet models outperform BERT models by up to 4.0 or 5.0% in many cases. Furthermore, when used in the area of sentence classification, XLNet models outperform BERT models by up to 4.0% or more in many cases. These advancements can also be attributed to the fact that our pretraining approach is fully autoregressive, thereby allowing the model to be viewed as an auto-bidirectional model. Our research also demonstrates that this enhanced pretraining approach is universal, thereby yielding similar improvements across various models. Our research includes an interactive demonstration. In the field of computer vision, researchers often utilize expansion methods for categorization problems. This approach involves a learning representation where positive examples of a class are pulled closer together while being pushed further away from negative examples. This method has been successfully applied to various problems such as metric learning and information retrieval. Although previous research has demonstrated that using a lower-dimensional space for this learning representation can reduce computational costs, maintaining inter-class distances in these lower-dimensional spaces can become challenging. To address this limitation, this research proposes HyperExpan, an efficient and effective categorization distance expansion method that learns a non-Euclidean, hyperbolic representation. By leveraging the properties of hyperbolic space, HyperExpan creates a more compact, class-based structure that preserves inter-class distances. To achieve this, HyperExpan integrates a variational autoencoder with a hyperbolic loss function and incorporates an information maximization constraint to maintain a stable, hierarchical structure. This research demonstrates that HyperExpan outperforms existing methods on various datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and MNIST. Additionally, HyperExpan's learned representation is evaluated for its visual clarity and ease of interpretation. Experiments reveal that HyperExpan's learned representation graph is more modulated and hierarchical compared to other methods, and its depiction of the learned space can effectively guide human prediction. Consequently, HyperExpan offers an efficient, hierarchical structure that preserves inter-class distances, making it a practical choice for many computer vision tasks. A major concern with modern computing systems is the possibility that they might be harvesting user data unknowingly. To explore this issue, we conducted two user studies. The first study involved asking participants to wear devices that could track their movement, and we found that both adults and children could distinguish between being touched by a device collecting subtle biometric data and a non-data collecting touch. The second study replicated these findings and also showed that users could identify when they were near a device that was disguised as a everyday object and was collecting their movement. Our studies suggest that physical interactions with computing systems, such as accelerometers, can provide users with a sense of their system's 'purpose'. Based on these findings, we suggest systems could operate in different modes, and possibly even be turned off completely, if users express uncertainty about a system's purpose. Our ultimate goal is to address the issue of shadow substance inquiries by making the system's intentions more clearly known throughout, and allowing users to have greater control over their data collection. However, our studies also highlight some challenges to this goal, such as users being unsure about certain everyday objects' data collection purposes and having difficulty expressing their uncertainty. Ultimately, we believe that users should have greater transparency and control over their data, and we believe our findings can contribute to this effort. This paper explores the approximation of solutions to a nonlinear diffusion equation on a complete, infinite-dimensional Riemannian manifold. Specifically, we consider equations governed by nonlinear operators with polynomial growth or singularities. Unlike previous studies that focused on bounded domains, we examine the manifold case, allowing for more general operators and initial conditions. However, the principal challenge posed by the manifold setting involves the approximation of gradient vectors, which we address through the introduction of specific regularity criteria for functions on the manifold. These conditions ensure the approximation of gradient vectors by sequences of smooth vector fields, which in turn enables the derivation of error estimates for function approximations using the vanishing viscosity method. Autonomous vehicles and robots require precise self-localization capabilities, 3D visual information being particularly beneficial for this purpose. While 3D geometric data can store detailed scene context like road lanes and buildings, it may not always match the appearance of a scene. Excluding external GPS and sensor data, visual localization can either rely on sequential images alone to infer a location, or utilize pre-built 3D geometric maps. Image-based localization has proven effective, but builds scene knowledge slowly and may not consider sensor noise. Geometric map-based localization, on the other hand, uses pre-built 3D maps to determine a vehicle's location, yet typically doesn't accurately represent a scene's appearance. This research combines the benefits of both approaches: first, a system extracts both geometry and appearance from a pre-built map; then, when the vehicle needs to localize, it uses both geometry and appearance to determine a location, with both methods being learned with deep neural networks. This research also employs a novel method to combine the vehicle's current camera view with the pre-built map, further improving localization accuracy. Specifically, there exists a predetermined, yet sufficiently large integer $N$ such that any logical function semifield over $X$ can be represented using a combination of at most $N$ tropical functions. Consequently, we demonstrate the existence of a basis for the vector space formed by the logical function semifields, consisting of finite combinations of tropical functions. Furthermore, for the specific case of chains of tropical points $X_n$ in $k^n$, we identify a detailed description of the logical function semifields by expressing them as finite combinations of tropical polynomials over $k$. Our findings have an application in modifying Wilson's theorem. Specifically, we establish that the product of all multiplicative inverses of numbers in $k$ that satisfy a polynomial equation with coefficients in $k$ and a fixed positive odd characteristic is a tropical zero of a polynomial expressing Wilson's theorem for chains of tropical points $X_n$ in $k^n$. Consequently, the logical function semifields enable the construction of new tropical curves in $k$, specifically those satisfying a polynomial equation with a specific form involving the product of multiplicative inverses, for instance, the Tate curve in the context of elliptic curves. Ultimately, our proof reveals that the logical function semifields over a tropical curve can be expressed using a finite combination of elements from the tropical semifield of a specific curve with a modified set of coefficients obtained through an induction process starting from a specific simple case. The significance of the modification process and the structure of the sets of coefficients involved remains an open question for further exploration. In stochastic network planning, researchers have focused on creating efficient methods for obtaining desirable strategies from a set of policy options. Specifically, the Q-procedure and its variants aim to determine optimal or suboptimal policies for making decisions about entering or exiting networks. While these procedures have been effective in small-scale systems, their ability to adapt has been unclear when dealing with large data sets. We investigate the ability of these methods to produce consistent estimates, especially in the context of i.i.d. data, and explore the relationships between these approaches using the Markov decision process and dynamic programming frameworks. Our results include new estimators with proven consistency, a generalization of the Q-procedure, and new asymptotic normality results for variance calculations. Furthermore, we apply our findings to a multi-product inventory control problem to develop a new class of policies that yield improved outcomes and minimize disruptions. We also devise a new class of policies with reduced complexity that still achieve substantial benefits. Additionally, we discover a connection between bootstrapping these methods and a family of stochastic approximations, which enables us to recommend practical approaches for their improvement. While our work primarily focuses on stochastic processes, we also discover that these ideas can be adapted to other fields, such as graphical models and credit risk evaluation. With the ability to produce consistent estimates and expand upon existing approaches, we can expect these methods to be applicable in a broader range of contexts. Such adaptations are suggested for future research. Our Estimators for Quantization Problems (EEQP) framework provides a comprehensive understanding of these methods and their potential applications, while our numerical results demonstrate that these techniques are practical and yield improved outcomes when tested. While our approaches may not always be feasible for real-time decisions, they provide a foundation for systems requiring sampling or data analysis. Such sampling conditions include network planning and simulation-based credit risk evaluations. Furthermore, our work highlights the desirability of using sampling to improve these methods, a topic to be further explored in related research. Our analysis also reveals a connection between sampling and testing, which may lead to expanded applications of these methods. While our results primarily focus on i.i.d. data, we also investigate the ability of these methods to produce consistent estimates under mixing conditions. While our approaches may not always yield finite samples, we recognize that these methods are practical and provide general insights that can be adapted to other fields. Our most significant discovery is the development of a family of stochastic approximations, which may have a range of potential applications. Such approximations are suggested for future research. The connection between unconventional superconductivity, antiferromagnetism and nematic order in iron-based superconductors is still an open question. In the study on LiFeAs, it was found that while it exhibits superconductivity at relatively high temperature and displays mesoscopic electronic fluctuations, it does not show any nematic response to its magnetic field. As a result, it can be concluded that the nematic instability is not necessary for the realization of unconventional superconductivity in these materials. This further implies that LiFeAs's unique combination of properties should not be directly compared to that of BaFe$_2$(-As)$, where it has been observed. Instead, it is suggested that the superconducting properties of LiFeAs might be attributed to the metal-doped, isoelectronic replacement band mechanism. Moreover, it has been observed that the metal-doped, isoelectronic replacement band mechanism can be implemented in compounds where it was initially thought to be impossible. For instance, it was found that NaFe$_2$(-As) can be generated through this mechanism, and exhibits a replacement band characteristic of high-T$_{c}$ iron superconductors. Nonetheless, the superconductivity in LiFeAs and other related compounds cannot be explained by this mechanism alone. In contrast, it can be seen that the iron 3$d$ states in these materials show notable hybridization with the anion states, and this can be understood within the free electron approximation. Consequently, it is proposed that the metal-doped, isoelectronic replacement band mechanism might be successful in compounds where there is little or no interplay between the metal 3$d$ and anion states, and where the hybridization is with the band formed at the interface between these two groups of states. Ultimately, it is suggested that the band formation in these compounds might be successful in leading to unconventional superconductivity in certain groups of materials. As for the case of NaFe$_2$(-As), it was found that the metal-doped, isoelectronic replacement band mechanism could result in a density of states at the Fermi energy that is comparable to high-T$_{c}$ iron superconductors. Nonetheless, it can be seen that NaFe$_2$(-As) and other related compounds exhibit magnetic behavior, and it is suggested that this might be attributed to the presence of a small moment on the Na atom. In contrast, it is proposed that such an arrangement could be removed through application of uniaxial pressure

We examine a type of two Higgs doublet models that can account for the Standard Model's results and the significance of the Higgs boson via a hierarchical structure of the vacuum expectation values, with one being significantly smaller than the other. Our analysis encompasses a broad range of models, however, we limit our focus to the NP8w type due to computational constraints. We use the most current data from experiments including fit4DNM (global $\chi^2$ fit), experiment measurements of $\Gamma_{h}$, $\sin^2 \theta_W$, $m_W$, $B^0\bar{B^0}$ mixing, $\epsilon_K$, and other constraints to investigate this type of model. The findings indicate that the models align with experimental data when considering the latest results from BaBar and ATLAS. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the models can accommodate a broad mass spectrum with doublet masses ranging from 600 to 3500 GeV. In addition, our analysis of the complete one loop corrections for $m_h$, $\Gamma_h$, $m_W$, and $\sin^2 \theta_W$ indicates that they do not deviate significantly from their SM counterparts. We also found that the size of crucial parameters like $\lambda_6$ and $\lambda_8$ can be substantial, allowing for a mechanism to mitigate several potentially large terms. We leave the detailed discussion of these parameters for future research. Ultimately, our short-term outlook suggests that upcoming results from high-energy experiments like HL-LHC, Belle-II, and ILC can potentially determine some of the model's key parameters with relative precision. We also acknowledge that our analysis has some limitations, primarily stemming from not incorporating loop-level corrections for $\epsilon_K$ and $n_+/\bar{n}$, and missing constraints from $B\to X_s\gamma$ and the electric dipole moment of the electron, though it's essential to note that these topics will be explored in greater detail in future research. In summary, our analysis provides a comprehensive assessment of NP8w's capabilities to adjust to experimental data, and we believe that further research in this model is highly warranted. This research introduces two modifications for Loidreau's code-based cryptography system. 
Originally, the security of this system relies on the Gabidulin matrix problem within a degree-$d$ multivariate polynomial ring of size $q$.
Our first modification swaps the role of the public and secret matrices, requiring a public matrix that does not have a zero column, is of full column rank, and can be easily multiplied by a pre-defined non-zero scalar. 
On the other hand, the secret matrix undergoes a unique multiplication by a pre-defined non-zero scalar. 
On correct parameter selection, this setup provides the same level of security as the original system.

Our second modification involves adding a publicly known $m$-column matrix $B$ to the secret code $s$. 
Here, the user receives a public code $c = s + b$, along with the secret code $s$. 
To decrypt, the user subtracts the public code $c$ from a randomly selected code $c'$, where $c'$ differs from $c$ by exactly $m$. 
Therefore, the user can recover the secret code $s$ as $s = c' - c$. 
This setup allows for the sharing of secret codes, thereby increasing both bandwidth and efficiency. 
To ensure security, $m$ should be less than the size of the code, and the size of the code should satisfy certain minimum requirements to prevent frequency attacks. 
The two proposed alterations offer a significant decrease in key storage, as explained below. 
For alteration 1, the size of the public matrix can be made significantly smaller than the secret matrix, thereby reducing key storage by a factor of $d$. 
For alteration 2, the size of the shared matrix can be made significantly smaller than the size of the shared code, thereby reducing key storage by a factor of $m$. 
Both alterations provide a significant boost to performance. 
For alteration 1, the size of the shared matrix can be adjusted to minimize computation while maintaining maximum security. 
For alteration 2, the size of the shared matrix can be adjusted to minimize communication while maintaining maximum security.

We introduce Dict-BERT, an enhanced pre-training method for BERT that utilizes a dictionary to capture general meaning, thereby improving its pre-trained capabilities. By incorporating the dictionary, the model can effectively tackle denoising objectives where word-level masks are employed. The word-level dictionary provides a clear understanding of the general meaning in language, facilitating the generation of plausible masked words during the pre-training process. As a result, the model can accurately predict masked words based on their general meanings. Furthermore, to refine dictionary look-ups in pre-training, we develop an optimized approach using a additional regression model and an extra noise reduction task. Experiment results on GLUE and IMDB datasets demonstrate that Dict-BERT outperforms BERT and various benchmark models, attaining a significant improvement of 0.3% on GLUE dataset and reducing training time by 27%. Moreover, Dict-BERT's performance surpasses BART, another robust baseline model, by 0.4% on GLUE dataset. The code used in this research is available at https://github.com/autumn-WS/Dict-BERT. In the complex field of federated learning (FL), several concepts such as federated transfer learning and vertical FL continue to evolve.  Vertical FL focuses on generating a collaborative machine learning model through entities who possess complementary data elements.  Although it is particularly useful in the creation of models for adult classification, this research reveals that it is vulnerable to certain attacks that exploit the privacy of the data.  Two such attacks have been developed within this study: the first one selectively breaches the data verticality parameter with the aim of lowering the cost of model creation, while the first attack to breach privacy breaches the parameter within which it operates by only attacking at specific points.  It is revealed that both attacks are highly successful.  In order to counteract these attacks on privacy, two methods of protecting against such attacks on privacy have been proposed within this study: the first one protects against such attacks on model creation costs, while the first attack to protect against such attacks on model creation costs also protects against attacks on privacy.  An experimental evaluation of these proposed methods is then conducted, while it is further established that FL is particularly susceptible to such attacks on privacy in comparison to the protection of privacy in the non-federated model.  Furthermore, it is even more vulnerable to such attacks on privacy when a form of data augmentation is used.  An additional finding is that several methods of protecting against such attacks on privacy are ineffective, while it is even more difficult to breach the data vertically parameter as the data becomes more complex. As the boundaries between physical and virtual worlds converge, cities are exposed to sophisticated non-physical attacks that could be as destructive as physical warfare. While there has been research on responding to such threats, developing effective strategies to defend urban areas against combined physical and virtual threats is still a topic of inquiry. In response, a new game called Intelligent Urban Defense is being proposed, which aims to simulate urban defense against hybrid attacks. The game will focus on resource allocation within urban infrastructure to counteract enemy strategies in an immersive game environment. By exploring this game concept, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of how to manage resources effectively to protect urban areas from integrated physical and virtual assaults. The research will focus on developing and refining this game concept through player testing and iteration, ultimately aiming to contribute valuable strategies to defend against hybrid attack scenarios. The project will also develop an intelligent, adaptive version of the game called Urban Defense, which will utilize artificial intelligence to simulate defense tactics on behalf of human players, enabling researchers to test different defensive approaches. The project's primary outcome will be a game platform that can be used in a variety of applications, such as educational tools for teaching resource management and strategic planning within urban infrastructure. The project's secondary outcome will be a game demo that serves as a visual representation of its research findings. The project expects to generate papers detailing its research, as well as a functional game prototype that can be showcased at conferences and demonstrations. The project plans to involve three Ph.D. students and two M.S. students as research assistants, with support for conference travel expenses being provided. The project envisions its research outcomes to have various applications in fields such as defense, intelligence, and education. The project budget for travel will be up to $1,000. The project expects to last from Summer/Fall 2020 to Summer/Fall 2022. The project's principal investigator will be Dr. M. B. Chandrasekhar. The project seeks to understand the effective management of urban infrastructure resources in the context of integrated physical and virtual assaults, with a focus on developing strategic planning skills through game-based education. This research develops a systematic framework for determining the optimal configuration of Chain Event Networks using Bayesian Model Selection, where the likelihood is calculated as the predicted probability of event sequences by the network, and the prior is based on the network's topological complexity. Applying this method to the networks related to the 2011 British wildfires and the 2018 California wildfires indicates that modeling only interconnected events that trigger and depend on each other yields accurate results. Specifically, it accurately replicates the low occurrence of multiple concurrent events in both the wildfire networks and the network of lightning that caused the California wildfires. This framework proposes and recommends various CEN configurations based on their topological characteristics. Notably, it effectively differentiates between true interdependent events and co-occurring events in the California wildfire network, leading to a significant reduction in false positives. Furthermore, it suggests that event networks should focus on distinguishing between different degrees of interdependence between events. Applying this method to the California wildfire network results in a substantial 31% reduction in the false positive rate and a 42% reduction from the current best practices, respectively. Additionally, it highlights the capacity of CENs to model sequences of multiple dependent events, which can lead to more accurate predictions. Specifically, it results in an almost four-fold improvement in the accuracy of predicted event sequences based on the network's topological complexity. In summary, this research systematically analyzes the effects of varying CEN configurations using the Bayesian Model Selection framework. It demonstrates that modeling only interconnected events that trigger and depend on each other yields realistic networks and accurate predictions. Furthermore, it suggests that event networks should focus on distinguishing between different degrees of interdependence between events. In the case of the California wildfire network, it leads to a substantial reduction in the false positive rate and significantly more accurate sequence predictions. Finally, it highlights the feasibility of CENs that model sequences of multiple dependent events, which can lead to more effective predictions and analyses. In a 100-page paper, we explore and demonstrate robust asymptotic convergence towards the minimum norm solution, applying a Tikhonov regularization framework within a 20-kernel dimension. This involves inertial dynamics with damping, and our work expands on existing research. We begin by establishing the dynamical system and then proving its asymptotic convergence towards the minimum norm solution. Furthermore, our study also reveals that the trajectory of the dynamical system can be expressed as a convex combination of trajectories derived from the strong convergence towards the minimum norm solution, and we identify the set containing the minimum norm solution and potentially additional elements. Additionally, our work includes an examination of the inverse problem of magnetic induction and illustrates the application of the Tikhonov regularization framework and our convergence findings in this specific context. We also discuss the feasibility of implementing a first-order inertial mechanics algorithm with a 100-kernel dimension, and our work at times adopts a numerical approximation perspective. Throughout the paper, we strive to ensure clarity and completeness of our proofs by providing detailed and rigorous support. Although our primary focus lies in the stability of the dynamical system, we also explore the minimum norm solution's robust asymptotic convergence towards itself. In particular, our study reveals that the trajectory of the dynamical system can be expressed as a strong convergence towards the minimum norm solution within any finite-dimensional subspace containing the minimum norm solution. This finding is then potentially extended by considering the problem within the closure of the exponential attractor set. We also explore another direction towards establishing the minimum norm solution's robust asymptotic convergence, centered around the concept of Carath\'{e}odory's existence theorem. Finally, our work at times adopts a more traditional and detailed approach to optimization methodology. We hope that our findings may serve as a foundation for generalizing towards other optimization problems and dynamic processes. In dynamic environments, robots need to be robust against external influences. We are working on developing a strategy for a mobile robot moving along a straight line, where the goal is for the robot to maintain a set distance from a fixed barrier on the path. The approach relies on a PDA control system, which uses feedback from sensors to guide the robot and keep it at a set distance from the barrier. The study examines the situation where the robot is subject to unknown disturbances, which could compromise its ability to adhere to the barrier path. The research reveals that, in this scenario, the robot is only able to stay on the barrier path for a limited time and only with occasional corrections, rather than maintaining a continuous path shift. The shift itself can take on a wide range of states, leading to an infinite number of possible states that the robot can take on. The study also considers a variation of this scenario where the robot is subject to disturbances that slow down its movement, which complicates its ability to move forward by maintaining a set distance from the barrier. The resulting behavior is captured through a dynamic system model with an attractive component, which determines when the robot can move forward by maintaining a set distance from the barrier. The study reveals that, in this scenario, the robot is only able to move forward by maintaining a set distance from the barrier for a limited time. The study was carried out using physical simulations, which validate the findings. The full details of the research can be found at https://arxiv.org/submit/2103.11116. The code used for the research can be found at https://github.com/faculty-iitd/BarrierAdheringRobot. This research presents an innovative shape space exploration method for modeling plant growth. By modifying our prior work on growspace, a plant-modeling system that uses appearance-based optimization, we have developed an innovative technique for generating stylized plant models. A novel non-parametric representation of shape space enables the use of a kernel-based smoothing method to decrease noise after perturbing the leaf geometries. Furthermore, our method allows users to incorporate preferred features by localizing points within the space and guiding the search in a top-down manner. It also introduces a pre-processing technique to boost search efficiency in shape space. We have demonstrated the capabilities of this method through both interactive and automatic sculpting operations, and showed its practical applications in computer-generated imagery for creating stylized plants in botanical gardens. Our approach has yielded striking results and outperforms existing sculpting techniques both in an interactive scenario and in an unsupervised setting. Moreover, our method has become the go-to tool for generating stylized plants in a botanical garden. The method's source code is available for download at: https://sites.google.com/view/shapespaceplants under the MIT License. 2022 IEEE. Additional Videos.

The initiative aims to establish a set of consistent datasets and clear guidelines for the development of new image processing algorithms. We have revised several well-known datasets, created new ones, developed standardized annotation tools, and made all resources available on the Phantasia Platform, a web-based portal for the creation and comparison of vision benchmarks. This paper outlines the concept of the initiative, its benefits, and how it can facilitate research in the field of computer vision. Furthermore, we describe the resources and data available for both research and education, and provide a web-based platform enabling researchers to run benchmarks and evaluate their performance. We have also launched a competition to develop new metrics that can compare vision models in a quantitative manner. The resources and platform described in this paper serve not only the standardization initiative but the broader computer vision community as well. We intend for this resource to be continuously updated and expanded to support research and education in the field of computer vision. We concentrated on investigating the effects of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances on two photoproduction reactions: one involving $K\Lambda$ and the other $K\Sigma$. Our analysis was based on a complete-birth matrix approach. We focused specifically on the contributions of high-spin nucleon and delta resonances, in addition to the well-known quasi-bound states, quasi-delta and rho bremsstrahlung. Our research revealed that high-spin nucleon and delta resonances play a crucial role in generating the observed angular distributions and differential cross-sections in the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction. We specifically found that the $K\Lambda$ cross-section receives a significant contribution from high-spin nucleon states, whereas the $K\Sigma$ cross-section receives a substantial contribution from high-spin delta states. We compared our findings with experimental data from various facilities, including IASTATE, LEPS, E93-085, SASA, Jefferson Lab, and MAMI. Our analysis demonstrated that high-spin nucleon and delta resonances are indispensable in explaining the experimental data. We also discovered that the high-spin nucleon and delta resonances do not primarily contribute to total cross-sections, as suggested by some other models. Our research primarily focused on the role of high-spin resonances for $K\Upsilon$ photoproduction with $\Upsilon=\Lambda$, $\Sigma$, or $\Lambda_0(1405)$. Though total cross-sections from high-spin resonances are negligible, these states have a prominent effect on partial cross-sections, $Ep$ cross-sections, and angular distributions. Therefore, it's necessary to consider these states in theoretical models that describe the $K\Upsilon$ photoproduction reaction. Our analysis may also have implications for $\bar{K}\Upsilon$ photoproduction within the quark-meson coupling model. We observed that total cross-sections from $\bar{K}\Upsilon$ are not significantly different from those of $K\Upsilon$, indicating that total cross-sections do not adequately convey the effects of resonances. Therefore, it is recommended to consider the effects of resonances in near-threshold photoproduction reactions via partial cross-sections, $Ep$ cross-sections, or Goody Boxes, in addition to total cross-sections. A close examination of MORPH-II's image repository uncovered numerous non-standard formats, including watermarked and elongated faces. A series of pre-processing steps were therefore developed to rectify issues such as illumination distortion, face segmentation, and facial distortion. By exploring alternative image representations through conversion, normalization, and segmentation, we ultimately increased the dataset's processing speed. Notably, our findings demonstrate the efficacy of utilizing OpenCV's open-source toolkit to optimize the retrieval and analysis of morphable morphable morphing models. A comprehensive evaluation of processing times for each method was conducted, providing valuable insights for researchers to design and implement efficient pre-processing algorithms. The breaking of time-reversal symmetry in certain systems results in the creation of topological chiral magnons that facilitate the propagation of heat. This phenomenon is predominantly observed in magnetically ordered systems with ordered structures but can also occur in more complex systems with disordered or polymorphous arrangements.  We show that the emergence of topological chiral magnons is possible even in systems without a an ordered structure, provided they exhibit certain low-frequency dynamical response characteristics. This insight significant because it suggests these systems could efficiently dissipate heat through thermal manipulation. As an example, we demonstrate this principle in systems formed from coupled and interacting loops consisting of non-magnetic particles. These loops can adopt various configurations - as in the case of knotable defects or by dividing into separate segments - leading to diverse low-frequency responses. Furthermore, we found three distinct ways in which time-reversal symmetry breaking occurs in these loop systems, involving the magnetic properties of coupled loops, their collective motion, and any existing magnetic field applied. This research therefore extends the scope of time-reversal symmetry breaking to include a broader range of systems with disordered magnetic properties. It also opens up the possibility of efficiently transferring heat within complex systems with engineered loop structures. These loops can be manipulated using various mechanisms - at a mechanical level by applying stress, chemically by introducing magnetic properties, or dynamically by modeling their movement. Our findings have significant implications for the development of chiral magnonic systems and efficient heat transfer technologies.  Experimental verification of these concepts could lead to novel thermal management applications in materials science, physics, and chemistry. Moreover,  chiral heat transport could significantly contribute to the development of efficient heat dissipation mechanisms in nanotechnology.  As an example, to illustrate this concept, we successfully created chiral loops in nanoscale systems to demonstrate the experimental feasibility of efficient heat transfer. Our study opens up various areas of research in heat transfer, spin physics, and thermal management of materials with looped arrangements. These loops can be achieved naturally or through processing these materials. This work significantly extends the possibilities of time-reversal symmetry breaking by introducing a previously unexplored class of systems where this symmetry might break efficiently. It also introduces a new paradigm in heat transfer based on spin physics and magnon propagation, which distinguishes this mechanism from other heat transfer processes involving temperature-driven effects and diffusion-like processes in materials science, physics, and chemistry. In systems exhibiting multiple stable states or oscillatory behavior, identifying the routes to important transitions is a significant historical challenge. By developing a theoretical method known as the Transition Path Theory, scientists have been able to study these transitions in various areas. Nevertheless, in systems showing periodic behavior, discovering the routes to important transitions remains a difficult task. This is mainly due to the fact that, in such systems, the Transition State Path does not clearly define a single transition route, as it does in systems with multiple stable states. To address this issue, the authors propose an approach based on optimizing the Action along dynamic trajectories that begin at stable states and reach the system's saddle points. This novel method, Global Enhancement of Action along Transition Paths, can accurately identify the dominant routes to important transitions in systems with periodic behavior or other complex dynamics. To overcome this limitation, we introduce antagonistic patch creation, a method that generates opposing virtual bases according to the polymorphic function graph structure of a program.
