By comparing repair times, the modified Autopatch emerges as the fastest fix finder. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that antagonistic patches facilitate more efficient repair approaches and suggests opportunities for further exploration of this concept in code transformation techniques. This study presents a knowledge distillation technique called InDistill, designed to reduce large models by leveraging their intermediate activations. InDistill is unique in that it utilizes the same data flow to train the compact model, utilizing a differentiable optimizer to replicate the intermediate activations of the larger model. We examine a scenario featuring a single producer, one intermediary, and multiple buyers, with the intermediary having the option to withhold information from the buyers, creating uncertainty about available supplies. Our analysis focuses on the interplay between the prices set by the intermediary within an auction and the prices buyers offer to pay, which determines the optimal lot sizes for the intermediary to auction to maximize their revenue. Our findings reveal that in equilibrium, the optimal prices in the auction will align with the prices buyers are willing to pay, causing the distributor's curve will be downward-sloping. Additionally, if the auction is perfectly competitive, prices and the distribution of prices buyers are willing to pay will be influenced by demand elasticity, resulting in a rent being paid to the intermediary. Conversely, if the intermediary controls prices, equilibrium quantities will not be affected by demand elasticity. We also identify scenarios in which the optimal prices in the auction will not align with the prices buyers are willing to pay and show that the rent paid to the intermediary can be maximized or minimized depending on specific conditions. Finally, we discuss how our findings apply to a variety of real-world situations involving prices for used books, out-of-print books, rare items, and other unique items. Our analysis concludes that in the presence of intermediaries, producers do not always maximize profits by producing more units at a lower cost, which can lead to inequality in the optimal prices setting up a rent-setting mechanism. Which price-setting method is used will significantly impact the size of the rent paid to the intermediary. To the knowledge of the authors, this is the first study to analyze the effects of intermediaries on optimal prices settings in the presence of asymmetric information and auctions. A complete draft of the paper may be accessed at: https://www.brown.edu/academics/econ/faculty/streich/eqinc-intermediaries.pdf. The findings presented in this document have been published in an article titled "Equilibrium income with intermediaries" in 2021 in the Journal of Economic Theory. Our analysis is an initial step in a more comprehensive game-theoretic model that was presented in "Asymmetric information, auctions, and price setting in oligopoly markets" at the International Meeting of the Econometric Society in 2019. Reconstructive Summarization generates detailed information-based summaries from highly structured input sources like articles with explicit fact statements. To produce such summaries, systems need to incorporate various types of entities and their relationships from the input. Current approaches rely on pre-defined prompts or sentence embeddings to extract and organize this information. However, since entity types in the training and testing data are not always identical, and fact statements can be missing, these methods often fall short. To overcome these limitations, this paper focuses on a novel approach where human editors create entity-specific and fact-based prompts through an analysis of the summary structure. We apply this strategy through an interactive process with an editor who fine-tunes HuggingFace transformers for a novel low-fidelity summarization task. We evaluate our approach on 200 summaries from the TAC KBP dataset and demonstrate significant improvements in F1 score, specifically 19, 22, and 24 points when generating prompts from abstracts, body text, and both respectively. We discover that engaging editors in this process increases summarization quality by 44% and reduces the need for expert knowledge in prompt development. Ultimately, this research explores the potential for prompt engineering as an important and underappreciated aspect of language model customization. A collaborative system comprising an end-effector equipped with force sensors and a base equipped with vision sensors offers the potential for simultaneous achievement of two main objectives: controlling the robotic arm's movement and directing the movement of the arm's end-effector. By leveraging neural networks to analyze visual data, this system can achieve goal-oriented robotic arm control using adaptive control techniques for end-effector movement tracking. This approach allows the robotic arm's movement to be fully controlled by the vision-based neural network, eliminating the need for further processing or optimization. Furthermore, this system can adapt to changing dynamics without requiring detailed modeling of the environment, utilizing only real-time input from the force and vision sensors. By simplifying the control problem, this solution enables more efficient use of sensory data and reduces computational complexity. To validate this approach, simulations were performed to examine how various factors like the complexity of the virtual environment and the presence of noise affect the system's movement. Additionally, this collaborative system was tested in a physical environment where the robotic arm's movement was controlled by the vision-based neural network, resulting in successful tracking of a moving target. A demonstration of this technology showcases its potential in human-robot collaboration, where a robotic arm is used to prepare a meal while being guided by a computer-generated character. This collaborative system offers promising applications in various areas of autonomous systems, including robotics, computer vision, and machine learning. Deep learning models' effectiveness relies on large training datasets, with depth information being particularly beneficial for this process. While using depth data for model development can be costly due to its high resolution and complexity, we argue that its relatively simple labeling process makes it a more efficient choice for pre-training models. In this study, we assess the impact of pre-training on a dataset containing only depth information on the performance of a semantic segmentation model, comparing it to pre-training on a color-based dataset. We investigate the conditions under which pre-training with depth data results in significantly better performance. We observe that this condition is primarily influenced by the size of the dataset used for model pre-training, with better results typically requiring larger depth-based datasets. However, we also demonstrate cases where smaller depth datasets can still yield performance improvements. In general, our experiments suggest that pre-training with depth data provides superior results when the color-based training dataset is significantly larger than the depth-based one, leading to a reversal of a previous finding. We attribute this discrepancy to several factors, such as the fact that depth information contributes to both edge and depth cues, enhancing the generation of edge maps in this process. These edge maps benefit the feature learning process by providing more effective spatial context, with our code being made publicly available on the GitHub repository 'DepthForSemSeg'. Our name reflects the main contribution of this study, with further details on the underlying methodology being documented in the relevant repository. In summary, our research indicates that employing depth information for model pre-training offers advantages over traditional image-based approaches, with potential applications in a broader range of computer vision tasks beyond the focus of this study. Ultimately, our experiments demonstrate the feasibility of utilizing depth information for model pre-training in a more efficient and cost-effective manner compared to traditional color-based approaches. With ongoing advancements in depth reconstruction techniques, we anticipate even more efficient acquisition of depth data in the future, with our findings providing a significant step towards developing efficient public datasets for model pre-training, potentially leading to a wide array of applications in computer vision beyond the scope of this study. Consequently, we expect to see numerous future works exploring depth-based pre-training for a variety of computer vision tasks starting from the current state-of-the-art models. In a future automotive network, the computational capability of the edge node and local privacy policies may hinder data sharing. We explore the feasibility of collaborative structures for edge cognition within the context of automotive networks. We introduce the concept of an intelligent string topology, a decentralized network paradigm where nodes collectively prioritize transparency and trust in data sharing. Theoretical analysis reveals that this structure enables reliable achievement of a global optimum. Furthermore, a simulation study based on an object detection use case demonstrates that collaborative edge cognition can reduce data transmission to 8.6% of original values while maintaining performance comparable to full data exchange. Our research findings suggest that collaborative structures for edge cognition could protect user privacy while facilitating efficient edge cognition in automotive networks. Nonetheless, a comprehensive assessment of various scenarios, factors, and user types is necessary to validate the practicality of this concept. If successful, it could facilitate the adoption of edge cognition in automotive networks. The concept and related challenges and limitations are presented in this dissertation. The goal of this work is to contribute valuable insights towards developing collaborative systems for edge cognition and ultimately advocate for the inclusion of collaborative structures in automotive networks. The study proposes a new iteration-bound concept, analogous to (weakly) optimal efficient pivot choices and efficient faces. This bound is achieved with the Aspect Pivotal Algorithm (APA), a method that utilizes specific properties of the facial pivotal algorithm to establish this bound. By analyzing the algorithm's iteration limit, we find that it converges under certain conditions. Moreover, we consider a generalized version of the algorithm by relaxing certain assumptions and show that it remains convergent even in the relaxed setting. Lastly, we consider a particular case of the Hirsch conjecture. While we cannot prove the entire Hirsch conjecture, our results show that a modified version of the generalized algorithm has an iteration limit of n+1 in the m-dimensional space, where n is the number of variables. This satisfies the Hirsch conjecture for m >= n and also provides a new iteration limit bound of 2n-1 for certain cases where m < n. Recent advancements in object representation have been primarily driven by attention-based transformers, which have shown superior performance in various computer vision applications compared to traditional convolutional neural networks. Notably, vision transformers are gaining traction in facial action recognition, notably in robust zero-shot facial action recognition, which is more difficult due to a lack of knowledge on the target movement. This study sheds light on the high success rate of vision transformers in zero-shot facial action recognition and proposes that this outcome is largely attributed to the capability of feature transformation rather than attention focusing. Furthermore, this research investigates the resilience of vision transformers in environments with strong noise and variable pose transformations and reveals their high performance even under these adverse conditions. Interestingly, it is observed that vision transformers often perform worse than other models, such as ResNet, when tested on synthetic data. These findings are supported by an in-depth analysis of the features extracted by different neural network architectures, which reveals the inherent advantages of vision transformers in effectively encoding both global and local features. Moreover, it is noted that the success of vision transformers in zero-shot facial action recognition is largely attributed to their strong innate capabilities rather than the proposed transformation-based evaluation approach. This research also proposes a novel transformation-based evaluation technique to assess the impact of different pose transformations on the performance of various vision transformer models. This research concludes by suggesting that future research in zero-shot facial action recognition should focus on accounting for a broader range of target movements. In the realm of digital forensics, creating sophisticated image classification systems to aid law enforcement is a significant challenge. Researchers have developed various methods to build accurate models, but there is a growing concern among researchers to safeguard their intellectual property. Consequently, there is a need to analyze the extent to which their models can be transferred to other domains, and if so, how much of their model remains intact. This study aims to investigate domain migration issues with image classification models, particularly those constructed with Deep Neural Networks. To accomplish this, we conducted an extensive survey of current limitations and pitfalls in domain migration, and then performed an in-depth examination of two transfer learning methods on a large, publicly available dataset. Our findings suggest that with proper preprocessing and a suitable learning approach, it's possible for models to adapt and perform effectively in target domains, but the success is heavily dependent on the quality of data in the target domain. Our results indicate that poorly maintained datasets can cause models to struggle and perform poorly compared to a basic benchmark. Ultimately, we hope our findings and insights can provide practical guidance for engineers and researchers working with domain migration on large datasets. This research was primarily based on a dataset of car images from the used-car price estimation competition, with a total of 280 unique brands across 17 categories present in the dataset. We utilized 12 datasets for training and testing purposes, and performed 117 model transfers during our experiments. Our research was a thorough and extensive investigation, covering a range of model architectures, training techniques, and evaluation metrics. We hope that through our research, we can inspire future investigations and provide useful insights and practical knowledge for domain migration research in image classification. Our research has been thoroughly documented, and the code is available for public use, along with the results. We believe that by making this information public, it can facilitate collaboration and drive innovative research in the future. is characterized by a pronounced non-linear regression characteristic in the
course of its initial phase. This nonlinear regression makes it difficult to
accurately determine the rate at which performance improves. Consequently, it
is difficult to compare the outcomes with substantial theoretical basis. This
difficulty is compounded by the fact that there is a shortage of consensus
regarding the LM's training protocols. To address these challenges, this study
investigates the application of parallel training to the LM. By leveraging
inter-correlations between elements in the initial attended trajectory, this
paper develops a novel method for partitioning the attended trajectory. This
partitioning enables parallel training, thereby eliminating the non-linear
regression observed in the traditional approach. Furthermore, the paper's results
confirm the effectiveness of parallel training at accelerating LM training. Additionally, by employing parallel training, the accuracy of LM models is
shown to be comparable to state-of-the-art models with 20% reduced parameters. This
research facilitates a deeper understanding of the LM's internal workings, and
ultimately, provides a substantial step towards developing standardized testing
for recurrent models and their performance evaluation. Finally, the paper's
outcomes lay the groundwork for enhancing the model's scalability through
distributed training. Experimental validation of the latter, however, remains
outside the scope of this study's current iteration. The proposed method's code

Numerical methods used to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) have inherent limitations in approximating certain complex phenomena. Neural networks, when employed as an alternative, also exhibit similar restrictions despite their potential for more expressive representations. The root of their limited performance lies in the'spectral bias,' a built-in tendency for neural networks to learn low-frequency information first. We have discovered that utilizing a momentum-based optimization approach can mitigate this spectral bias, thus enabling neural networks to more effectively tackle PDE-related tasks. By experimenting with the stationary diffusion equation and focusing on the influence of spectral bias, we were able to develop a theoretical understanding of the problem and identify momentum-driven reductions in reconstruction errors. Additionally, we found that our proposed framework could successfully predict non-linear flows where state-of-the-art methods had failed. Ultimately, this investigation underscores the significance of accounting for the inherent characteristics of the data-generating process in order to unlock the full potential of neural networks. $$\begin{aligned}
\ddot{u} - \nabla \cdot \sigma \nabla u + \int_{\Omega} \dist (x, \Sigma) \dot{\sigma} \nabla u \,
dx = 0 \quad \text{in} \ (0, \infty),
\end{aligned}$$

where the damping function is only active in a sub-set $\Sigma$ of $\mathbb{R}^d$. We show that this system develops the property of exponential stability, coupled with an optimal L^2 decay rate, when the associated abstract operator becomes a generator of an analytic semigroup with sectoriality expansion. Additionally, when the sub-set $\Sigma$ is compact, we prove that this system develops the property of global stability, along with energy dissipation due to the effect of Voigt damping. We further investigate the long-term behavior of its solutions using the theory of generalized anabolic semigroups. A consequence of this finding is the existence of a generalized version of the classical supercritical surface boundary damping problem. We achieve these results through the use of decoupling techniques, operator decomposition, and the application of the basic principles underlying the theory of anabolic semigroups. Ultimately, the major challenge we face is to develop a novel, innovative approach that connects the underlying mathematical principles underlying the damped wave equation with those of non-active damping mechanisms and the theory of semigroups of operators.

These components are often required in areas such as reinforcement learning (RL) applications. While explainable AI approaches can tackle this, they have been found to be overly complex in most cases. Formal verification through Hoare logic has been a failed endeavor thus far.
This method has seen success only in the simplest programs, while more 
complex ones have proven too challenging to annotate. The chief hurdle 
arises from the necessity of specifying pre- and postconditions in a 
clear and concise manner using a predetermined notation. In an attempt
to address this problem, we propose a new approach called Natural Hoare
Reasoning. This approach requires Hoare logic annotations that reflect
the structure of input sentences rather than the conventional, syntactically defined format. By adopting logical forms and utilizing them in the specifications, we believe that Hoare logic will become a more feasible verification tool. To test this idea, we developed a prototype that translates sentences into the Hoare logic domain without pre-encoding the program logic. The prototype demonstrates some limitations in handling the most intricate aspects of programs, but our results show that it performs well on a substantial number of examples. In particular, we found that this approach allowed us to specify and validate a significant program, called the Collins basic parser, which prior methods had been unable to comprehend. The extensive, yet still restricted, domain of our experiment includes a limited collection of relatively simple programs, as well as more complex routines, including recursive functions, mutual recursion, and a rigorous method for dealing with lists. Importantly, we discovered that our Hoare logic specifications were often selectable by algorithms designed to parse natural language, regardless of whether they relied on shallow or deep analysis. These results open up the possibility of extending this method to an even broader range of programs, as well as more intricate domains that have so far resisted formal verification. In particular, we believe that fully formalizing more sophisticated parsing algorithms, including those used in high-end neural models, is within our reach. Further details about our method, along with a comprehensive collection of our experiments, can be found online. Our online resource includes a step-by-step guide that allows users to specify and validate programs using a logical form translation that we developed. Although this tool is still relatively basic, it enables users to efficiently specify more complex programs than those that have previously been successfully verified. Ultimately, we plan to replace the current approach to annotation with a new method that uses more advanced technology. By leveraging improvements in natural language understanding, we intend to remove the need for manual specifications altogether, marking the beginning of a new era in the formal verification of programs. This research introduces an end-to-end, Bayesian neural network approach specifically designed for object detection tasks. The proposed method generates a multidimensional output, representing a probability distribution over object confidence levels, location, and class categories. This probability distribution enables the computation of multiple sampling noise estimates for object detections, which in turn facilitates a reliable assessment of uncertainty in deep object detectors. The model is named BayesOD, a Bayesian object detector. It incorporates the traditional sampling noise estimate into a novel loss function, thereby enabling the training of a Bayesian object detector on which uncertainty can be quantified. The efficacy of BayesOD is verified through its performance on the COCO dataset for image-based object detection, with the model's performance measured in terms of both accuracy and uncertainty. The model's performance in these areas significantly surpasses that of non-Bayesian object detectors. The research also explores the relationship between uncertainty and reliability in BayesOD, demonstrating that its uncertainty and reliability patterns conform to theoretical predictions. Lastly, this study examines the estimated sampling noise of BayesOD through an analytical model based on the variational inequality loss. The model's loss term of BayesOD includes the estimated sampling noise. The estimated noise model's accuracy reveals that the scale of sampling noise has a positive correlation with the density of objects in a given image and a negative correlation with the size of objects. The model's performance is measured in terms of its average mean absolute error on the test set for different scenes. The model's performance in this area is measured to be between 0.11 and 0.57. We created a Monte Carlo model to simulate how cosmic rays interact with the Earth's atmosphere and magnetosphere. This model was particularly focused on capturing protons produced within the Earth's atmosphere due to interactions between galactic and solar particles. By analyzing data from the LEO spacecraft, we verified that our model accurately captures these protons at low Earth orbit. Our research found that the number of available protons increases with energy intensity from lower to higher energy ranges. We observed significant increases in proton flux, with rates changing by factors of 3-10 per unit increase in energy intensity. Notably, our model suggests that the primary source of these protons originates from ~100-1000 GeV cosmic rays rather than solar events. Our study has implications for understanding particle interactions and potential radiation hazards for spacecraft. It also highlights the need for further research to investigate the solar particle source of these protons and potential effects on Earth's radiation environment. Our model can serve as a valuable resource for forecasting radiation levels and guiding research into the Earth's radiation environment. Based on our calculations, the number of available protons per second at 400 km above the sea level is approximately 2.87 x 10^9, with energy intensity distributed across a wide spectrum. Understanding the energy spectrum of these protons will be crucial for accurately predicting radiation levels and preventing potential damage to electronic systems. The energy spectrum at 400 km above the sea level can be described by the function y(A) = -1.92A + 1.76 * 10^9. When plotted, this function demonstrates that the rate of proton flux changes significantly as energy intensity increases. For example, between 200-300 GeV and 300-400 GeV, proton flux increases by 50%. However, between 400-500 GeV and 500-600 GeV, proton flux increases by 25%. This difference highlights the importance of researching proton flux behavior across various energy ranges. Furthermore, our study suggests that the rate of proton flux change at the boundary between galactic and solar particles may significantly increase. In recent years, the field of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) has experienced rapid growth, with significant advancements in network architecture design and underlying theory. Research findings have revealed that pyramid-like shrinkage skeletons are essential for boosting model performance and adapting to various network architectures. Furthermore, link redistribution among local structures can help enhance GNN models. However, existing models still underutilize the potential of link redistribution and some problems, like compatibility issues with explicit skeleton design, and inefficient computations, hinder high-performance model development. To address these limitations, we present a novel framework called LLR-GNN that combines a universal skeleton design with local structure link redistribution. Our framework consists of two main components. First, we propose a two-stage decoupled framework to automatically extract the skeleton, whose multi-level features from each layer are condensed into pyramid-like features. Second, we introduce a link redistribution mechanism that establishes connections between neighboring structures to facilitate information exchange. Our LLR-GNN framework demonstrates superior performance over 114 datasets and outperforms 226 competing models, thereby serving as a best-practice guide for GNN design. The source code is available at https://github.com/whwuphd/LLR-GNN. Our model has won the 2022 IEEE Data Science Competition on COVID-19 Screening Algorithm (https://dx.doi.org/10.7797/COVID-19SA/ABBA). Additionally, we have won the 2022 Challenge on Medical Graph Masked Prediction at IJCAAI 2022 \& 2022 IEEE Data Science Competition on COVID-19 Infection Inferring (https://dx.doi.org/10.7797/COVID-19SI/ABBA). The model related to the winning challenge can be accessed via https://github.com/whwuphd/COVID-Inferring. The model also won the 2021 Challenge on Modelling the Impact of Government Interventions on COVID-19 Hospitalizations at AI4D 2021 https://dx.doi.org/10.7905/2021/ghr.g.0002. To protect users' privacy, we are focusing on a low-rank matrix completion framework with stringent accuracy requirements and robust noise constraints, as dictated by differential privacy regulations. This is an advancement of the existing low-rank matrix completion problem and requires completing a partially observed matrix containing sensitive information. Our solution integrates the Huber loss function, a gradient boosting algorithm, and Least Squares SVR to provide a versatile solution for this challenge. The proposed approach can be based solely on gradient minimization, or it can incorporate an iterative process incorporating the first derivative of the Huber loss function. Theoretical analyses are provided to verify the objective function's fidelity and the rank of the estimated matrix. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through synthetic data experiments, generating results that surpass current differentially private low-rank matrix completion methods in terms of fidelity. The proposed code is available at https://github.comxingjw256/Huber-low-rankmatrixcompletion.py. In this research, we revise the principles of Abstract Interpretation by splitting the effects of abstract abstractions into distinct 'ascent' and 'descent' phases, which can be applied in various orders. This reformulation enhances ABNonlinear, a class of Abstract Interpretation techniques used to identify program regions that trigger infinite loops by disregarding their actual computational effects. We present a new decoupling method for ABNonlinear, called dec-ABNonlinear, that identifies areas of a program not influenced by its infinite loops and exhibits comparable precision to ABNonlinear while performing better numerically. Dec-ABNonlinear can be utilized with other state-of-the-art Abstract Interpretation techniques to determine program segments that enter infinite loops regardless of other computational processes. We demonstrate the improved precision of dec-ABNonlinear over traditional Abstract Interpretation for a significant method implementation by 50%. Additionally, our experimental findings show that dec-ABNonlinear outperforms ABNonlinear in time by 20% with representative program benchmarks. Ultimately, dec-ABNonlinear offers promising potential for integration with other Abstract Interpretation techniques to further enhance precision. Although our initial evaluation of overall precision is similar to ABNonlinear, future advancements are anticipated. The proposed decoupling abstraction framework can be applied to other Abstract Interpretation techniques as well, offering a potential general improvement in precision. We present a general algorithm for abstract domains to overcome potential issues during the descent phase and demonstrate its utility in improving the precision of Abstract Interpretation. This decoupling algorithm is available under an open-source license on GitHub. We use non-linear abstract domains in our experimental evaluation but the decoupling can be applied to any Abstract Interpretation algorithm to improve precision. We present a variety of program examples to showcase the improved precision of dec-ABNonlinear over ABNonlinear. Several of these examples highlight the utility of dec-ABNonlinear in identifying infinite loops that cannot be captured by ABNonlinear due to its inability to account for computational effects during the ascending phase. On the other hand, there are also examples that illustrate a complete disregard for infinite loops during the descending phase leading to a precision loss compared to ABNonlinear. Lastly, we present examples highlighting the difficulties encountered by dec-ABNonlinear in accurately predicting program behavior due to inaccurate over- or under-estimation of infinite loops during either the ascending or descending phase. These challenges, along with other related issues, are investigated in more detail. The main contribution of our research is the improved precision achieved by integrating ABNonlinear

Detecting abnormalities in data is a crucial step in many processes, such as
model training and quality control. However, traditional methods are often
inefficient due to reliance on histogram-based representations. In contrast, a
new approach employs a graph structure where each node represents a data point
and connects adjacent nodes with a specified proximity. By analyzing the
proximity graph, this method can accurately identify and quantify anomalies
in a very short time. Our empirical analysis using real datasets reveals that
the proposed CloGraph method surpasses existing techniques in speed, precision,
and scalability. Notably, it is the only method that can be applied to data sets
where the values are not unique. CloGraph is also capable of processing data
where the values are not numerical by replacing the distances with similarity
measurements. To facilitate the use of CloGraph, we created a user-friendly
interface that can be used as a Google Chrome extension or a standalone tool. 
Furthermore, we introduce a publicly accessible database of pre-analyzed datasets to support clograph-based research. 
The code for CloGraph is available at https://github.com/andreaborella/CloGraph.

By spurring digital innovation, the rise of data richness has generated various formats of data, necessitating innovative strategies for extraction and analysis to derive valuable insights. By leveraging a computer's processing power, we can swiftly identify similarities and differences among neighboring areas, thereby enhancing the detection of anomalies and supporting decision-making processes. The associated code has been made publicly available for further development and use. This research contributes to the development of a versatile tool for graph analysis from a neighborhood perspective, ultimately leading to deriving actionable insights for supporting decision-making in real-time. As a result, we expect our method to benefit various applications, such as early detection of at-risk individuals, across the digital spectrum. This research focuses on a specific class of stochastic models, namely continuous-flow stirred-tank reactors, to analyze reversible enzyme reactions. To determine the concentration values of species over time, we calculate the system's moment dynamics from the associated microscopic description, which is a generalized version of the chemical master equation. Subsequently, we develop an iterative technique to approximate the system's stochastic solution, leveraging the moment dynamics. Notably, our analytical findings reveal that the iterative approximations consist of a probabilistic recursive formula and an ordinary differential equation, with the latter requiring adjustment to account for higher-order terms. We compare the accuracy of our analytical solutions with Monte Carlo simulation results for three scenarios: the Michaelis-Menten interaction, a two-step protein-ligand interaction, and a three-step multienzyme reaction. Overall, our iterative approach exhibits excellent time efficiency for a wide range of parameter values. Moreover, to account for additional factors affecting the reaction system, we introduce a generalization of our analytical solution and validate its performance by simulating various relevant modifications. Finally, we analyze the correspondence between our stochastic enzyme reaction model and a deterministic Michaelis-Menten model. This study explores a theoretically grounded model of a quantum harmonic oscillator propelled by a jet of particles. By combining the propulsion particle's quantum dynamics with the oscillator's classical motion, researchers develop an exact expression for its wave function. Two distinct sets of coordinates are utilized: the Hilbert space representation focused on exponential variables which enables the derivation of an analytical expression for the partition function, and a numerical Monte Carlo approach focused on position-momentum coordinates which allows for calculating physical properties. In the second method, a Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation is applied to investigate how changes in jet force, amplitude, and frequency influence the partition function's decay rate as momentum increases. These changes are found to be described by a power law, and both methods yield the same exponent value. Moreover, the variation of the partition function with respect to the propagation variable produces the analytical momentum distribution obtained from the first method. These outcomes validate the utilized formalism and lay the groundwork for analyzing other driven quantum harmonic oscillators. This research also contributes to understanding the properties of microscopic propulsion mechanisms, such as those found in kinesin and dynein transport, as well as to investigating quantum harp driven by a jet of particles decoupled from its potential. Future studies will utilize these approaches to examine more complex and driven quantum systems. Evaluation-based recommendation seeks to enhance the quality of interactions between customers and products by providing useful feedback. This task is particularly challenging due to the scarcity of interaction data. To address this issue, we develop an innovative framework, called the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), which aims to leverage customers' reviews to improve recommendation precision. By using a sentiment classification model to determine relevant reviews and combine them with user-product interactions, SIFN learns a robust product representation that captures diverse aspects of user preferences. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets confirm the efficacy of SIFN, achieving better performance than existing methods across various evaluation metrics. Notably, we found that SIFN's recommended product rankings often align with human judgments in a majority of cases (57.11% on AmazonFashion and 65.25% on Taobao). This research makes significant contributions to both the interaction-based recommendation and sentiment analysis fields. The proposed approach successfully applies sentiment analysis to interaction data for the purpose of interaction-based recommendation, while also improving recommendation quality and providing robust user product representations that reflect comprehensive preferences. The research reveals that recommending products in accordance with defined rating criteria can be accomplished by incorporating relevant review sentiments into product representations and enhances recommendation precision with more robust and diverse user product connections. The approach expands the scope of interaction-based recommendation to capture various aspects of user preferences, akin to NLP's n-gram extension for token analysis. Moreover, this work bridges the gap between the evaluation-based and interaction-based recommendation tasks and evaluates the recommended product lists with human-like sentiment analysis. Finally, it highlights the practicality of recommendation models in real-world applications by showing consistency between the ranking order of recommended products and human preferences. The research utilizes an innovative sentiment analysis model to bridge the gap between evaluation-based and interaction-based recommendation and bridges the gap between the two tasks by combining evaluation-based and interaction-based models to achieve superior results. Training neural models on code-switched Arabic-English text using maximum likelihood can lead to switched word order, which hampers performance. Research has shown that using monolingual data and artificially augmenting it with a minimum of code-switched examples can sometimes be beneficial. However, models still struggle on tasks requiring a strong understanding of either language. We investigated the potential of code-switched data generated by replacing code-switched tokens with equivalents from either language in a neural machine translation dataset, revealing that this too can be counterproductive. On the other hand, manually gathered code-switched examples that focus on switching individual words can boost model performance across different task levels. Moreover, using code-switched examples up to a certain degree does not continue to improve the model's performance beyond that point. We observed notable performance gains of up to 3.48 BLEU points in an NLP task after using these targeted examples compared to standard data. Ultimately, we recommend a balanced mix of using code-switched examples that cater to varying levels of code-switching intensity. Discovering relations in a knowledge graph is now possible with large pre-trained models, but these relations must be present in the dataset or subset that the model was trained on. The main aim of relation discovery is to identify relationships between subjects and objects that the model has not been trained on before. Recent studies have employed pre-trained models, combining them with either learning-based or unsupervised techniques to discover new relations. The performance of these methods is subpar when judged by their ability to accurately predict relations in out-of-sample cases. The major limitation of these methods is that they suggest new relationships between two entities based on their connection to other unrelated entities. To improve relation discovery, we developed an approach to predict which entities of a subject are most likely to be connected. By incorporating this entity correlation information into the relation discovery process, our approach significantly boosts performance in relation discovery tasks. The established framework, known as Connection-Aided Relation Discovery (CARD), also allows for more accurate results when finding novel relations. The approach leverages an adapter transformer to map entities into a shared space where it predicts potential connections. By eliminating connections with entities that are connected in the knowledge graph, the approach then assesses the similarity between entities to identify novel relations. Experiments conducted on three prominent knowledge graphs - DBpedia, YAGO, and Wikidata - as well as two prominent datasets, i.e. NEWSTIME and CONDIV, demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework in discovering novel relations. Notably, the approach outperformed existing relation discovery techniques, achieving a 6.7% average improvement in MACE benchmark. To accurately analyze the performance of advanced analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), which exhibit nonlinearity in their conversion function, precise knowledge of their transfer characteristics is essential. These transfer characteristics are represented by parameterized functions that describe how input voltage levels are mapped to corresponding ADC output codes. Since nonlinearity affects how the ADC's output deviates from its ideal transfer, determining this transfer nonlinearity is crucial for simulating ADC performance using different distortion metrics. A proposed method utilizes a Matlab implementation of the Fourier series technique to parameterize ADC transfer nonlinearity and generates the necessary transfer function coefficients. The corresponding Matlab code is provided to facilitate analytical ADC simulation. By employing this approach, it's possible to accurately analyze ADC performance over various operating conditions and extract relevant metrics, such as signal-to-noise and distortion ratio (SNDR), effective number of bits (ENOB), and top-9 modulation frequency harmonic power for multitone tests, which can also account for the impact of dc offset and common-mode feedback circuit efficiency. The presented method is validated through comparison with spice simulation results for an ADC example featuring a proprietary dynamic element matching (DEM) modulator. The analysis highlights the importance of accounting for ADC nonlinearity and phase nonlinearity in determining its overall performance. The approach provides a cost-effective means of performing ADC performance analysis. The corresponding Matlab code can be accessed at https://github.com/mkacikarom/AADC-ANALYSIS.git. Key properties of function smoothness play a crucial role in developing and analyzing many Machine Learning and Reinforcement Learning algorithms. While the implications of smoothness are extensive, its definition can be quite abstract. In the realm of Reinforcement Learning, a more streamlined smoothness definition would likely streamline the development of policies. Unfortunately, most established smoothness criteria are tailored to gradient-based optimizations and do not directly apply to tabular RL. This study seeks to bridge this gap by introducing a new, function smoothness criterion rooted in metric spaces and suitable for tabular RL in finite or countable settings. This novel smoothness perspective not only reduces computational complexity but also provides a foundational framework for further research. Building upon this, we leverage our metric space-based smoothness and establish several RL algorithms, notably three TD learning algorithms - including an accelerated, adapted version of TD($\lambda$) - that are both efficient and versatile. These new algorithms are also demonstrated to be effective in both tabular and parameterized contexts. Finally, our smoothness analysis enables the generalization of existing RL algorithms to novel settings, such as interdependent MDPs. This research contributes a new perspective on metric space-based smoothness and its applications to tabular RL. It is anticipated that this smoothness criterion will facilitate the exploration of novel RL settings and properties. Multidimensional fluid dynamics simulations heavily rely on complex mathematical models that often require to be refined locally to capture essential physical processes. However, doing so typically disrupts the smooth structure of the solution, making it unappealing for practical purposes and even invalid in some cases. To address this, we have developed a new generic filter designed for simulated data with low noise and strong structural connections, particularly in multi-dimensional systems. By leveraging an optimization-based approach, our filter maintains the structure of the solution while reducing unwanted components. We have tested its effectiveness using multiple, highly complex models across three distinct mathematical frameworks, achieving impressive results. Moreover, we have obtained similar outcomes when applying it to realistic simulations of two distinct applications: a solar flare model and a simulation of ocean currents. Our results demonstrate that the simplicity and flexibility of the new filter make it a valuable tool for handling local events in diverse fields. It is open-source and can be easily integrated into existing projects at https://github.com/ahartin1/StructMaintFilter. Additionally, pre-trained models can be accessed at https://hubbion.github.io/StructMaintFilter. In collaborative learning between a student and a teacher, the associate's motivation plays a crucial role in understanding the transfer of learned capabilities to unreliable environments. By varying their level of engagement, associates can influence students to focus on specific task variations. To improve collaborative learning outcomes, it is essential for teachers to adjust their instruction methods according to associates' behavior. For instance, in training a graph neural network, an associate can provide focus on different nodes based on varying interest levels. While active learning aims to have teachers provide specific feedback on what is important, it places the burden on teachers due to the difficulty and cost involved. To resolve this, a system has been proposed called Social Inherent Motivation of Transfer Enablement (SIMTE), which places the burden on associates. It achieves this by creating a motivation framework that reflects the associates' level of engagement. As a result, the teacher only needs to provide guidance on this motivation, saving considerable time and effort. To determine the motivation of associates, a transfer enablement network (TEN) is employed, which measures how much a student has focused on specific task variations based on the supervision from the teacher. In turn, this student can serve as a role model for other students to focus on similar variations. A mechanism has been developed to update the motivation of associates by using a variational autoencoder to identify the motivation distribution. Moreover, a new training objective, called transfer enablement loss, has been proposed to update the motivation of associates. By enabling teachers to simply provide guidance on this motivation, it places the burden on associates. By testing the proposed method on various collaborative learning experiments, it has been shown that it outperforms other competing methods. Furthermore, it has been shown that the proposed motivation of associates can serve as a useful regularizer to improve training efficiency even in the absence of any specific collaboration. More importantly, it has been found that the motivation of associates can be naturally acquired through human-robot interaction and does not need any external assistance, as proven by conducting a human-robot collaboration experiment. It is expected that this research will serve as a starting point for developing various mechanisms to update the motivation of associates and also for integrating such motivation of associates into the existing state-of-the-art models. A related project is available on github at https://github.com/AI-SAILOR/SIMTE. The robot used in the research can be seen at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Oa4Hk1Oo4sI. Advancements in machine learning have led to increased efficiency across multiple industries, particularly in identifying substances. Our research focuses on visual identification in environments with minimal spectral variation. We've developed a comprehensive approach to substance identification, utilizing pre-trained Vision Transformer-based models and post-hoc refinement using specialized rules. Furthermore, identifying a substance in real-time requires a well-designed and efficiently processed data stream. To achieve this, we employed contrastive learning with pre-trained physics-informed visualizations. Our implementation of this approach involves pre-training a model to take a pair of inputs, real and fake, and determining their similarity. To create a variety of fakes, we employed color mixing as our hyperlens. The pre-trained model is then used for post-hoc refinement by projecting the model output onto a pseudocolor space and applying a set of rules. Our method was tested using XRF phone vision, leading to 100% accuracy in laboratory settings and 95% in real-world settings, outperforming traditional approaches such as mass spectroscopy and using human observers. Our method allows for a single-shot identification and can be done with minimal expertise and specialized equipment. Our study demonstrates that a trained model can overcome spectral variations by applying a understanding of color in between spectrograms and images. 2-Lie algebras, being central components of two-stage Lie-theoretic constructions, have been studied for about five decades, yet research on Lie 2-groups remains relatively underdeveloped compared to other areas of differential geometry and Lie theory. This underdevelopment is particularly evident in the lack of a comprehensive reference on Lie 2-groups. To address this gap, the current work aims to provide a accessible introduction to Lie 2-groups by surveying the fundamental theory and notable results in the field, with an emphasis on Lie 2-groups derived from 2-Lie algebras. This foundational account aims to lay the groundwork for exploring more advanced topics, such as the geometric properties of Lie 2-algebras and their connections to foliations. A accompanying online resource includes illustrative Mathematica code for the construction of Lie 2-groups. We anticipate that this introduction will serve as a reference for future research on Lie 2-groups and their connections to related areas, such as foliations and Lie groups. This survey has been initially published in 'Banach Center Publications', volume 115, edited by A. Naldona and A. N. We introduce a novel, unsupervised method for object feature matching called LoFTR. This approach bypasses object detection and leverages deep regional feature matching instead. By using a decoder-only transformer architecture, we enable our method to efficiently handle large image sets. Our experiments show that LoFTR surpasses state-of-the-art performance in both abstract and semantic alignment, achieving this with deep regional features that require minimal computation. Specifically, we achieve a 43.6% increase in average AVE (mAP) on the EPIC-KITCHENS dataset compared to a baseline model. Our code and method are publicly available.

The comprehension of everyday knowledge, especially in human relationships, requires extensive training in neural networks, necessitating substantial datasets to learn from. Such resources are scarce, with existing large datasets often defined by rigid, categorically-structured rules, making it difficult to scale. To address this limitation, we've developed COMET-ATOMIC 2020, a significantly expanded version of the original ATOMIC dataset. This updated release records over 1 million descriptions of social interactions, surpassing the previous record by tenfold. To further facilitate research, we've developed COMET-NEURAL, a large neural network-based knowledge graph containing over 52 million connections that define everyday relationships. By comparing neural network-trained models using this dataset to those trained with a symbolic counterpart, we've demonstrated the effectiveness of combining neural networks with symbolic patterns in understanding everyday relationships. By assessing models through both symbolic and neural connections, we've identified a substantial advantage in using both approaches to fully grasp everyday relationships. We've also discovered that by employing a neural network that predicts symbolic patterns, we can significantly enhance our understanding of these relationships. By promoting dual-research methods that utilize both symbolic and neural techniques, we can accelerate the development of AI's common sense knowledge. The updated COMET-ATOMIC 2020 dataset, along with related resources, can be accessed at https://comet-atomic.org/comet-atomic-2020.html. The source code for ATOMIC 2020 can be found at https://github.com/comyetl/comet-atomic. The benchmark results can be accessed at https://comet-atomic.org/comet-atomic-2020.html#results. In an outdiffusion process with an isolated source, the initial exit time of the source region plays a pivotal role. This study investigates the distribution of the initial exit duration and its relationship with the source region's shape for a confined Brownian motion in a two-dimensional, convex domain. The exit time is demonstrated to be a Markovian process with a specific renewal property, and corresponding exit probabilities are computed analyticly for any domain bounded by analytic curves. Moreover, the study shows that the distribution of the initial exit duration is characterized by a heavy-tailed function with a exponent determined by a universal Kullback-Leibler divergence of the uniform probability in the domain and its renewal polynomial. This finding is further generalized for the case of file diffusion, where multiple sources are involved. Estimates for the exponent powers, including Kullback-Leibler divergence, Renyi entropy, and Tsallis entropy, are provided. These estimates depend on the shapes of the source regions and their positions relative to the domain boundary. Furthermore, the study illustrates how these estimates change for specific domain configurations. They depend on either the domain's perimeter or the smallest distance between the source region and the domain boundary. These findings are verified through numerical simulations. They have significant implications for the performance evaluation of caching systems. The findings suggest that multiple caching strategies should be adapted based on the specific domain configuration to achieve optimal performance. Based on the known state of the QCD matter in larger systems at the same renormalization scale, a key formula for determining the state of the QCD matter in small systems at lower renormalization scales is developed. Using known states in larger systems and a set of known parameters in small systems, numerical calculations of the state of the QCD matter in proton-proton and proton-nucleon collisions over a range of energies and rapidity ranges are performed. The results reveal that the states of the QCD matter in such collisions are dominated by a particular phase of the QCD matter known as 'quark-gluon plasma' across a wide energy range, rapidity range, and also in electron-proton and proton-argon collisions. Astronomers observing the Lyman ultraviolet wavelength range have long been hindered by the Lyman-alpha line, which overwhelmingly dominates other spectral signals and necessitates careful filtering. Although effective filters to block Lyman-alpha are scarce, especially for ground-based telescopes, a new approach using a Lyman-alpha screen prototype has shown promising results. By leveraging the screen's absorption of Lyman-alpha light, it is possible to significantly reduce the line's intensity, enabling accurate photometric measurements. Our prototype, which employs a rotating screen to modulate the light, has facilitated unobstructed views on both the Telescopes Pierre Auger and the Grand Rapid Impactite Telescopes. Furthermore, it has been successfully tested on the telescopes 20 times in the last two years and a new order has been placed with the manufacturer to enhance the filter's U-band response. Future applications of this technology could also involve space-based Lyman-alpha filters to allow for multi-wavelength photometry. Our prototype has also demonstrated the potential for ground-based photometric surveys with the Grand Rapid Impactite Telescopes once an improved version of the screen is implemented, making it feasible to conduct a Hubble constant campaign in the Lyman ultraviolet spectrum. Additionally, the prototype may be adapted for ground-based spectroscopy at various observatories. It is possible that a similar approach could be applied to the James Webb Space Telescope's spectrograph to eliminate a major photometric limitation of the instrument. By leveraging the screen's absorption of Lyman-alpha light through a broadened path length, it is possible to eliminate the Lyman-alpha forest, which is a critical factor in the instrument's ability to study the formation of galaxies in the cosmos. Our prototype has also sparked proposals for similar technologies to be developed for other space-based instruments. For instance, a similar approach could be applied to the PLATO spacecraft, which is in the final stages of its development, to facilitate a complementary photometric search for exoplanets. Lastly, the prototype has also been used to determine the movement through space of Lyman-alpha emitting clouds that are in the process of being carried by the wind of the cosmos. By analyzing the data from these clouds, scientists are being able to study the physics of the wind of the cosmos with high precision. Our prototype has also facilitated a new research direction in which the movement through space of material can be studied by analyzing the shift in the wavelength of light emitted or absorbed by astronomical objects. In recent years, the world has witnessed an explosion in wireless connectivity needs. to address this challenge, the concept of graph symmetry has been introduced as a solution. This approach allows for the creation of a virtual network topology by combining multiple spatially dispersed wireless devices into a device that provides a graph-based network structure for all connected stations. This topology offers an ideal solution for applications such as distributed storage, often requiring a specific graph structure. However, connecting stations under a general graph symmetry framework is complex due to the need to find an optimal node mapping that minimizes the impact on existing wireless connections. this problem is particularly difficult because of its non-linear and nonconvex nature. in this research, we introduce a new framework, called the minimum spanning forest (MSF) graph symmetry), that focuses on creating a tree-like network structure while maintaining existing wireless connections. the proposed approach breaks down the problem into an optimization subproblem for each station, allowing them to independently find an optimal solution with minimal global coordination. the MSF framework offers an ideal platform for applications such as distributed storage by providing a graph structure that can be tailored to specific use cases. The study not only derives the optimal solution for the MSF framework but also incorporates a bounded suboptimal solution for the general graph symmetry problem within the proposed framework. The practical effectiveness of the proposed approach is demonstrated through analysis and numerical evaluation, which shows that it performs close to optimal solutions while maintaining efficient network connectivity. The results reveal that the proposed solution significantly reduces the latency by an average of 30% and surpasses existing schemes by a margin of 85%. The performance gap between the proposed and optimal solutions averages at 6% with standard deviation of 3%. The choice of large or small solution largely depends on the application requirements, the trade-off between the performance and latency for the proposed MSF framework. The proposed solution sits at the middle ground between the two established approaches by providing generalization, specialization and scalability capabilities for the graph symmetry problem. The study not only offers novel distributed algorithms for the proposed MSF framework but also provides a framework to study the interplay between the graph structure, the node placement problem, and the existing wireless traffic for the general graph symmetry problem. The study has been made available to the public as a competing interests page to allow for the continued advancement of the field. The study has also been shared with the testpool of the IEEE to support the creation of a new standard. The study has been nominated for the best paper award at the IEEE LCN conference in 2021.

We are examining the numerical behavior of a particle moving in a washboard potential. When the quasiperiodic driving force has a fast frequency, the particle exhibits an intriguing behavior where it can move without spreading, under specific conditions. We are exploring this phenomenon in two distinct systems - an oscillating washboard and an oscillating washboard with a ball - to understand their dynamics in the limit of fast driving frequency. We are then leveraging these models to develop insights into the behavior of an experimentally studied system. We are focusing on the parameter space where the particle moves without spreading and investigating how it is affected by changes in force strength, $k$, and phase, $\theta_0$. We are observing that for certain types of forces, the particle moves in a limit cycle with a specific period and the particle's spread scales with the square of the applied force for a wide range of washboard heights. We are exploring the possibility of creating a theoretical model that describes this behavior thoroughly. We are achieving this goal by establishing conditions for stationary states in the system's phase space and leveraging ideas from rotator systems to develop a simplified model. We are then validating the simplicity and accuracy of this model through numerical simulations and analyzing its practical applications. We are demonstrating that for a specific type of washboard potential, the particle's spread exhibits a linear relationship with the applied force for small values and a robust robustness against variations in phase. We are also showing that this model can be utilized to control the particle's spread by adjusting its phase in specific ways. For instance, we are demonstrating that by advancing the phase by a fraction of the driving frequency, the particle's spread decreases exponentially and this model can be leveraged to achieve this goal with high accuracy and for a wide range of types of forces. We are acknowledging that this model needs to be validated through direct comparison with high-precision numerical simulations for other types of forces as well. We are also acknowledging that this model's applicability should be evaluated based on the specific experiment under consideration through direct comparison with data. We are then suggesting potential experiment and strategies to test this model and its predictions. We are also acknowledging that this model's general validity in other systems where the particle moves without spreading in the numerical simulations needs to be evaluated through direct comparison with high-precision numerical simulations and theoretical models. We are achieving this goal by establishing a theoretical model for the particle's spread that captures its behavior across multiple phases by leveraging the concept of the system's phase space. We are then validating the accuracy and simplicity of this model

This is characterized by sporadic, resource-hungry tasks that are hard to manage with traditional cloud computing methods. This issue becomes even more critical due to the varying nature of simulation resource demands. To tackle this problem, we developed a virtual cloud platform to provide cloud-based simulators as a service. This platform ensures fair resource allocation to users via a virtual interface, simulates the resource consumption of virtual machines with simulators, and allocates real virtual machines to balance the load while maintaining a high throughput. Moreover, we observed that Prepartition's efficiency could be further improved with the introduction of a more sophisticated partitioning function. Additionally, this paper provides a detailed description of the partitioning algorithm, which was missing in the original research. Finally, the experimental results have been revised to show that Prepartition's efficiency could be improved by applying partitioning. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our method through present two real-world applications: one involving a water treatment system and the other a chemical plant. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the feasibility of LSTs and the impact of attacker's characteristics and reveal that our approach is resilient to the very attacks it aims to detect. In a competitive context, individuals typically strive to achieve or find the optimal outcome. However, when contests are nonlocal in nature and involve hidden or unobservable states, the process of identifying the winner becomes more complex. Typically, one relies on the release of signals or cues that indicate relative strengths or qualities. The conditions under which a competitive outcome can be accurately determined are known as the "resolution" of the contest, and research has established that for certain types of signals or noise patterns, resolution is possible, though not necessarily fair or just. Building on previous studies, our research has found that even when states are as complex as maximally correlated with each other, and accompanied by significant noise, resolution remains possible under specific types of nonlocal contest designs. Moreover, our results indicate that for certain types of signals or noise patterns, resolution can be achieved both with and without the use of equilibrium strategies. The implications of our findings are significant, suggesting that under certain conditions, nonlocal contests can be designed to be more efficient and adaptable. The current research has focused on a broad class of nonlocal contests, and our methods are anticipating applications to a wider range of competitive contexts. The key technical aspects of our study involve leveraging tools from nonlocal quantum state tomography and the use of variational problems to determine the most effective states that maximize competitive outcomes. Our study aligns with a broader research tradition seeking to apply quantum-related concepts to analyze economic and political competition. The current paper represents an advancement in this line of research, and its findings could potentially shed light on real-world applications by providing a deeper understanding of the characteristics of nonlocal contests. The key technical aspects of our study are significant, and our study has the potential to connect quantum physics to the study of economic and political dynamics. The research has been published in a leading journal, The Bulletin of Mathematical Biology.

Our study reveals that thermal photons emitted during ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions exhibit an asymmetrical distribution in momentum space, primarily due to interactions with turbulent quark-gluon plasma (QGP) in an over-rotating environment. The magnitude of this asymmetrical distribution is directly correlated with the ratio of photon scattering on plasma particles and photon dissociation, driven by turbulent plasma's viscous forces. The rate of photon dissociation is, in turn, influenced by the QGP's viscosity. The resulting relationship between the asymmetrical distribution and QGP viscosity serves as the basis for an innovative method, dubbed "photon viscometry." This approach was applied to the largest collisions of LHC experiments (Pb-Pb at 2.76 TeV) and (Pb-Pb at 5.02 TeV), yielding a viscosity-to-entropy ratio of $\frac{\eta}{S}=1.0(0.5)$, independent of the QGP temperature but expressing a distinct relationship with the momentum spectrum's gradient. The study further discusses the complex interplay between turbulent plasma's viscous phenomena, such as plasma waves, jet Tomography, and thermal phenomena like photon dissociation and multiple particle correlations. The obtained ratio of $\frac{\eta}{S}$ aligns with the results from other approaches to study the QGP, while its value significantly exceeds its critical value by at least three orders of magnitude. The obtained ratio of $\frac{\eta}{S}$ also expresses a distinct relationship with the momentum spectrum's gradient, dubbed "parabolic rise." Furthermore, our study provides evidence that early stages of over-rotation develop in turbulent plasma, characterized by a transition from turbulent plasma with parabolic rise to turbulent plasma with the Mottola-Wipf spectrum, thus advancing the understanding of turbulent plasma's transition from incoherent to coherent turbulent states. The study of the ratio of $\frac{\eta}{S}$ also reveals that it can serve as a universal scale for the quantum chromo-color transition temperature of QGP, thereby significantly advancing the understanding of QGP properties. The study of the ratio of $\frac{\eta}{S}$ in peripheral Pb-Pb collisions (high multiplicity events) provides conclusive evidence of QGP existence. The study of the ratio of $\frac{\eta}{S}$ in Pb-Pb collisions (high multiplicity events) significantly advances the understanding of QGP properties, while its measurement in proton-proton collisions rules out the possibility of surviving high-momentum turbulent plasma even at lowest collision multiplicities

Intervention science, a rapidly growing field focused on changing observed relationships, is crucial in various real-world applications, as it allows researchers to identify specific intervention effects under strict statistical controls. Our study tackles the challenge of positively identifying intervention impact in the presence of strong negative correlations, a common issue in child development experiments. To address this, we developed a framework with framed false discovery rate (FDR) control, applied it to the simplest cases of single and multi-arm experiments, and proposed a computational tool called PathFinder to optimize paths for analyzing such experiments. Our method can handle various intervention models and assumes no distribution other than exchangeable data. Our computational simulations demonstrate our approach's efficiency in path optimization, and an actual application of our techniques is shown through an analysis of the NICHD Study of Early Child Care research findings, where we successfully identified intervention effects using different comparison groups in the context of strong negative correlations. Our results highlight the limitations of the current thresholding strategies for dealing with highly correlated data, and we show that our approach provides more accurate and comprehensive intervention impact identification compared to existing solutions. Our work also offers an alternative to deal with dependent data, and it sheds light on future research directions to identify intervention impact in the presence of strong negative correlations. In question answering, question reformulation is a critical step that contributes to several information retrieval tasks. Nonetheless, manually creating a set of reformulated questions can be a time-consuming process. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel task known as the Inquiry Reformulation Task, which aims to transform a given question into a set of more precise and compact reformulated questions that capture key concepts. To tackle this new task, we develop QUICKAR - Query Understanding and Information Conditioning for Automatic Reformulation - a model that takes a question as input and generates a set of refined and compressed queries that better represent core concepts, with the assistance of crowdsourced data. By treating the task as a combinatorial optimization problem, we establish a training objective and train the model using the crowd-sourced data. Evaluations on two datasets reveal that the model successfully captures concept positioning, thus facilitating downstream applications such as explaining model decisions with improved accuracy and explaining the positioning of ads on web pages by enhancing the correlation between ad relevance and user search queries by 50%. Furthermore, we observe a significant 43% increase in the accuracy of compressing questions while retaining their semantic preservation, thus showcasing the practical utility of this research. The proposed model and associated datasets are now publicly available at https://github.com/ericliufong/QUICKAR. By leveraging the trained model, we are able to provide compressions and explanations for questions, thus highlighting key concepts within questions. To the best of our knowledge, we initiate a novel research direction centered on inquiry reformulation that aids in understanding the core ideas within questions. To facilitate further advancements, we provide publicly accessible code at https://github.com/ericliufong/QUICKAR to enable others to adapt and enhance the model. Entrainment refers to the adaptive adjustment in interaction between individuals, which can be categorized into categories such as convergence and divergence. This paper focuses on developing a framework to measure convergent entrainment in dialogue by modeling the tendency of conversational partners to mimic each other's speaking style. We are unable to find existing datasets that have explicit entrainment labels, thus we are compelled to create a model that operates in an unsupervised manner. This paper achieves this through training a neural network to predict the speaking turn order in dialogue without any guidance. Notably, our findings reveal that the entrainment tendency can be inferred from the model's performance using permutation tests. This un supervised approach is then tested on eight dialogues and demonstrates a significant positive correlation with human-assessed convergence values. Furthermore, the developed entrainment measure is capable of accurately predicting the convergence of human-human conversations across domains using minimal textual features. We also compare its performance with other baselines that are also trained in an unsupervised manner. While the proposed entrainment measure is not as effective as supervised models, it is able to capture convergence in dialogue without requiring labeled data, making it a viable option for applications such as evaluating dialogue systems without the need for additional annotations. This work is also compatible with transformer architecture, thus it can be applied to other unsupervised tasks within the field of natural language processing. We are releasing the code and data used in this study, which can be accessed via https://github.com/ExplainableAI-Lee/Entrainment-measure. Our study is based on the analysis of the experiments conducted by Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) and transformer models to understand how each layer contributes to entrainment at the turn-level. This analysis highlights that the transformer model's use of multi-head self-attention facilitates the detection of entrainment by adapting to conversational data at different scales. This study provides the foundation for future research to uncover the underlying reasons for entrainment detection at the turn-level, which could potentially lead to the identification of the hidden layers responsible for entrainment through attribute-based entrainment measurement. To tackle this issue, we present a new method, Self-supervised SSCAP, that is capable of performing unsupervised temporal action segmentation. SSCAP focuses on modeling the relationships between action durations in an unsupervised environment and uses a feature enhancement technique to improve performance. Additionally, SSCAP incorporates a cross-model to combine individual predictions from distinct models, thus enhancing overall accuracy. We validate the effectiveness of SSCAP through experiments on standard datasets, achieving superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Notably, we observe a significant performance boost averaging 2.5% to 4.5% on HMDB51-24 and UCF101-24, respectively.
