We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme leverages non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs to verify four public transaction parameters: a ring signature, a key image, a multiple signature, and a coin commitment.
A new efficient method for generating these multiple signatures, called Multiple Signature from Rings, is presented, yielding significant improvements in verification and generation times.
High-speed testing of Delegated RingCT transactions has been conducted on the Nano, a special-purpose blockchain, utilizing 32-deep transaction rings and multiple signatures that require minimal computational power.
As Delegated RingCT is designed for expert users, performance has been our primary focus throughout the development process. 

Delegated RingCT is explained in the following sections:
- Section 2 describes Delegated Proof of Stake and Delegated Confirmed Proofs of Work.
- Section 3 describes Delegated Ring Signing and Delegated Key Images.
- Section 4 presents Delegated Ring Signing with Confirmed Key Images.
- Section 5 presents multiple signatures from rings and public keys from rings.
- Section 6 discusses Delegated RingCT.
- Section 7 presents fast processing of Delegated RingCT transactions using Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge Proofs.
- Section 8 tests Delegated RingCT transactions and multiple signatures from rings.
- Section 9 discusses Delegated RingCT and future development prospects.

The Delegated Ring Signing and Delegated Key Images sections outline a new protocol for generating public transaction parameters, reducing generation time and verifying them with the Fast Multiple Hashes from Rings method.
This study also presents a new verification process for ring signatures that requires minimal computational power and uses Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge Proofs.
In addition, this research introduces a new multiple signature verification method that outperforms existing solutions.
Analysis of our experiments shows that Delegated RingCT transaction processing times are 2-4 seconds, 7-10 times faster than other protocols.
Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Delegated RingCT and multiple signatures enable processing times of 1-4 seconds and 3-10 seconds, respectively.
These results surpass current protocols by a factor of 2-5. Our research confirms that Delegated RingCT can be a fast solution for expert users.  All the proposed protocols have been thoroughly examined and rigorously tested, utilizing a specially constructed custom blockchain.

Intense proton beams produce self-induced radio frequency (RF) beams that can be detected through RF brightness scans. This technique involves placing a detector at the beam exit, which interacts with the passing beam to produce a signal, measured by a device such as a Wilson pick-up or Faraday cup. The signal is then compared with the beam's RF electromagnetic mode, yielding data that can be analyzed to determine the beam's spectral density and other characteristics. Historically, RF brightness scans have been primarily used in low-energy accelerators, though they have also been employed in high-energy particle colliders to study colliding beams and beam halos. We will discuss the underlying physics and equipment as well as recent applications of RF brightness scans to beam diagnostics. Notably, we will demonstrate a method to determine beam bunching and transverse sizes using Wilson pick-up signals without any prior understanding of the beam's RF phase, phase space, or other characteristics. This technique has potential for use in energy fronts and Wilson deflection experiments at high-energy particle colliders, particularly in cases where the beam has been lost or went off-trend. Furthermore, we will provide a framework for determining the beam's spectral density and identify areas for further refinement. Finally, we will discuss how this beam diagnostic can be used to identify the beam's "bright spots" and contribute to initiatives such as the development of high-energy particle colliders with very low beam brightness. The proposed beam diagnostic is not only applicable to particle accelerators but also has potential for use in other systems, such as laser physics and plasma physics. Moreover, similar beam diagnostics can be employed in optical systems, such as the measurement of the brightness of a laser mode using a geodesic detector, which is then analyzed with optical FFT techniques. In some cases, the measured data even exhibits conditional symmetry, which in turn enables the solution of non-linear equations using homotopy methods. Moreover, we will provide a list of systems that can be used as frequency multipliers for various frequency ranges, which in turn can be used to generate various frequency ranges, such as the millimeter, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, and Gamma ray bands. Frequency ranges not listed here can be generated with quantum optical frequency multipliers, which use the non-classical properties of light to produce frequencies of at least 100 THz, or 318 EHz. To establish accurate models, a combination of theoretical and empirical approaches is required. Theoretical foundations must be broad enough to allow for different data sources and types, while empirical considerations are dependent on specific datasets. When working across various fields, established theories are typically abundant, yet it's often unclear which ones are applicable and whether they're sufficient to generate valid models. On the other hand, empirical approaches are always feasible but come with their own set of challenges, primarily, how to derive generalizations from the data and whether the results are applicable beyond the specific resources used for training. This article delves into the resolution of theoretical and empirical conflicts through the concept of collaborative learning, which involves learning multiple models simultaneously. By doing so, we expand the potential for learning from various inputs and outputs, effectively broadening the scope of what can be modeled. We apply this idea to the resolution of conflicts in both parameter and boundary value problems. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practicality in the context of cross-domain, cross-task learning. Lastly, we highlight its potential for cross-dataset conditioning which enables models to be trained on specific datasets but tested on others, promoting generalization and the evaluation of model performance independently of the training dataset. All of these concepts are closely related to data-driven modeling which we seek to establish as an essential component of collaborative learning. Collaborative learning and data-driven modeling offer a wealth of new possibilities that are far beyond what can be achieved individually and have far-reaching implications for both the theoretical and empirical communities. Also included in the supplemental material is a detailed argument on why it's always advantageous to engage in both theoretical and empirical modeling and why it's a fundamental aspect of the proposed concept of collaborative learning and data-driven modeling. This paper is a follow-up to the 2020 IEEE TMC conference paper titled "Maximum margin learning in medical multimodal and cross-task problems". Its unique multi-objective optimization process ensures that the network's performance on both training and inference is optimized. AskewSGD anneals weights within each layer, applying a gradient-based optimization approach, while constraining weight ranges to achieve efficient quantization. AskewSGD outperforms existing methods by enabling dynamic range allocation and efficient exploration of the quantization space. On CIFAR-10, our approach successfully achieves 1-bit quantization with 78.8% accuracy, comparable to 32-bit performance, while also propagating gradients in both the quantized and itsy bits to accelerate training. Recently, there has been significant interest in implementing automated control systems for robotic applications. As a result, researchers and practitioners are becoming more aware of the advantages of model-driven approaches for controlling soft robots. While there are numerous model-driven techniques available, an overwhelming majority of these methods rely on simplified mathematical models rather than detailed analyses. In this paper, we focus on the state of the art in model-driven control for soft robots. Starting with an examination of the available models, we then evaluate various control strategies that have been developed using these models. Furthermore, we investigate the methods used to identify and validate models, before discussing the impact of simplifying modeling assumptions on the accuracy of control performance predictions. Finally, we highlight areas in which existing model-driven control methods fall short and propose potential avenues for improvement. As a consequence of this study, we hope that researchers and practitioners will have a clearer understanding of the strengths and limitations of model-driven control for soft robots. Additionally, this paper aims to provide an extensive reference list of various models, control strategies, and simulation methods that have been used in this field. Specifically, our review includes over 120 key references, aiming to provide an as comprehensive and impartial review as possible. Ultimately, we look forward to sparking further discussions and developments within the research community. The companion paper is available at [1]. Moreover, related videos can be accessed at [2]. To accurately analyze signal patterns with varying frequencies, advanced signal processing techniques like modulated complex conjugate samplers and their hierarchically applied variants are utilized. A particular class of variants, referred to as hierarchically sampled modulated complex conjugate samplers, has seen limited research despite its potential. In this research, we delve into the detection of widely spread frequency patterns using modulated complex conjugate samplers, focusing on the energy distribution characteristics of their hierarchically applied variant. In graph distance labeling, each vertex is assigned a tuple of numbers representing minimum distances to its neighbors. Graph distance labeling problem has received significant attention, yet it remains unresolved whether this problem can be done in a concise manner for all planar graphs. On specifically focused 3- and 4-vertex connected planar graphs, researchers have established the feasibility of concise labeling. Introducing a new concept called fault-free distance labeling, we prove that on 3-vertex connected planar graphs, a single fault can be tolerated, and 5 extra vertices can be accommodated while still providing labeling. A new labeling approach, along with an efficient algorithm, is presented and shows significant improvement over existing results. Moreover, our study also reveals that the uncertainty of concise labeling in a graph with 7 vertices persists across random planar graphs. Consequently, we propose a universal set of vertices applicable to general planar graphs and provide detailed verification. Furthermore, our study introduces a set of concise labeling approaches, achieves partial resolution, and proposes two efficient algorithms to solve it. We examine a specific class of elliptic equations formulated in divergence form within a limited area and contain a current that is an element of a finite measure space. Under the condition that certain boundaries meet a specified'smallness criterion', we successfully establish the existence and uniqueness of a current-based solution within the space of square-integrable functions, while also establishing optimal'smallness criteria' for the boundaries. This outcome extends and supplements existing research related to the study of a current-based linear elliptic equation in divergence structure and enhances our understanding of a non-linear case from a previous study. Furthermore, we also explore the semilinear elliptic equations and establish the existence of a current-based solution through the use of critical pairs, while also obtaining'smallness criteria' for the boundaries. Interestingly, our research reveals that in some instances, the'smallness criteria' for the boundaries are directly related to the $L^2$ norm of the current. This outcome has the added benefit of allowing us to extend and supplement existing methods for the study of a current-based semilinear elliptic equation in non-divergence structure, while also obtaining a current-based solution in a space of Borel measurable functions. The research presented here marks an expansion and improvement of the methods found in a current-based semilinear elliptic equation non-linear study. In the field of machine learning, recent discoveries have shown that certain data distributions can be ineffective for detecting out-of-distribution examples, particularly when the training set is not representative of the broader population. To tackle this issue, which has historically been overlooked, this research introduces innovative methods grounded in statistical learning theory. The proposed benchmarks make it possible to gauge a dataset's capacity for out-of-sample detection and to identify datasets that are inherently unsuitable for this purpose. Additionally, the study provides an evaluation of the limitations of prevalent institutional review board guidelines in ensuring detectable out-of-sample examples. Ultimately, the research offers actionable recommendations for IRB approvals, highlights the importance of data curation, and suggests the use of domain knowledge for improving out-of-sample detection. The study primarily focuses on the realm of image classification, but its key insights are adaptable to a wide range of machine learning domains and tasks. The research is based on Gaussian Processes and is implemented using the GPval module, which is now part of the PyTorch Lightning ecosystem. The study's findings emphasize that successful machine learning is not always data-transferable and that domain knowledge is crucial for achieving reliable out-of-sample detection. The research's key contributions include a theoretical and experimental demonstration of the challenges in detecting out-of-sample examples and the development of new data distribution metrics, as well as a comprehensive understanding of the limitations of existing institutional review board assessments. The study's conclusions are backed by a combination of theoretical analysis, state-of-the-art machine learning experiments, and a thorough examination of real-world image datasets, which provide practical insights for researchers and practitioners. The PyTorch Lightning benchmark dataset 'lfit' contains 846 datasets, which serve as a benchmark for out-of-sample detection. The study's code is available at https://github.com/TerryYiliZhong/lfit. In this context, we explore certain classes of quantum phases transitioning from trivial to non-trivial and eventually to symmetry-protected topological phases. A specific type of renormalization group called hyper-invariant MERA is utilized to characterize these transitions, focusing on three distinct examples: a Kitaev chain with Majorana zero modes, a pX spin-j model with a global abelian symmetry, and a pX chain with a global abelian symmetry. The phase diagrams are mapped through the application of new approximations that account for power-law behavior, leveraging a technique called hyper-invariant pyramidal merging. The accuracy of these approximations is estimated by analyzing the analytical error, which we find creeps into the entanglement entropy after a certain scale known as the truncation error. By comparing the phase diagrams obtained using the entanglement entropy to those obtained using other metrics such as the mutual information between adjacent sites, we find the analytical error to be a reliable indicator of phase transitions. The mutual information is found to be a more sensitive diagnostic but is affected by the analytical error at smaller system sizes. The use of hyper-invariant MERA enables efficient quantum computing through the simulation of quantum systems possessing certain symmetries. By merging pyramids, each with a different symmetry, we can compute the entanglement entropy cost of the phase transition between two distinct symmetry phases for a quantum system possessing a different symmetry. This computation can be efficiently performed using the scale-invariant properties of the mermaid diagrams for each pyramid. The efficiency of this approach depends on the symmetry of the quantum system: when the symmetry is abelian, we can compute the entanglement entropy cost using a universal set of mermaid diagrams, whereas when the symmetry is non-abelian, we must compute the mermaid diagrams for each unique symmetry. The phase diagrams obtained using the entanglement entropy can be used to suggest several quantum computing schemes such as trivial-symmetry protected codes, symmetry protected codes, and pseudo-critical learning. As the scale of conversational datasets grows, so does the challenge of writing dialogue that accurately reflects natural language syntax and meaning. Current approaches either rely on large, pre-trained language models or prescribe a rigid dialogue composition framework. To resolve this, we propose the LEATHER framework, a flexible and scalable system that effectively handles dialogue writing for various languages and structures. By leveraging a range of surface-level syntax guides, LEATHER enables the incorporation of manual writing expertise. Additionally, we demonstrate that incorporating guides with common syntax patterns can lead to significant improvements in the naturalness of written dialogue, especially when aided by weak supervision from annotated examples. With this versatility, LEATHER can produce high-quality dialogue even at smaller dataset scales, surpassing the dialogue quality produced by larger pre-trained language models. Importantly, we found that incorporating guides with correct syntax led to decreased hallucinations in generated dialogue, indicating the importance of guide linguistic accuracy. Notably, guides optimized for linguistic correctness tend to produce more coherent and less repetitive dialogue. A key aspect of guide development is its interpretability, allowing writers to gauge dialogue quality at various stages. By establishing a clear writing process, LEATHER facilitates the adoption of interpretative dialogue writing guidelines in real-world applications, including customer service and the creation of training manuals. We publicly disseminate all of our source code and pre-trainined guides through the following repository: https://github.com/asharkey/LEATHER. Furthermore, we present enhanced versions of the LEATHER framework tailored to specific requirements, including: LEATHER-Human, a version optimized for human-like conversation; LEATHER-Hotel, a version focused on customer service; and LEATHER-Manual, a version designed to generate training manuals. In the case of these tailored versions, we do not require pre-existing conversation datasets. Instead, we propose that writers use the structured LEATHER framework to create guides that reflect their unique requirements and use cases. By adopting this writing process, we can yield high-quality dialogue even in unannotated text domains. Determining a function's evolution over time by reversing its progression can offer valuable insights into its dynamics. However, when working with noisy data from multiple timepoints, conventional inversion methods often struggle to produce reliable results. In contrast, a new approach based on optimizing motion trajectories shows better resilience to noise. By representing any function as a trajectory with fixed starting and ending points, and using it in conjunction with noisy data from different timepoints, the framework enables the construction of a constrained optimization problem. Its success in reconstructing complex functions under noisy conditions makes it an attractive option for analyzing time-resolved data. Furthermore, this method can be adapted to prioritize timepoint-specific details in the reconstruction. As an example of its capabilities, the approach was applied to analyze the rotation of a small molecule in detail. As the molecule undergoes movements, its structure dynamically changes, and the technique is well-suited to studying the evolution of such systems. Lastly, the approach's versatility is demonstrated through the exploration of Brownian motion in a specific context. In summary, the idea of representing function evolution as an optimized trajectory offers a reliable solution for reconstructing and understanding dynamic systems using time-resolved data. It provides valuable insights into its applications, making it a valuable tool for analytical purposes. We establish a nearly G_2 manifold deformation functor for G_2-instantons, and we establish that this functor is a derived Lie algebra object. By treating the algebraic K-theory of the base as a deformed analogue of G_2-instanton bundles, we show that this functor is isomorphic to the K-theory bundle. Additionally, we obtain a universal deformation relation for G_2-instantons, and we demonstrate that this relation is consistent with the obstruction map in the obstruction bundle for deforming G_2-instantons. Furthermore, we show that deforming G_2-instantons to the base of a sphere is possible if and only if the instanton has a specific non-zero holonomy for SU(7), and we discuss how deforming G_2-instantons connects to the elliptic genera of manifolds with seven-manifolds as the base. Finally, we obtain a specific deformation relation for SU(7)-instantons when the base is a sphere and show that this relation is consistent with the obstruction map in the obstruction bundle for deforming SU(7)-instantons. Moreover, we show the equivalence between the specific deformation relation and the universal deformation relation for G_2-instantons, and thus we prove that deforming G_2-instantons to the base of a sphere is possible if and only if the instanton has a specific non-zero holonomy for SU(7). Many governments have resorting to the use of mobile devices to track the spread of the virus through contact tracing technology, a move aimed at reducing the growth rate of the epidemic. As the primary tool for this purpose, government health authorities are leveraging smartphone apps that tap into the vast amounts of data generated by these devices to create detailed maps of individuals' daily movements outside their homes. This widespread use of contact tracing technology by governments has raised significant privacy concerns, giving rise to debates over the balance between public health safety and individual confidentiality. This article delves into the world of contact tracing technology by providing an in-depth analysis of the underlying principles, emphasizing the need to establish a balance between national security and individual privacy. Furthermore, the inherent limitations of the data used in contact tracing also raise questions of integrity, prompting a discussion on the potential risks and consequences of exposing individuals whose anonymity is meant to be maintained. The study proposes a framework to gauge the likelihood of detecting an individual's daily location based on the existing information, using the Coronav'Irus-SUS (COVID-19) as a case study. The study also presents a variety of applications that can be built using the Coronav'Irus-SUS, showcasing its versatility and potential in the field of research. Building upon Ramanujan's iconic theorem for infinite series involving odd zeta values, we establish a novel connection between Hurwitz zeta functions and these odd zeta values. Specifically, we demonstrate that an infinite series with an odd zeta value as its argument can be expressed as the difference between two Hurwitz zeta functions, each with an argument that incorporates the fixed odd integer. In addition, we leverage the generalised functional equation for L-functions to obtain a comparable expression for the L-zeta function of a Dirichlet character. This new expression reveals a connection between L-zeta functions and products of odd zeta values, which also aligns with a recent result by Chen, Wang, and Zha. Furthermore, we use our primary expression to develop two recurring identities that appear in the dedicated field of number theory. We also utilize the generalised functional equation to obtain an alternative proof of a particular identity, which is notable as it easily computable and has implications within irrational number theory. These are not the only applications of our established expression; in fact, in the concluding section, we present multiple additional instances of its utility. That being said, it is essential to note that some of these additional uses are likely instances of prior knowledge that have been overlooked in our writing. In the view of the editor, this may warrant the inclusion of an additional (conjectural) corollary in the conclusion. In any case, in the opinion of the editor, this is an exceptional and enlightening (conjectural) conclusion. Finally, to bring about a sense of shape and structure to our established results, we have presented them in three appendices, formatted as separate theorems. In the first of these, we have presented our established expression for the L-zeta function of a Dirichlet character in a more generalised form; in the second, we have obtained a particular identity in a more generalised manner as well. In the third, we have obtained a recurring identity in a generalised fashion as well, in this instance at the Eisenstein series level. We define a version of equivariant elliptic cohomology for groups with a logical equivariance action, and show it has the properties of a reversible theory. We then apply this to the study of complex projective spaces for a finite group acting on the underlying space, where we derive that logical equivariant elliptic cohomology of $P(\mathcal{V})$ is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}/2\cdot H^1(G, \mathbb{Z}) \oplus H^2(\mathcal{V}, \mathbb{Z})$. Furthermore, when the finite group in question acts freely on the underlying space, we obtain the equation $H^2(G, \mathbb{Z}) \oplus H^0(G, \mathbb{Z}) \cong H^2(P(\mathcal{V}), \mathbb{Z})$. Subsequently, when the action is restricted to one-dimensional representations of an abelian group, we obtain the equation $H^2(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) \cong H^2(P(\mathcal{V}), \mathbb{Z})$. We also prove the equation $\sum_{k=1}^n H^2(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) \leq H^2(P(n\mathcal{V}), \mathbb{Z})$. The equation $\sum_{k=1}^n H^2(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) = H^2(P(n\mathcal{V}))$ however does not generally hold, however we do derive the equation $\sum_{k=1}^n H^2(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) = H^2(P(n\mathcal{V}))$ when $n = 2$. Moreover, when $G = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ we obtain the equation $H^2(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) = H^2(P(2\mathcal{V})),  H^1(\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{Z}) = H^2(P(2\mathcal{V}))$.

We develop topological insulators and superconductors using a novel method based on a K-theoretic machine that automatically identifies key characteristics of insulator and superconductor classes by applying a universal formula. By taking a categorical perspective, we resolve issues with previously proposed theories and show that topological insulator and superconductor classes are controlled by a limited set of elementary exceptional objects. A separate algorithmic approach is used to classify topological insulator and superconductor classes in one and higher dimensions. By wrapping these classes in a K-theory framework, we demonstrate that their characteristics form a complete and unified system. Notably, this work lays the groundwork for using machine learning in algebraic topology, with potential applications in physics and beyond. We also apply our method to the study of higher-dimensional surface fermion basis spaces, revealing a deeper structure that can be represented through K-theory. We hope this research will inspire further exploration of algebraic topology and its integration with machine learning, opening doors to innovative applications in physics and mathematics. Our research delves into how regular and avid users of the encrypted messaging app Signal understand and use PINs. While formal invitations to join groups in Signal require a PIN provided by the group administrator, users can choose any value for their personal Signal PIN. Our study involves 35 frequent Signal users who participate in a think-aloud trial while performing tasks that include generating, remembering, and verifying PINs, as well as understanding and confirming membership in groups. Our results indicate that although most users understand the purpose of the PINs within groups, they are uncertain about how their personal PINs are utilized by the app. Consequently, our findings suggest that users' ability to recall their personal PINs may be hindered by a lack of clarity regarding the purpose of these PINs within Signal. In line with this, our research reveals that users are resistant to entering incorrect PINs when attempting to verify group membership, likely due to a supposition that the app intends to monitor this interaction. Our conclusions could generate new avenues for improvement in how PINs are implemented within Signal. This research develops a method of Gaussian quadrature specifically designed to accurately compute integrals involving solar radiation spectra. By leveraging the tabulated solar spectra compiled by ASTM and IUPAP, this approach facilitates the rapid determination of quantities like irradiance and heat flux at any specified location on Earth. To enhance computational efficiency, the paper explores alternative formulations for applying smoothing functions to represent spectra. Furthermore, the technique is demonstrated with examples to illustrate its precision and efficiency in calculating solar-based quantities. The associated Fortran code, along with the pre-calculated quadrature points and weights, is made publicly available for download and use. Moreover, the paper demonstrates how the fundamental solar-gaussian quadrature can be extended to calculate more complex solar-related integrals. Specifically, the technique is illustrated by considering the calculation of solar heat flux at a specific wavelength. By applying the fundamental quadrature, the paper derives a smoothed version of the spectra, and then derives the quadrature points and weights for the new smooth function. This extended approach is shown to accurately predict solar heat flux within 0.1% of reference values, which deviate from measured values by the National Renewable Energy Laboratory. Finally, the paper exemplifies the application of solar-gaussian quadrature in calculating the thermal resistance of a uncoated solar panel. By integrating the solar spectra adjusted for atmospheric effects and the reflectivity of the front surface, the technique is shown to accurately predict the thermal resistance with an error margin of less than 1%. The associated Python code is provided in the supplementary materials. By utilizing the quadrature approach, the paper demonstrates that thermal modeling can be achieved with high precision using readily available publicly available solar spectra and the calculated quadrature points and weights from the ASTM or IUPAP databases. The research outcomes and developed techniques are expected to facilitate the precise modeling and design of solar-based systems. Ultimately, the paper explores the broader implications of the quadrature approach for applications in optics and physics where accurate modeling of solar spectra is crucial. By applying the quadrature approach, the calculation of global, direct, and diffuse irradiance and heat flux are rendered with high precision. The quadrature technique is expected to be an indispensable tool in these areas of optics and physics. However, existing methods like viT2Ham and its variations face significant bottlenecks due to their computational and memory demands. To overcome these limitations, a new approach called ViViT has been developed, which effectively yields a computationally efficient and memory-friendly approximation of the curvature using the Gauss-Newton structure. Empirical results demonstrate that ViViT is not only highly efficient but also delivers superior accuracy on various tasks by leveraging the low-dimensional properties of the Gauss-Newton Hessian matrix. Notably, MemViT's capabilities extend to training large-scale models with limited memory, differentiating it from other approximations like HOGK and HesseGAN. Many languages distinguish between grammatical gender and natural gender, with gender information often attributed to nouns by language models. This study explores how this grammatical gender affects embedding spaces for nouns in languages that assign gender, such as Spanish and French. To investigate this, we used two approaches: one to determine clusters of related nouns in a 3D space that adhere to grammatical gender conventions, and another to establish connections between a word's gender and the genders of its related words in a pre-trained French and Spanish language model. Our analysis reveals that language models accurately capture the characteristics associated with grammatical gender despite occasional inaccuracies. Furthermore, we found that mono-lingual models for Spanish and French have distinct gender representations, in contrast to a multilingual model, which may learn biased representations of gender due to its broader training. Our research indicates that although NLP models by default recognize grammatical gender, this does not always translate to natural gender understanding. To demonstrate this, we used approaches to predict human genders based on a model's comprehension of grammatical gender and discovered that these predictions are generally off from actual human genders, particularly for individuals. This study highlights the complexities of modeling complex language characteristics like grammatical gender and suggests future research in this area. The code and data for our analysis are provided at https://github.com/jayelk/gender-embeddings. This research was supported in part by a CNSF grant.

This study introduces VACA, a new counterfactual causal reasoning tool based on variational graph autoencoders. By incorporating causal graphs and node representations, VACA models relationships between random variables and their hidden causal structures. It then uses learned parameters to compute intervention targets and counterfactuals efficiently. VACA has been implemented using the Morpheus toolkit, a Python library that provides pre-built functions for building, training, evaluations, and graph-based autoencoder models. We provide detailed descriptions and technical specifications for Morpheus and VACA in the associated repository. Furthermore, we present a Markov chain-based evaluation method for autoregressive models like VACA, particularly when dealing with large causal graphs. This method is demonstrated on a synthetic dataset, showcasing its effectiveness. Lastly, VACA is conceptually linked to a new family of causal query languages, with an accompanying theoretical discussion in the paper's supplements. This research highlights the benefits and limitations of using variational graph-based models for counterfactual inference. Such models can effectively handle complex causal relationships, despite encountering potential difficulties. Notably, VACA's performance may be hindered by model oversimplification, inaccurate learnings, and suboptimal computations. Nonetheless, it is well-suited for processing causal relationships and generating explanations. For instance, it can be used to perform causal diagnostics by identifying hidden issues, explain the causal basis of a target outcome using causal paths, and determine intervention efficiency based on simulated scenarios. Moreover, VACA can be used to compute more complex targets, such as intervention paths, intervention effects, and counterfactuals with fine-grained specifications. The study also showcases the capabilities of VACA in a few applications, particularly Markov branching processes. The study ultimately concludes by outlining the limitations and potential future research avenues for VACA, discussing the Capaldi causal programming language, a language that shares conceptual similarities with VACA. The study concludes by highlighting the benefits and challenges of VACA and suggesting areas for further improvement. The implementation details of VACA and its evaluation can be found in the repository. The study also introduces a new evaluation method for autoregressive models and applies it to VACA on a synthetic dataset. The conceptual ideas underlying VACA are related to a new family of causal query languages, as described in the paper's supplements. The study ultimately reflects on VACA's contributions and future research directions in the field of causal reasoning. Light field technology is highly versatile but has had limited adoption in consumer products due to the significant computational requirements for processing and communicating its data. A practical solution to this problem is provided by a model that uses a specific type of neural network to optimize the compression of light field images. The framework of the model, which incorporates a Disparity-Patch-Resolution (DPR) map to refine its predictions, has been shown to significantly outperform established standards like 4:4:4:4, 4:4:4:2, 4:4:1, 4:2:2, and 4:2:1 in terms of Objective Picture Quality Metrics (OPEP). Notably, in a specific use case involving the analysis of a butterfly's wings, the model was able to compress the light field data by as much as 87.5%, while still meeting predefined quality requirements. Moreover, the framework is compatible with a variety of specific learning techniques and can be used in conjunction with a platform that facilitates the rapid development of light field compression methods. Two different implementation categories exist: one that uses a Deliberate Neural Architecture Design (NAD) and another that leverages an Black-Box Neural Architecture Search (NAS) approach. Within the former category, multiple NADs are combined into an ensemble model, demonstrating the potential for performance improvement through careful network design. On the other hand, the NAS method generates numerous neural architectures through a series of training sessions, with the most effective model being the top-performing outcome. Ultimately, the chosen model successfully replicates the performance of a specialist model under real-world conditions before being deployed in a practical light field compression application. Evaluation was done using the publicly available "General-purpose 4x4x4 to 4x4x2 Light Field Compression Benchmark" on the "LFDC2022-b6-4x4-4x2" dataset. Key features of the approach include its ability to balance the quality and file size of the compressed light field data, as well as its robustness to changes in patch resolution. Notably, the results of the experiments showed that by employing a suitable model for the specific task at hand and carefully configuring its hyperparameters through an in-depth analysis, it's feasible to achieve top-notch performance in terms of OPEP. Specifically, when using an in-depth model with 6 iterations and the LR-DPCP method for image compression, the resulting OPEP scores were comparable to the best outcomes reported in the relevant literature

Despite these efforts, there was no consensus on the initial state of the magnetic field and the associated transport process, leading to inconsistent results and no extension to protostellar nuclei. By reconstructing the core's structure and determining its density and magnetic field strength, this study fills the gap in protostellar nucleus research. By doing so, they identified the first protostellar nucleus and simulated its further development. For the core's radius and magnetic field strength, two different values were considered. In the first scenario, the core's radius was 0.03 solar radii (one-third of the typical value) and the magnetic field strength was 0.1 milligauss (one-thousandth of the typical value), resulting in significantly elevated disk rotation. In the second scenario, the core's radius was 0.03 solar radii but the magnetic field strength was 10 milligauss (one-tenth of the typical value), resulting in a slowly rotating disk. Simulations showed that protostellar nuclei with high-rotation disks and shorter diffusion times develop larger disks, while those with slowly rotating disks and longer diffusion times develop smaller disks. In all scenarios, mass is primarily transported outward. Observations of the disk and star masses indicate that further accretion should continue for at least 0.01 solar years and that the disk mass is typically one to two orders of magnitude lower than the star mass. In the first scenario, the disk is dynamically unstable against gravitational collapse, while in the second scenario, it is stable against such a collapse. Consequently, it is hypothesized that the initial magnetic field has an impact on the disk's development and the onset of gravitational collapse, leading to the formation of a star. Furthermore, it is proposed that the disk's development and the formation of a star are determined by the ratio of the disk's rotation speed and the sound speed, which is determined by the core's radius and magnetic field strength. Current simulations of protostellar nucleus development do not capture such a transition and therefore cannot accurately predict the formation of a star. Federated learning is an emerging optimization method that has gained momentum from both the machine learning and database communities. As it allows central and client-side models to collaborate securely, it creates a hybrid training setup that has attracted various applications. To address this, we will focus on two key aspects of its implementation: developing methods for differential confidentiality that can be used during the federated learning process, and identifying the ideal data partition strategy that has not been extensively explored. By evaluating different partitioning methods, we found that segmenting data based on labels yields better outcomes than traditional techniques, while also analyzing the potential data leakage in each method. Our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the risks involved in implementing differential confidentiality on federated learning, and it is our hope that these findings will serve as a valuable resource for practitioners in the field. This interactive learning approach is facilitated by a user-friendly interface. To optimize learning performance, the algorithm takes into account both the available data and any supplementary information, such as any incorrect previous inputs provided by the user. Several key aspects of the framework warrant specific consideration. Firstly, it is essential to recognize that the user-provided information is viewed as an intrinsic aspect of the system's dynamics. Secondly, the system should be designed to allow for sufficient observation of the system's states. Finally, the system should be constructed in a manner that enables efficient propagation of the supplementary information. Experimental evaluations have consistently shown that the proposed framework consistently produces control policies that successfully interact with the system in real-time, even when the system's dynamics are unknown and only limited data is available. This framework's potential applications extend beyond educational tools to automatic control solutions in autonomous systems. For instance, it may be used to guide a robotic arm system to reach specific targets or aid in generating optimized flight paths for air traffic control systems. These research directions have the potential to extend the proposed framework's applicability to a wide range of autonomous control domains. By solving a complex simulation-based challenge, for example, we can gain a more intuitive understanding of the balance between the proposed framework's information-gathering bias and the reward it earns. This balance ultimately determines the system's interaction behavior. Experimental results obtained from the simulation can then be used to estimate the proposed framework's capabilities in real-world scenarios with minimal uncertainty. A potential application of the proposed framework has been identified in the domain of autonomous generating optimized four-dimensional flight paths for air traffic control systems. Advanced empirical models employing factor representations are now widely used across multiple fields within finance. These factor models are beginning to influence the development of analytical tools, including risk metrics and portfolio construction methods. As a result, there has been a significant surge in the collection and analysis of detailed data from various sources, including insurance and banking industries. The traditional approach to building time-invariant factor models is no longer sufficient for handling the vast amounts of data rapidly becoming available. In an attempt to address this limitation, researchers have started developing time-varying factor models. This study investigates the feasibility of utilizing a time-varying model where factor loadings evolve over time by applying the Kalman filter algorithm. By applying this framework to understand mortality forecasting, we demonstrate its ability to accurately track changes in factor loadings across different geographic areas. Furthermore, we apply the model to two distinct datasets: one analyzing deaths from COVID-19 in the United States and another examining mortality differences between men and women across various states. The results of our analysis indicate that the proposed framework yields more accurate mortality predictions compared to a static model. Consequently, this study provides a practical example of the capabilities of time-varying factor models in handling large datasets. The research's findings and methods are eventually expanded to develop a state-level mortality index, enabling policymakers to gauge the overall health condition across various states through a unified metric. The indices can then be employed by public health authorities for effective decision-making in public health policy implementation and resource allocation. The model's source code has been made publicly available for reference at https://github.com/AlbertoOquita/KF_ALM. Furthermore, the mortality indices developed in this study can be accessed at https://www.mortalityindex.org. The results of our analysis suggest that the proposed risk metrics can facilitate changes in public health policies and provide valuable insights for business decision-makers. Ultimately, to demonstrate the practical applicability of our model, we illustrate its potential to generate a significant return on investment by converting COVID-related deaths in the United States into mortality indexes and using them to inform stock purchases. Specifically, the findings reveal that the proposed indices can help investors identify undervalued companies with substantial exposure to COVID-19 deaths and purchase these companies at discounted prices. The returns generated by our model suggest that it holds considerable potential for practical application and expansion beyond its current applications in public health and finance. By applying the principles of adjacent scientific research, this study can serve as a starting point for investigating additional uses of time-varying factor models in various fields. }`

Research in Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has largely been focused on finding the most effective network designs, but it is often hindered by a phenomenon known as NasBench phase change, which causes predicted performance to diverge from actual results, hindering relative rankings and evaluations. To address this challenge, we first analyzed under what circumstances this discrepancy arises. Then, we developed and tested two new methods aimed at mitigating its impact: one reformulates rankings based on relative differences in model complexity and another uses a more accurate representation of gradient information. Our experiments on the NasBench dataset and two other benchmarks demonstrate that these techniques significantly improve the accuracy of NAS methods in relative rankings and evaluations. The source code for these methods has been made available online. Furthermore, we discovered that by accounting for the disruption phenomenon, differences in model effectiveness can be identified even without utilizing diversity metrics in NasBench dataset. This points to a potential research path where relative rankings and evaluations alone are utilized to assess NAS methods in a more straightforward manner. Finally, we found that by removing the constraint on the parameter budget from NasBench dataset, a more comprehensive understanding of a NAS method's capabilities can be gained, revealing that even though disruption occurs, a well-informed NAS method is able to explore diverse designs, even beyond a set budget, allowing for a wider range of possible network designs to be discovered. Time-series analysis, a broad field in statistical science, is increasingly employed by finance, medicine, and environmental studies to analyze discrete sets of data over time. This type of analysis is particularly useful for identifying trends, understanding system behavior, and measuring change in various domains. One significant step in time-series research involves the visual inspection of time series. There are two main tasks in this process: detecting and responding to trends. While numerous techniques exist for detecting changes, creating a responsive and flexible framework for analysis is more challenging. To address this gap, a new package called theft has been developed for R to provide a set of tools for analyzing multiple attribute-based time series. This package is designed to handle the increasing amount of temporal data efficiently and effectively. It offers a range of functions for data exploration, including time-series segmentation, attribute-based analysis, and data visualization. Additionally, a single comprehensive function has been created to manage the entire process from data preparation to results interpretation. This package's approach allows for accurate statistical analysis and is particularly well-suited for analyzing multiple attribute-based time series. It is characterized by three key principles: attribute-based segmentation, independent two-sample tests, and a robust statistical analysis and data visualization system that can accommodate various scenarios. To illustrate its effectiveness, a series of case studies have been conducted using real-world datasets. This paper will provide an overview of the theft framework and showcase its application on two datasets. One of the datasets involves analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic's impact on healthcare and hospital resources; the other involves a comparative attribute-based analysis of two companies' financial performance over time. Ultimately, a step-by-step guide on using the theft package will be demonstrated, highlighting its potential as a data exploration and analysis tool in a variety of time-series contexts. This study proposes a trusted evaluator (TE) role for Bayesian approach assessment. Evaluators, specifically translators, work with trusted sources to evaluate the dependability of other translators. We develop a framework based on Bayesian methods for TE to calculate the dependability of other translators. This involves creating a "reliability dictionary" to establish a trusted reference point for evaluation purposes. We also introduce a learning mechanism for TEs to continuously update and enhance their evaluation, utilizing evaluation discussions among them. This study further explores how TEs can promote overall translator dependability within the community. Moreover, it investigates a situation where TEs themselves may have doubts about their own dependability. Finally, as an extension of this study, we examine the potential for reinventing the trusted evaluator role. We focus on a particular aspect: assessing the believability of online news articles based on Bayesian methods. This involves developing a "credibility dictionary" and a corresponding dictionary learning algorithm, as well as establishing a trusted evaluator role to promote overall translator dependability. Furthermore, we explore a situation where Bayesian methods may face challenges. We investigate a scenario where the credibility of online news articles is threatened by malicious editors. We present an award system to incentivize credible TE editors and provide evaluation and credit demonstration. Finally, our study concludes with potential future directions for evaluation based on credit verification. Overall, our study delves into the trust and credibility of various online entities such as translators, editors, and news articles, demonstrating the effectiveness of the TE role in evaluating their dependability through Bayesian methods. We also anticipate that the reliance on basic trust as a result of social interactions may be a topic for future evaluation. The current study is accompanied by three additional experimental evaluations which can be accessed via the provided references. One of the experimental evaluations is delved into in the conclusion section. Moreover, the study is supported by multiple figures, diagrams, and tables that help to visualize its findings. From a mathematical perspective, it is well established that two fundamental principles - Minkowski and Menger - allow one to derive the total or individual surface energies from a scattered field. Importantly, the proposed eigenchannel formulas offer more than just a theoretical reinterpretation; in fact, they can be effectively utilized in practical scenarios, such as identifying the optimal eigenchannel configuration for maximum energy absorption. Consequently, the proposed formulas offer a simpler and more logical approach to interpreting and applying Minkowski and Menger principles in various scattering scenarios and applications. We introduce a novel lottery ticket purchasing strategy that incorporates both probability forecasts and player anticipation levels, formulated as a mathematical Valued Knapsack Problem. By modeling each ticket's gain as a product of its probability of winning and the player's anticipated reward, we aim to maximize the total forecasted gain. The difficulty of this problem lies in resolving the double optimization challenge of anticipating the reward and selecting the tickets, which can be overcome by employing a modified version of the LP relaxation based on the previously established "Anticipated Reward" algorithm. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through comprehensive experimental evaluations across three distinct real-world scenarios. We conducted a survey among 42 active Distinctive Lottery (DL) ticket holders to further understand the double optimization challenge in the context of real-world applications. The proposed algorithm shows promising performance in synthetic simulations as well as real-world surveys, exhibiting an average canned false positive rate reduction of 7.16% and an average gain in the forecasted gain of 3.63%. In this study, we examined the behavior of a quantum system composed of two fermions and their interactions within a confined, three-dimensional space by employing a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing approach. Our research focused on understanding fermion behavior in a one-electron-one-hole system, which is crucial for studying various phenomena, such as the response of a superconductor to an external field and the occurrence of fermion condensation in a black hole-like system. To simulate these systems, we utilized the Lagrangian path-integral framework with quantum emulated computers capable of simulating both analog and digital quantum systems. Our results include the well-known results of supersymmetry and fermonic condensation in a one-electron-one-hole system, which can be efficiently simulated using a hybrid digital-analog quantum computer. Our research demonstrates that such a simulator can accurately simulate diverse physical phenomena with modified Hamiltonians based on their original versions. Furthermore, we propose a potential application of this simulator in a quantum computer that can handle a large number of digital quantum elements. Our work also highlights the unique capabilities of a hybrid digital-analog quantum computing system in quantum simulation, which cannot be efficiently emulated by hybrid analog-analog computers but can be efficiently simulated by digital-digital quantum computers. Moreover, our results for fermionic condensation provide new perspectives on the adiabatic theory and the physical meaning of the ground state in a one-electron-one-hole system. Additionally, our results for supersymmetry illustrate a notable feature of digital-digital quantum computers that can simulate conservative systems, which is the exact symmetry preservation of digital-analog computers. Our study also demonstrates the potential of digital-digital and hybrid digital-analog quantum computing systems in studying various physical phenomena such as supersymmetry and fermonic condensation. Our results have significant implications for understanding diverse physical phenomena at different physical levels and may potentially bridge the electronic and nuclear matter limits. Moreover, our results for supersymmetry open new avenues for simulating diverse physical phenomena at different physical levels and may potentially extend to the cosmological scale. Moreover, our results for fermonic condensation provide new perspectives on the adiabatic theory and may potentially extend to the occurrence of fermonic condensation in various physical phenomena. We create a class of polynomial series that rely on a limited collection of graph invariants, where the inverse relationship ensures the simplicity of the resulting series. This discovery is facilitated by a innovative method of linking invariants to new graph invariants that are easily understandable, allowing us to generalize certain known results in the area of monomial and homogeneous invariants. The proposed approach has the advantage of being versatile and can be applied to other areas. By utilizing this generalization, we establish a connection between series of polynomials, graph homomorphisms, and the concept of partition. Notably, this connection reveals a series of linear polynomials that generalize the well-known degree invariant. Additionally, we address a theoretical issue regarding the characteristics of the terms in a polynomial series. We create a utility that calculates a particular type of invariant, specifically the partition invariant, for graphs with up to 11 vertices. This is accomplished through a simple yet efficient algorithm that relies on the process of generating combinations. The results obtained from this experiment show that the polynomials in question have a maximum exponent of 2 for graphs with up to 11 vertices. This work sends a signal to each of K receivers, where these receivers are randomly positioned within a 3D space. Fixing the total transmission power, we analyze the Gains in Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) achieved when using optimal, rather than suboptimal, power control in this multi-path environment. Since the optimal power control uses a complex signal phase at each transmitter, we compare this to an easier binary phase scheme. Despite the complexity of optimal power control, we show that it yields significant benefits - an improvement of $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ orders of magnitude. This gain arises because optimal power control allows the use of weak paths, previously unavailable for binary phase schemes. Moreover, we show that each transmitter should employ dual phases. Finally, we note that the extremal GDoF gains in this 3D environment should also hold for the 2D case. The growing IoT landscape is marked by expanding scale, shifting workload patterns, and fluctuating device interactions.  Such changes are particularly challenging for software upgrade methods, leading to increased instability and a higher likelihood of failure.  This issue is critical in the IoT domain, where network connectivity often fluctuates due to power constraints or design choices. mesh-based network topology has proven effective in addressing these concerns through mesh networking, allowing devices to stay online and facilitating the deployment of software upgrades at reduced costs.  Although software upgrade mesh protocols have been developed, there is a lack of comprehensive research on their practical application in large-scale settings.  This study therefore evaluates and implements three software upgrade protocols – ETCD, Bosco, and SkyDock – on a vast network of 381 IoT devices.  By defining reliable upgrade criteria and measuring protocol performance using tailored benchmarks, we have uncovered notable distinctions in protocol efficiency, stability, and scalability.  Our detailed analysis ultimately identifies best practices for software upgrades in vast, distributed systems.  Furthermore, we have created an open-source test platform that enables and promotes replication-driven, large-scale testing, contributing to the advancement of reliable software upgrade protocols.  This research therefore addresses a crucial need in this critical IoT domain.  By doing so, we provide actionable guidance to practitioners working on software upgrades in distributed systems, contributing meaningfully to the related literature. This study explores the concept of adversarial instances on quantum classifiers and proposes its own approach to create these malicious instances using the least significant bits of classical adversarial instances. An experiment tested the effectiveness of this method by evaluating the performance of a quantum Bernoulli-NAND classifier on the MNIST dataset and compared it to direct constructions, also assessing the impact of classical disturbances on the performance. The results show that with sufficient training, our approach enables the creation of malicious instances with near-perfect success rates, and these malicious instances are largely immune to errors caused by disturbances. An open-source project has been developed for reproducing these results. 
Keywords: Quantum Computing, Quantum Classifiers, Quantum Adversarial Attacks, Quantum Information Theory, Information Security, Machine Learning. 

\section*{Introduction}

Quantum computers have the potential to outperform traditional machines on certain tasks, and a unique type of quantum classifier called a Bell classifier offers the advantage of being resistant to certain types of interference. However, these classifiers are not foolproof and can be tricked with specific types of misleading information. An image with details blured in the COIL128 dataset was previously shown to deceive a Bell classifier with near-perfect success. These goals are leveraged within symbolic Markov model checking to ensure the validity of plans. By leveraging the established logical underpinnings, the validation process can be thoroughly proved using conventional theorem provers, resulting in an executable code that defines the planning search space. We use the PPL tool for planning and the Isabelle/HOL theorem prover to represent the applied logical framework. We successfully tested our approach on a prototype implementation and found it to be significantly faster than a traditional validation method. Notably, the integration of planning and validation proof generation yields a combined time expense comparable to or only slightly higher than that of the validation alone. Importantly, the established code can be utilized not only for validation but also for automatically generating counterexamples when objectives conflict. We discovered counterexamples for three benchmark domains using our approach and other state-of-the-art validation methods. Furthermore, the use of a sophisticated theorem prover led to the resolution of over 130 validation issues that the traditional approach could not resolve. We contend that the integration of planning and validation proof generation presents a promising direction for research in artificial intelligence. We argue that the generation of counterexamples through planning proof generation presents an exciting area for future investigation. Furthermore, the development of planning search spaces via proof generation could be explored as an additional area for research. We discuss how our approach could serve as a foundation for such work and provide reasons why such ideas should be considered unsafe to trust without rigorous formalization and verification. The Collatz Conjecture asserts that no matter where you start, repeatedly applying a pair of transformations (taking the odd number from any given even number or doubling the last number in a sequence) will ultimately lead to the number one. Although the conjecture has been tested for extremely large numbers with the aid of computers, it remains one of the most profoundly enigmatic and unresolved problems in the field of mathematics. This document examines and explains the Collatz Conjecture, including a look at the underlying mechanism and evidence for its validity. It also includes a brief discussion on why the conjecture is considered particularly complex. Furthermore, a hypothesis regarding the conjecture's validity is proposed and tested in this document. The hypothesis suggests that any sequence leading to a divergence from the numbers' natural ordering must necessarily culminate in the number one. Our analysis will verify this hypothesis using sequences originating from up to 21, which is a prime number. Although this does not offer any new insights that might crack the conjecture, it provides an opportunity to explore number theory in a more in-depth and intricate manner. Importantly, it also serves as an enhancement to the existing number-theory knowledge presented in the "A Course in Number Theory" by Robin Hartman and "Introduction to Number Theory" by Michael Rosen texts. Additionally, a related idea is proposed in the "Recurrent Patterns in Natural Phenomena" section, which considers the possibility that sequences and numbers might hold more significance than typically assumed within the context of the conjecture. It's also worth noting that any attempt to verify the conjecture for numbers up to 23 using my own analysis may exhibit mild inaccuracies due to computational and algorithmic limitations. Users are encouraged to generate an accurate version using their own programming efforts and share it, potentially leading to a improved version. Similarly, users are invited to create a more efficient, recursive version of the "Collatz Conjecture Numbers" spreadsheet listed in the references, which describes all the number sequence divergence occurrences. This project draws inspiration from a "Number Game" project developed by Robert Bradshaw, although the specific focus and scope may differ. Lastly, any version of this document can be accessed at http://www.math.columbia.edu/~woit/TS/ and I kindly request that users report any found bugs or shortcomings by email at TristanWitkowski@gmail.com. Research in STEM fields relies heavily on formal mathematical expressions, which pose challenges to categorization and semantic analysis. To accurately categorize documents and capture their semantic scope, it is essential to utilize both textual and structural features specifically governing STEM content. Although prior studies explored document categorization in STEM, they often overlooked the complexities of mathematical co-authoring and graph-based topology within the community. In this study, we address these limitations by focusing on clustering STEM publication graphs to discern the role of co-authorship in category modeling. We also examine how introducing mathematical entities affects model performance and features, particularly those that are intrinsic to STEM content. By leveraging the Collection of Academic Literature for Science (CALS), which merges publication graphs and text documents, we conduct an in-depth analysis of STEM document categorization from both structural and textual perspectives. We discover that co-authorship and community topology significantly influence categorization, and that incorporating mathematical entities and graphs further improves model performance across eight STEM categories. Our results suggest that a two-model approach, consisting of one graph-informed and one text-informed model, is a robust strategy for STEM document categorization. We believe that this dual-modelling strategy can be adapted to other disciplines within STEM. We showcase the feasibility of our proposed method by implementing it on a large, recently published dataset of CALS and demonstrating its results through human evaluation. We publicly release our code and data for the benefit of the research community. Importantly, we address ethical considerations surrounding the use of graph-based models for categorization, particularly those related to community structure and writing conventions. We ultimately contribute to the understanding of STEM document classification as a whole. Mechanism design theory relies on the assumption of rational decision-making, but in practice, individuals making multiple choices may not always act rationally.  To design effective mechanisms, it is crucial to understand and address the potential for irrationality.  We examined a fundamental mechanism, the dictatorial veto, used in numerous applications, and investigated its performance when faced with irrational agents.  Our study makes a significant contribution by developing the first quantitative model to describe how veto mechanisms interact with irrationality.  It appears that irrationality can significantly impact the performance of the veto mechanism - whereas it excels in environments with low levels of irrationality, its effectiveness plummetes in environments with high levels of irrationality.  We investigated ways to mitigate the veto mechanism's vulnerability to irrationality.  One approach involves making selective suggestions, a strategy that effectively enhances the veto mechanism's performance.  Our study provides strategies for determining when and how to employ this approach.  Furthermore, we investigated the potential for the group to contribute to the identification of the desired outcome, either by imposing external constraints on the veto mechanism or by allowing it to adapt to individual preferences.  Although external interventions may provide temporary relief from the veto mechanism's vulnerability to irrationality, they generally do not provide lasting solutions.  Conversely, we discovered that adopting a particular adaptation, namely the product adaptation, can endure and cause the veto mechanism's performance to improve as irrationality increases.  It is worth noting, however, that implementing the product adaptation comes with its own set of challenges.  Interestingly, our study reveals that the veto mechanism's performance in environments with irrationality but without product adaptation can be better than its performance in environments with low levels of irrationality but no irrationality.  In general, our study provides valuable insights into the veto mechanism's behavior, and we found that the veto mechanism's performance is highly dependent on a particular parameter, which we call the VAT parameter.  Our study provides valuable guidance on how to manipulate the VAT parameter and achieve desired outcomes.  Ultimately, our study emphasizes the importance of and strategies for identifying the desired outcome, and we found that the veto mechanism's performance is highly dependent on a particular parameter, which we call the REL parameter.  Our study provides valuable guidance on how to mitigate the impact of irrationality and achieve desired outcomes.  Ultimately, our study provides significant contributions to the fields of mechanism design and the study of irrationality.  Specifically, our study provides valuable insights and strategies for identifying and addressing irrationality, and we distinguish between irrationality and external interventions

CrossEncoder, which can accurately assess summaries through their semantic connection with the original text, offers an alternative. In this paper, we introduce SummScore, a pioneering summarization evaluation metric that relies on CrossEncoder. Our approach uses the Probing Technique to determine the extent to which generated summaries effectively convey the original text's essential information. Different Probing Techniques lead to distinct evaluation metrics, namely, F scores for objective metrics and correlation and Delexicalization metrics for subjective assessment. F scores evaluate a summary's fluency and its ability to convey the original text's main ideas, while other scores evaluate a summary's ability to convey the original text's ideas despite using less descriptive wording. In our study, SummScore outperforms the current best metrics in the coherence and fluency qualities of the generated summaries. Additionally, having established SummScore, we expand on this concept by defining three distinct qualities that an ideal summary can possess: Coherence, Fluency, and Informative capacity, which enable comprehensive analysis of the generated summaries. Furthermore, we introduce properties that make CrossEncoder a more versatile tool, such as its ability to assess summaries written in any language by pre-training it on a large, multilingual dataset as evidence that XE can handle multilingual summaries. Finally, we propose a pre-training strategy for CrossEncoder that does not involve the original text's retrieval, making it a more viable tool for the generation of abstracts in fields such as law and medicine where such retrieval is difficult. In our final analysis, generated summaries of various writing styles and from numerous domains have shown to greatly benefit from CrossEncoder as an efficient tool. It can learn and assess various styles and domains using a single model, in stark contrast to the current state where one model is trained for a single style or domain. In our testing, our pre-trained CrossEncoder has shown to generate highly precise and detailed summaries that are often indistinguishable from those written by humans in various domains including technology, law and medicine as evidenced by our test on specific datasets in these fields. The development of autonomous vehicles depends heavily on fusion between camera and LiDAR data, which provides spatial and temporal data in an efficient manner. Current methods combining camera and LiDAR data mostly rely on self-supervised auto-encoders to measure their similarity. Although effective, this approach has significant drawbacks, particularly in scenarios where LiDAR signals are weak or interrupted. This study presents a novel idea to match 3D LiDAR features with 2D camera data in 4D space and then use attention-based cross-modal encoding to merge LiDAR and camera information. Our novel method, named BEVFusion, has been evaluated and compared with other approaches using the MapNet dataset. The results show that MapNet with the BEVFusion technique achieves a mean average precision (mAP) of 65.12 on the "car" category, representing an impressive 11.83% enhancement over the current top-performing method. Moreover, the research highlights the advantages of integrating LiDAR and camera data within the context of autonomous driving through the creation of an interactive 4D map. This innovative framework has the potential to improve object detection and scene understanding when processing real-world data effectively. At the molecular level, thermal noise can alter the spatial arrangement of surface elements, causing them to fluctuate and approach equilibrium. This fluctuation has a characteristic scale determined by the momentum transfer from these structures, causing them to deviate from optimal conditions, leading to increased angular momentum and rotation. As this surface structure rotates, it creates and maintains large-scale circular flows that facilitate efficient momentum transfer along the wall normal, explaining why fully developed turbulent flows require a minimum thickness and why momentum is often transferred along odd-numbered scales. A pioneering data pipeline approach known as the Multi-Stage Data Pipeline (MSDP) is introduced in H-STREAM, incorporating real-time data selection, aggregation, and computation functionalities. Within an industrial setting, H-STREAM was applied to enhance the efficiency of online advertising management and maintenance processes. The present research builds on existing studies in data pipeline technology and stream data processing, introducing an innovative and practical solution known as the Multi-Stage Data Pipeline (MSDP), said to offer superior performance and greater versatility in real-world applications compared to current data pipeline models. The study showcases the practical value of H-STREAM by illustrating its effectiveness in resolving complex problems in online advertising management and its broader potential to contribute to various data-intensive fields. The primary contribution of this study is the development of an innovative data pipeline model, which through evaluation and assessment, demonstrates its superiority over established pipelines in terms of computational efficiency and practical applicability.
