The increasing use of artificial intelligence in critical systems raises concerns
about transparency, as users cannot evaluate their reliability. To address
these concerns, we investigate the potential approaches to verify and validate
neural networks. By examining existing validation methods in regulatory
contexts, we analyze their applicability to neural networks. Given the current
lack of suitable validation methods for these models, we explore ways to
adapt or modify existing techniques, such as validation procedures for
safety-critical software. We also discuss the importance of developing
validation methods for neural networks and outline steps for establishing such
methods in regulatory contexts. Further, we investigate the feasibility of
utilizing validation methods for other types of machine learning models and
clarify the distinctions between these models and neural networks. This study
ultimately aims to facilitate the development and implementation of neural network validation methods within regulatory environments. To support these efforts, we provide case studies that illustrate the application of validation methods in regulating neural networks and apply them to real-world scenarios to evaluate their effectiveness. One case study involves a vehicle driving system and finds that existing validation methods can be challenging to apply, highlighting the need for additional guidance. Another case study examines a model using an established validation method in a regulatory context and demonstrates its usability. Through these case studies, we address practical concerns and goals related to neural network validation and confirmation in regulatory environments. Finally, we conclude by addressing open questions and predictive issues related to neural network validation and confirmation. Regulatory bodies face significant challenges in addressing the increasing deployment of artificial intelligence in critical systems. To mitigate these concerns, we investigate the application of existing validation methods for neural networks and identify the feasibility of adapting or expanding these methods to verify and validate neural networks. By analyzing the possibilities and constraints of validation in a regulatory context, we explore the development of new and innovative approaches to neural network validation and confirmation. This study ultimately aims to introduce neural network validation and confirmation guidance to facilitate the assessment of reliability in artificial intelligence. To achieve this goal, we delve into technical, practical, and procedural aspects of validation in a regulatory environment, including the selection of and guidance for models, data, and procedures. Through case studies, we apply the developed guidance on neural network validation and confirmation. To conclude, we predict future developments and challenges in validation in a regulatory context. By examining the artifactual, and universal aspects of the verification and validation process, we can conclude whether the challenges stem from the model form (e.g. neural network) or whether they are due to limitations in current verification and validation techniques

Clustering is an essential technique in data analysis for recognizing patterns 
by condensing similar data into more compact representations. Unlike other 
methods, this research introduces a functorial clustering method that accurately 
maps hidden structural patterns in multilevel data. We have developed a novel 
functorial clustering method, called funclu, in combination with a mapping called 
funmap. These can be applied to data from various domains with or without 
overlapping groups. Funclu is capable of discovering the underlying pattern 
at any hierarchical level, enabling novel interpretations of the data from both 
a statistical and a mathematical perspective. A key benefit of funclu is its 
ability to accurately identify patterns in multilevel data without relying on 
predefined parameters. We have implemented funclu in R and demonstrated its 
usefulness through its application to simulated data, data from the presence of 
sources challenge, and real-world datasets, including breast cancer and CO2 
envelopes data. This approach is available on GitHub under the open-source 
license. Furthermore, a associated predictive mapping tool has been developed 
under the terms of the GNU General public license. We present both funclu and 
predictive mapping in updated versions that are accessible directly from their 
original sources or through GitHub's zip function.

Recent technologies have enabled the efficient recovery of sparse and low-rank tensors in data retrieval, significantly contributing to improving both the speed and quality of processing. Despite this advancement, there are significant drawbacks to achieving streaming tensor ring restoration for the retrieval of visual data. These shortcomings include the loss of valuable information, degradation of restoration performance, inability to respond to user interactions, and inadequate support for more complex and abundant 3D visual data. To address these issues, a novel method called Patch Monitoring-based Streaming Tensor Ring Restoration (PSRTR) is proposed. The PSRTR model successfully predicts and corrects errors that occur during tensor restoration, thereby enhancing the overall restoration quality. The development of a cost function and an algorithm to monitor and correct patches (PatchCorr) are also presented. The PSRTR is evaluated using various 3D visual datasets, demonstrating its superiority over traditional restoration methods. The PSRTR has been successfully applied to several data retrieval systems. The system utilizes the PSRTR's ability to correct errors and maintains the highest processing efficiency even with the most complex and abundant 3D visual data. The proposed method and system are respectively named Enhancer and StrongEnhancer. The system achieved top rankings in both the NUS3D and Stanford2D3D datasets in various evaluation categories over leading data retrieval systems. The system's source code and detailed information are available at https://weiyingwu.github.io/StrongEnhancer. 

The main contributions of this research are two-fold:

1. A novel enhancement algorithm, called PatchCorr, is developed to address the PSRTR's error correction aspect, thereby enhancing the overall restoration quality.
2. The Enhancer and StrongEnhancer system is introduced, achieving state-of-the-art performance in processing the most complex 3D visual data with high speed and efficiency. The system successfully surpassed 12 leading data retrieval systems in various evaluation categories, cementing its position as one of the top-performing data retrieval systems. 

It is worth noting that there are several potential issues with this research paper, which may decrease its impact on the reader. Firstly, some of the key concepts and technical terms, such as tensor ring restoration and visual data retrieval, are not clearly explained, making it difficult for readers without a background in the field to fully understand the context. Secondly, some of the sentences are excessively complex and feature dense object-related words, which may increase comprehension difficulty. We observed the system Cr Dra, which consists of a binary made up of active stars CR Dra and DR Dra, using multiple frequency beams at 1.4 GHz. Over 100 days, we tracked a strong, periodic signal from CR Dra's low-frequency radiation, which lasted for almost a decade. This signal exhibited a frequency drift of 5.8 x 10^-3 day^-1. While the exact mechanism behind this drift remains unclear, it's likely due to complex magnetic field structures. We also observed rapid, high-frequency changes in frequency, which could be explained by mode switching or a source with moving electron cyclotron frequencies. This discovery confirms that active stars like CR Dra can produce powerful radiation, which could be used to study magnetized plasmas. We suggest that CR Dra's low-frequency radiation is the result of a source near the star's pole, which could provide insights into electron cyclotron maser radiation theories. Additionally, we propose that CR Dra and DR Dra, which is a less active star, could have distinct radiation patterns that are influenced by their respective magnetic fields and coronal features. Long-term observations from the Nanshan radio telescope in China have enabled us to study the behavior of active stars and magnetic field structures in the solar corona, which could provide insights into active stars like CR Dra's low-frequency radiation, which could be relevant for studying magnetized plasmas in the solar corona. Finally, we highlight the importance of a radio source near the star's pole, which could provide insights into active stars' circularly polarized emission and their circularly polarized emission patterns. Moreover, we investigate the active stars' radiation patterns and assess their potential for astrophysical radio astronomy. This research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China and the Yunnan Provincial Science Foundation. There is consensus among both human and machine vision that the same image can be interpreted differently based on the surrounding context. However, our understanding of how this happens, particularly in extreme cases, is still scarce. To investigate this, we created DeviantArt2, a massive, extensively labeled dataset comprising 89,626 images with dramatic modifications and their corresponding context descriptions. By analyzing this dataset, we discovered that while both humans and machines can identify altered images, their patterns of variation are distinct and specifically, human tendencies to notice such changes more frequently occur near the image's center and are often associated with higher-level semantic information, whereas machines show a more uniform pattern of focus across the image and do not show semantic influences in their preferences. Our research further reveals that, despite these differences, both humans and machines can learn to predict these patterns, thereby enhancing their performance in extreme cases. Interestingly, according to our findings, machine learning improves at predicting these changes almost immediately, whereas human performance improves significantly with practice. Our study provides new insights into these visual phenomena and highlights the value of collaborative learning from both human and machine vision. Importantly, our research delivers a significant step towards creating a general understanding of visual context that can be applied across various situations by highlighting that intense image modifications with context-dependent variability might be a key feature for developing such a theory. The high temperature and dense matter environment where a phase transition to a quark-gluon plasma is predicted, is also characterized by significant dynamics at the interface between this state and various forms of hadronic matter. In Deconfined Quark Plasmas that exist for short periods at lower values of the coupling constant, the process of deactivation may occur before the transition to the plasma phase. We investigate multiple variations of this transition in a model where the underlying symmetry is known, and demonstrate through various simulations that the process of deactivation is linked to the spontaneous formation of gluon-baryon bound states. If true, this would imply the presence of a particular type of phase transition in SU(3)-Higgs theories at higher temperatures. A distinctive characteristic of this transition would be a sudden limitation in the plasma's energy density, occurring simultaneously with the disappearance of deactivation-induced modifications to the transition line. We confirm through multiple simulations, both at fixed symmetry temperature and for zero temperature variations of the Deconfined Quark Plasma, that this sudden limitation in the plasma's energy density is a universal property of the phase transition. This is linked to the process of deactivation being suddenly delimited, and also to the sudden appearance of the gluon condensate, a complex composite object. We note that this is a unique type of phase transition, one where the process of deactivation becomes the opposite process of activation, and simultaneously, the disappearance of the gluons' collective behavior is replaced by the formation of this collective behavior. Furthermore, we simulate the thermodynamic properties of the SU(3)-Higgs and the gluon-baryon liquid phases that exist just before and after this sudden limitation in the plasma's energy density has occurred. HD58260 is an exciting B-type star that demonstrates significant magnetic field changes, especially in its metal lines, in contrast to the photospheric H$\alpha$ line. Conducting rapid, precise measurements of the star's magnetic field is achievable through high-resolution spectroscopy with a 0.7 meter telescope. The analysis focuses on the star's magnetic field cycles, characterizing its temporal behavior and examining how the magnetic field in individual cycles correlates with the star's rotation period. The research includes simulated observations to validate the spectropolarimetric technique on photometric data and discusses the differences between the magnetic fields measured in metal lines and the H$\alpha$ line. The results demonstrate a magnetic field fluctuation of approximately 600 Gauss over a 1.5 day period in the H$\alpha$ emission, while the magnetic field measured in metal lines reaches a maximum of nearly 3000 Gauss and exhibits a more complex variation pattern. The spectral lines show nearly opposite polarity, with the magnetic field measured in the red lines exhibiting a reversal. The magnetic field measured in the red lines corresponds to the star's magnetic field during the second half of its 1.5-day cycle. The team suggests that the magnetic field measured in metal lines originates from the star's upper upper atmosphere, while the H$\alpha$ magnetic field corresponds to the star's lower upper atmosphere. The presence of the chromosphere was confirmed through the analysis of the line intensity, revealing a positive correlation with the line's magnetic sensitivity. We propose an asynchronous federated training method for nonlinear regression that is highly efficient in terms of communication and computation. This training framework comprises two distinct phases - an optimization phase and an active learning phase - both designed with the goal of minimizing the time it takes for models to learn from participants. Our proposed framework focuses on two key resources - communication and computation - that greatly impact the training process. By applying a nonlinear regression model, we develop an optimization phase that identifies the most favorable training data and model parameters which results in significant model improvement with minimal model size. Next, we devise an active learning phase that efficiently selects the most suitable data for models to learn from, leading to notable reductions in model training time and a better trade-off between model performance and the time models take to learn. Our experiments using real-world data demonstrate that our proposed framework outperforms existing federated learning methods by achieving up to a 250 times speedup compared to standard asynchronous methods, learning from models 10 times faster than passive methods, and achieving performance comparable to centralized learning. Our models also require less memory and processing power than other methods leading to a better resource efficiency. This research introduces a new technique, called SSNE, for embedding nodes in large networks. 
SSNE uses localized embeddings to represent nodes, making it efficient for large networks, especially those that are sparse. 
Standard node embedding methods like Node2Vec and DeepWalk rely on the presence of a sufficient number of random walks per node. 
If the number of random walks per node is less than the dimension of the embedding matrix, the algorithm will not converge. 
This is typically the case in sparse networks, which have been found to benefit from SSNE. 
We evaluate SSNE on various networks, showing that it produces better node embeddings and has better performance on link prediction tasks compared to other node embedding algorithms. 
The results indicate that SSNE is able to create accurate and informative representations of nodes even in the absence of a large number of random walks per node. 
The embeddings produced by SSNE are similar to the ground truth node degrees, making it effective for predicting links in networks.

We've developed an innovative COVID-19 model that combines elements of two established models, the Kermack-McKendrick and SIR models, to simulate the spread of cases within a confined population. This new approach allows us to analyze near-term trends of cases, combining the accuracy of the Kermack-McKendick model for initial growth with the recovery capabilities of the SIR model for later stages. To account for ongoing spread, case rates, and death rates, we adjust our model using fractional stochastic equations and incorporate a stochastic element to reflect uncertainty. This method enables us to make accurate short-term forecasts by utilizing historical data and adjusting for contemporary factors such as social distancing, vaccination rates, and the prevalence of new variants. We apply our model to study the patterns of COVID-19 in the United States, specifically focusing on the trends observed in California and Texas. This analysis allows us to evaluate the potential impact of different variables on case growth and death rates, shedding light on the interplay between these factors. Furthermore, our model demonstrates that, despite differences in case growth during initial waves, the outcomes are surprisingly similar when adjusting for population size. This research reveals that, to mitigate the effects of a pandemic, it is crucial to maintain social distancing until a high percentage of the population has been infected or vaccinated, and that early gains in this direction can sometimes lead to false security if not sustained through continued effort. We also observe that economic recovery heavily depends on near-term case growth and death rates, making the early stages of a pandemic of outproportional significance. This method offers a valuable framework for understanding the long-term effects of a pandemic and identifying the critical variables driving those outcomes. It provides actionable insights for public health policy-makers, helping them make informed decisions when allocating resources, prioritizing vaccination and hospitalization, and determining the optimal levels of social distancing measures and travel restrictions. The model's source code and other supporting materials are publicly available at https://github.com/RobertALeeds/COVID-19-comp-model. This study builds upon and expands the findings presented at the International Conference of Artificial Intelligence in 2020 and the International Conference of Power and Energy Drive, under the auspicious leadership of Dr. Adarsh Khuntia and Dr. Deepak Khantia respectively. Following the conference, this research was enhanced and published in the Journal of Artificial Intelligence. Building upon this work, the model has been selected for a competition hosted by the Future of AI for COVID-19 Forecasting, where it finished as runner-up

We explore a general method for calculating weighted sums of polynomials in nonzero rows of $\mathbf{X}$, where $r_i$ varies from 1 to $n$. This approach relies on two existing concepts: the expectation of a low-rank matrix with a given number of nonzero rows and the distribution of eigenvalues in such matrices. To identify potential New Physics within the precision measurement of lepton flavor universality in $b\to s$ transitions, we investigated the semi-inclusive version of this observation. By analyzing additional hadronic characteristics in the vicinity of $D$ and $\bar{D}$ mesons at e+- collider experiments like Belle II, we can assess whether new interactions violate lepton flavor conservation across various decay modes. Unlike traditional $b\to X_s$ observations, semi-inclusive measurements are more susceptible to new physics affecting lepton production, even with no net transfer of momentum to leptons. We established a theoretical framework and relevant form factors to evaluate the influence of New Physics across various $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ processes. Our research indicates that if New Physics is detected in any $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transition, it is highly probable that it can be also identified through semi-inclusive Lepton Flavor Universality ratio, thus enhancing the sensitivity of this method to uncover New Physics. Moreover, we found that with sufficiently high statistical accuracy in $b\bar{b}$ cross-section rate, it is possible to determine the sign of $F_{Le}^L$ to a precision of 0.020, which is comparable to the statistical error of Belle II. We concluded that semi-inclusive Lepton Flavor Universality ratio and various semi-inclusive hadronic observables are complementary observables in the context of $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions. Finally, we have also examined the applicability of this method to $K^+\to\pi^0\ell^+\ell^-$ rare decay process within the SO(10) GUT framework, which is highly suitable for experiments at a high-intensity $\mu$ muon collider. Our assessment indicates that with $\sim$3,000-$6,000 $K^+\to\pi^0\ell^+\ell^-$ events, it would be feasible to identify New Physics consistent with the Full Monte Carlo Simulation of muon collider's detector and background response. This new approach has the potential to uncover New Physics with $K^+\to\pi^0\ell^+\ell^-$ decay process at muon colliders with significantly enhanced sensitivity compared to LHC and with complementary input from $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions observed at Belle II and in the future Super-Belle II. The present work may also be adapted to other rare decays

This paper addresses the challenge of developing a communication-efficient distributed regulator for multi-channel network systems. Despite the successes achieved in designing controllers for such networks, creating a decentralized system that transfers optimal information across the network channels to regulate output trajectories remains unsolved. To overcome this challenge, we present a new approach using distributed convex optimization in a specially crafted objective function, which leads to a robust, plug-and-play architecture. Under certain conditions, the proposed method guarantees global stability and stable operation in the presence of hardware or network disruptions. The method allows each node to autonomously design, implement, and update its regulator without affecting other nodes, making it highly efficient. The global output trajectory is stabilized through a novel decentralized information-sharing protocol, which ensures all nodes maintain identical channel properties. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through numerical tests. The proposed method offers superior performance compared to existing methods for large networks, reducing inter-node information exchange by 40% to 90%, while also providing robustness against node failure. Additionally, this solution expands the capabilities of existing distributed regulation frameworks. We expand the eco-evolution model to investigate the interplay between environmental changes and the evolution of species over vast periods. Our analysis reveals that the traditional model's dynamics are suited for shorter-term scenarios, primarily focused on the rapid response of species to fluctuations in their environment. In contrast, our extended model explores the long-term coexistence of multiple species, including the possible emergence of complex dynamics such as chaos, particularly when three species interact. When more species are involved, however, the eco-evolutionary equilibrium becomes increasingly unstable and more prone to sudden transitions. Our results also demonstrate that species can adapt to environmental changes more easily in the short-term than in the long-term. Furthermore, regulating the duration and adaptation rate of these processes is crucial for understanding the long-term stability and potential for complex dynamics in the eco-evolutionary model. Our study lays the foundation for future research by adapting the eco-evolution model to account for the distinct patterns and mechanisms observed at different timescales. Such an adaptation enables us to explore a broader range of ecological and evolutionary phenomena, from group competition to the potential for irregular patterns in three-species models, and opens the door for exploring more complex interactions among multiple species in diverse ecological settings. Our model can be applied to various types of eco-evolutionary phenomena, including the potential for irregular patterns in models featuring up to nine species and different adaptation rates. We create a specialized neural network, called NuSPAN, to tackle the challenge of non-uniform sparse model representation in artificial intelligence-based inverse problems. The world around us has numerous examples of a combination of smooth and sparse patterns. However, existing neural networks are not well-suited to handling the issue of representation in non-uniform sparse models because they rely heavily on assumptions of piece-wise smoothness or uniform sparsity. The newly developed NuSPAN is capable of learning a representation that effectively captures both the smooth areas and the sparse patterns in signals through its Proximal Mean Network architecture, which consists of a proximal network and a mean network. The proximal network is responsible for maintaining the sparsity of data, while the mean network learns the average features in areas where the signal is smooth. By using back-propagation, the gradient of the loss function is passed through the network to update the model parameters in an end-to-end manner. The effectiveness of NuSPAN is demonstrated through its application in seismic reflection imaging. The 2D seismic data sets used in this study clearly illustrate the benefits of representing non-uniform sparse models. Additionally, comparative studies using conventional deep learning methods and sparsity-based optimization techniques show that NuSPAN yields superior performance. One significant challenge to building large-scale quantum computers revolves around eliminating hidden errors stemming from inaccuracies in their functioning. We've proposed the concealed inverses (CI) protocol, a direct approach that identifies and corrects errors without positive operator projection. This method develops a representation of a quantum operation's inaccuracies without describing every possible error configuration. CI's application in superconducting quantum technology results in a significant reduction of errors affecting two-qubit gate performance, as supported by both experimental and numerical evidence. Furthermore, this reduced error rate facilitates the creation of more resilient multi-qubit states. CI can be integrated with other quantum error correction strategies and offers potential as a widespread solution for improving the reliability of quantum computers. This new protocol, along with its underlying insights, could play a crucial role in building a fault-tolerant quantum computer. CI offers numerous benefits over traditional Hamiltonian simulation approaches and other quantum error correction schemes. This work examines CI's application in the context of superconducting quantum technology but also explores its broader potential for use across various quantum systems. An instance of CI's noise-reducing capabilities is its ability to lower the probability of measurement collapse during the execution of a multi-qubit entangling gate. CI achieves this by first determining the uncalculated inverse of a quantum operation through the application of Krylov sub-spaces and then calculating the uncalculated inverse of a corrected quantum operation to finally calculate the uncalculated inverse of a complex quantum operation. This results in a substantial performance boost with which CI outperforms conventional approaches by seamlessly integrating error correction into a quantum operation while streamlining the description of errors and significantly reducing the complexity of calculations. Moreover, this work examines CI's application to the uncalculated inverse of a quantum operation derived from random Hamiltonianian model. Following the proposed protocol, this approach allows the creation of a resilient quantum state despite the quantum operation's imperfect functioning. This, in turn, facilitates the creation of a reliable quantum state despite the quantum operation's imperfect functioning. Specifically, VT-CLIP uses a pre-training objective where a visual feature is matched with a text feature that an optical character recognition model extracts from a given image containing optical character recognition-generated fake text. Although research has effectively addressed this challenge in noisy environments, a general solution remains lacking. In this research, we offer a precise explanation of the task and propose a method of using linear operators to achieve matrix recovery under noisy conditions. Building on the robustness of operator switching in matrix completion, we extend this concept to matrix recovery and establish that our approach is feasible. We provide examples of matrices that, when modified through any transformation, remain near-perfect replicas of each other, as well as general conditions that identify such matrices. Additionally, we outline the theoretical guarantees for our method and offer numerical evidence of its effectiveness, including comparisons to an existing matrix recovery method. Our research provides new insights into the universal nature of matrices and may have significant implications for a variety of fields. It has the potential to improve performance in fields such as computer vision and learning, where successful applications of matrix completion have been documented. We show that for an $F$-regular ring $A$ with dimension $d$, its Hilbert function $P_A(t)$ can be expressed using a polynomial with at most $d$ non-zero coefficients, specifically $P_A(t) = \sum_{i=0}^{d} c_i \binom{t+i}{i}$. Furthermore, the coefficients $c_i$ of $P_A(t)$ are positive integers that depend only on $A$ and $d$, rather than the specific ring $A$. In contrast, the coefficient $c_d$ equals $1$ plus the cardinality of a specified set $\mathcal{F}_A$. The set $\mathcal{F}_A$ consists of elements of the form $S^{\frac{d-1}{2}} \cap X_1 \cdots X_d$, where $X_1$ through $X_d$ are proper ideals in $A$, with the intersection taken over all possible choices. In related work, we establish that an $F$-regular ring $A$ admits an $F$-filtration on $K_{X_1,\ldots,X_d}$, the ring resulting from the intersection of the given ideals, with the dimension of the filtration equal to $d$. The result holds for an arbitrary number of ideals in $F_{d+1}$ positions. In the paper's final section, we explore the inverse problem of determining which polynomials with the specified properties correspond to Hilbert functions of $F$-regular rings. While an exhaustive answer remains out of reach, we do identify a fundamental constraint: the leading coefficient $c_d$ must equal $1$ plus an integer multiple of the cardinality of the specified set $\mathcal{F}_0$. In the ring context, this translates to saying that the cardinality of the set $\mathcal{F}_0$ must be at most $1$ less than the cardinality of the specified set $\mathcal{F}_A$ for an $F$-regular ring $A$ with the specified properties. We developed highdicom to create and verify compliant digital images, combining rules from DICOM and relevant scientific standards.  This paper focuses on highdicom's application in creating model predictions for pathology slides and x-ray images, along with its model training and prediction capabilities.  We also examine how it enhances image annotation with SD data sets and makes it easy to report model outcomes in DICOM format.  Furthermore, highdicom is highly compatible with other popular scientific libraries, as shown by its digital signatures.  We include step-by-step instructions and practical examples for using highdicom to produce compliant outputs, as well as highlight its numerous applicable use cases.  We also include model results that were obtained using the model training and prediction processes described here: https://doi.org/10.1002/pbe.5862 and https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-021-5990-y.  The related source code and packaged software can be found online. In the digital world, documents are represented by vectors in a high-dimensional space.
For DNA sequences, a document corresponds to a specific genome.
Unlike other text, DNA is not typically represented by vectors because it does not come with associated information like meaning or relevance.
However, DNA sequences can be converted into numerical documents by applying various functions such as counting occurrences of specific patterns.
Despite the conversion, there is no clear benefit because the resulting vectors do not capture any meaningful connections.
To fix this issue, a method called unsupervised embedding is proposed to organize these vectors in a more useful way, focusing on maintaining the inherent structure of DNA sequences.
By achieving this, a DNA genome can be represented by a unique point in a high-dimensional space, enabling new applications based on similarities between DNA sequences. 
A key aspect of this project is developing an effective distance metric in order to visualize and analyze DNA sequences.
We experimented with creating "close" or "far" relationships between different genomes by preserving the overall structure of DNA sequences.
The results show that using a specific distance metric reveal visually recognizable relationships between genomes based on their genetic similarities. 
In addition, we discovered some interesting connections among the tested genomes using this visualization tool.
Ultimately, we aim to make unsupervised DNA embedding more useful to the scientific community by enabling a variety of applications, including visualization, analysis, and discovery of relationships between DNA sequences. 
We plan to further develop this project in multiple directions, such as identifying relationships between DNA sequences and visualizing them on a 3D map. 
A demonstration of this project can be accessed at unsupervised-dna-embedding.org. 
A related GitHub repository containing the project's code and a pre-trained model can be found at github.com/kenjiy/nasun. 
Key project information, including results and datasets, can be found at kenjiy.com/dna-embedding.

The metal-insulator transition in V$_{2}$O$_{3}$ is well documented but the factors influencing it within the first few atomic layers are not fully understood. Low temperature scanning tunnelling microscopy (LT-STM) has investigated this transition in 3, 6 and 12 layered V$_{2}$O_{3}$ thin films grown on (0001) Al$_{2}$O$_{3}$ and established that they all exhibit bad metal behaviour due to strong electron scattering at the surface. However, the metal-insulator transition appears to be influenced by the presence of these surfaces. Moreover, the use of high temperature hydrogen flame treatment to clean and modify these surfaces significantly affects this transition. Out of the various surface treatments tested, only hydrogen flame treatment resulted in good insulating behaviour in V$_{2}$O_{3}$ thin films. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirmed the formation of a flat, oxidised, and metallic-like interlayer at the surface of these treated films. This interlayer behaves as an intermediate layer, concealing the metal-insulator transition that occurs within deeper V$_{2}$O$_{3}$ layers. Therefore, the use of hydrogen treatment surfaces enables the exploration of the metal-insulator transition in a well studied, 6 layered V$_{2}$O$_{3}$ system. This work showcases the role of a solid-state interface in regulating the metal-insulator behavior within thin films. 

Please note that this work was initially received prior to being confirmed by additional experiments such as low temperature 3He magnetometry. These experiments confirmed that the good insulating behavior observed was indeed caused by an intermediate layer rather than remaining bad metal at low temperatures due to elevated electron mobility. Moreover, the various surface treatments tested did not alter this behavior as previously thought. Primarily, the different metal-insulator behaviors observed were influenced by the presence of the interface itself. 

For the 3 and 12 layered V$_{2}$O$_{3}$ films, the metal-insulator transition occurs at the same temperature of 165 K. The Second Galactic Planet Search project aimed to analyze microlensing patterns in the second Galactic quadrant, with a particular focus on a thousand-degree sub-prime field (1600Q1), in-depth analysis of a hundred-degree prime fields (1600Q2), and thorough examinations of sixty-degree semi-prime fields (1600S). Our study of the 1600Q1 field discovered nearly a hundred microlensing candidates, most of which turned out to be genuine minor body influences. Unlike previous sub-prime fields, which showed a high proportion (20%) of planets passing very close to stars, we found this phenomenon occurred in only 13% of the candidates in 1600Q1. Our research covered nearly sixty-five thousand individual lensing observations from over three hundred different telescopes and volunteers. It allowed us to consult more than five thousand individual star charts for the analysis. Our findings revealed that about 5% of the candidates occurred in pairs and realized the hypothesis that a significant number of the candidates indeed have companions. It must be noted that only 57% of the candidates were handled by the AutoAnomaly system. The rest were discovered either manually by the observers or based on their comments. Our research discovered nearly five hundred minor body influences. It also confirmed that about 7% of the candidates closed in on a target star. Interestingly, we found that the time it takes for a lensing object to hit its star is roughly a distribution that is relatively uniform. While these approaches can provide simplified models for understanding complex phenomena, they also need to be consistent with conservation principles, albeit in some cases, implicitly. Furthermore, some of these approaches may lead to suboptimal results, such as additional dissipative terms, but are still viable, exemplified by their ability to handle the Fokker-Planck limit in incompressible fluid flows and apply to both compressible and incompressible systems. Predicting clients who will become unresponsive or non-paying is an essential activity for any company. This paper focuses on analyzing a dataset containing information about non-paying clients and evaluating supervised and deep learning models to prevent such situations. This involves creating a combinatorial formula using q-rook placement on a q-rectangular board with obstacles, adorned with colored squares. To derive this formula, we develop a strategy for placing two types of colored squares - subject to color and position constraints. In the process, we formulate two q-analogues for the Egeland-Kauflag generalization of the Hall-Littlewood symmetric function G_k(1^N), which are based on Dyck paths and colored square placement respectively. This research is facilitated by the extension of q-rook theory to colored square configurations. Subsequently, we extend this theory to the broader realm of Dyck paths. To achieve this, we propose a novel interpretation of Dyck paths as signed loop networks. This signed loop interpretation is then employed to propose a combinatorial formula for loop insertion in Schur Q-functions, which are fundamental to the study of Toda conjectures in algebraic combinatorics. This formula is derived by formulating a strategy for loop insertion in the context of signed loop networks. Notably, the strategy involves adjusting edges to satisfy the alternating height property, which is a hallmark of Dyck paths. This adjustment process is itself a recognized combinatorial mechanism for q-rook placement on a q-rectangular board with obstacles. As a result, we are able to leverage this mechanism to drive loop insertion in Schur Q-functions. The resulting formula is shown to be consistent with existing combinatorial formulas for elementary and homogeneous symmetric functions. Additionally, we are able to apply the formula to propose a combinatorial interpretation for the generalized Egeland-Kauflag function, which is a key element in the study of Toda conjectures. This proposed interpretation is based on the concept of t-Dyck paths. Notably, Schur Q-functions are integral to the study of Toda conjectures in the context of Schur posets. As such, we are able to leverage our understanding of Dyck paths and the generalized Egeland-Kauflag function to propose a combinatorial interpretation for Toda posets, which is facilitated by the extension of Dyck paths to the realm of Toda posets. This proposed interpretation is itself a novel direction in the study of Toda conjectures in algebraic combinatorics. Convolutional Neural Networks, or CNNs, are highly successful across various image classification and detection tasks. However, they are not optimized to determine the orientation of image objects. In applications where image orientation is crucial, like medical imaging or defect detection, it is necessary to align images with a reference frame. To address this, we suggest a set of CNN modules that can serve as a reference frame and can be trained with or without additional images. We also propose a simplified method to calculate image orientation. Our orientation-sensitive CNN modules perform better in many situations than traditional CNNs, according to our tests across various image identification tasks. Furthermore, we found that the two-step process including our orientation-sensitive modules and the conventional CNN is particularly effective. Our research is documented in the paper, along with demonstrations and test data available on our GitHub page. Our findings indicate that by integrating orientation-aware information into CNNs, they can identify images more accurately. To facilitate the development of such orientation-aware CNNs by others, we release our new orientation modules, pre-trained models, and source code under the open-source license. They can lead to improved results when used as is, or serve as a starting point to develop your own orientation models or integrate them with your existing CNNs. Our tests show that the resulting combined models are highly successful, achieving more accurate image identification in many situations. Our experiments also are with limited data sets, so it is reasonable to assume that the methods will work well with larger data sets. To summarize, we created a set of compact, open-source orientation modules that can be trained with just a few images and can be integrated with other models easily. They can be used as is, or as a starting point to develop your own models or combine them with existing models to obtain more accurate image identification results. Our source code is available on our GitHub page under the open-source MIT license. Users can clone it, run the pre-trained models, and use them to improve image identification results. Our research expounds the benefits and usage guidelines for the newly developed orientation modules and provides example code to illustrate their usage. As the use of machine learning learning ideas in mobile apps and other systems grows so does their complexity, making it difficult for users to comprehend the inner workings of these models.  Therefore, there is a growing need for interpretation techniques that can provide clear and culture-specific explanations to enhance user trust and engagement.  By providing easy-to-understand interpretations that are relevant to individual users, interpretation systems can improve this trust and engagement.  In situations involving recommendation systems, accurate individualized interpretations can lead to greater satisfaction with the recommended content and overall satisfaction with the application as a whole.  By providing clear explanations for why items are recommended, interpretation systems can satisfy a fundamental psychological need known as the need for explanation.  While previous studies, such as LIME, have attempted to provide explanations for machine learning models by analyzing how the loss of specific features impacts predicted outcomes, we introduce a unique interpretation algorithm for recommendation systems that takes into account how users modify their behavior when certain features change.  This new algorithm, LIME-RS, is based on two key principles: first that feature changes should occur in ways that reflect how users perceive their environment, and secondly that the modified behavior should be determined by how users perceive their environment, i.e. by a cognitive model.  By accurately reflecting how users perceive their environment and how they think, LOME-RS provides interpretations that are more culturally relevant, more realistic, and more comprehensible from a psychological perspective.  We evaluate the accuracy of our new approach by comparing it with a competing method that uses a pure analytical approach, through an analysis of 300 interpretable models, which demonstrate that our approach provides interpretations that are more consistent, more understandable, and more by-human.  Additionally, we show that the interpretations provided by LIME-RS are more effective in improving user satisfaction with the application as a whole compared with a competing method.  This is because while the competing method provides explanations that are accurate from a technical perspective but do not take into account how users perceive their environment and think, LIME-RS is designed to improve satisfaction by providing explanations that are accurate from a psychological perspective and culturally relevant.  In summary, our new approach provides interpretations that are accurate from a psychological perspective and culturally relevant, which in turn improve user satisfaction with the application as a whole.  A complete description of our approach can be found at: https://compliance-stability.github.io.  Furthermore, the interpretability library used in this research can be downloaded at: https://github.com/compliance-stability/limers.

In many scientific fields such as medicine and biology, categorizing objects is a common task that requires accurate prediction of their class labels based on available data. A widely employed method for classification is the nearest neighbor technique, which involves assigning a label to an object based on the class of its nearest neighbor. However, this simple approach can be unreliable when classes are nearly equal in number, as variations can lead to inaccurate predictions. A potential improvement to this limitation is the use of a majority vote from more than one neighbor. In this research, a statistical framework is proposed for evaluating the performance of a nearest neighbor classifier when data classes are not equally represented. A key element of this proposed method is the creation of weighted classes based on the relative size of each class and the assignment of weights to votes from nearest neighbors. By incorporating nearby data in the weighting process, this method can lead to improved accuracy of the classifier. The efficacy of the proposed framework was demonstrated in three real-world examples, including the classification of breast cancer and two multidimensional functional data categories. Furthermore, an algorithm based on this proposed method has been developed and made available for public use. A demonstration of its usefulness is the classification of unlabeled objects within the process of feature selection. A thorough investigation of the method revealed that it outperformed other competitive techniques such as the random forest and support vector machine. A relevant package, the knnunequalR package, has been created and made available for public use through GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/PhD-ChenDong/knnunequalR. A detailed description of its implementation can be found at the following link: https://github.com/PhD-ChenDong/knnunequalR/issues/1. Through numerical examples, the reliability and accuracy of the proposed method were shown to be consistent even with a relatively small number of training data, which addresses a long-standing concern in the field. As a result, the proposed method may be a trustworthy alternative to other existing classification methods. A comparison of its implementation with that of standard methods can be found at the following link: https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/equitable-nearest-neighbor-classification-new-statistical-chen-dong. The source code for these demonstrations can be found at the following links: https://github.com/PhD-ChenDong/knnunequalR/blob/main/appendix/A4.pdf. Utilizing this method, the proposed package was successfully applied to the classification of unlabeled objects within the process of feature selection.

Our investigation involves examining the process of charge tunneling between a quantum point contact and a region of superconductivity, as well as the associated normal metal regions in a triple-barrier device.  By employing advanced magnetic tuning techniques and the tools of quantum tunneling and superconductivity, the distinct electrical responses of the quantum point contact and the more deeply situated quantum dot are differentiated and analyzed.  The results reveal the existence of two primary charge-tunneling mechanisms:  Cooper-pair tunneling as a highly sensitive response to changes in superconducting domain size, and single-charge tunneling as an increased phenomenon in the presence of photoexcitation of the quantum dot.  The single-charge tunneling mechanism is found to be highly influenced by the quantum point contact's tunnel barrier width, as demonstrated through application of a gate electrode.  This work contributes to a deeper understanding of the complex interactions between quantum tunneling and superconductivity, as it sets the groundwork for exploring more intricate systems involving spin and light interactions.  Ultimately, the capabilities of advanced quantum tunneling and superconductivity tools have been thoroughly utilized in this investigation.  Interestingly, the results presented provide an opportunity for future research directions, as the single-charge tunneling mechanism may be influenced by the application of magnetic and electric fields, thereby potentially introducing a controllable element into the system.  Future research directions could involve the exploration of a variety of charge-tunneling mechanisms as they are modified by external influences such as light and magnetic fields, as well as as they are altered by changes in the characteristics of the normal metal regions and the positioning of the quantum point contact. A new method is presented that relies on a conditional generator model to generate panoramic images from single viewpoints, without needing supplementary data or semi-supervised learning. By contrasting the performance of model-trained and self-supervised learning approaches, it is demonstrated that self-supervised training yields better outcomes according to both qualitative and quantitative assessments. Further analysis explores the reasons behind the proposed method's effectiveness. It is revealed that using the latest model architecture, LLDM with 4-channel data, results in high-quality output with minimal artifacts. Furthermore, integrating moving object removal through the optical flow LLDM yields the best performance. Evaluations also confirm that the produced single panoramic images are compatible with CV2K-360E. The source code for this method will be freely accessible via https. The method achieved first place in the CVPR2023 DVIP Challenge on Single View Panoramic Image Generation. A key challenge in detecting hate speech is identifying the underlying text's semantic meaning, particularly with text that is ambiguous and open to multiple interpretations. In this paper, we employ a unique approach to extract key features, classify them, and develop a model that can predict hate speech with a high degree of accuracy. Our results demonstrate that our model's performance is comparable to that of existing models, achieving a remarkable 99.8% accuracy in one instance and averaging 87.5% across four distinct datasets. Notably, the features extracted by our model have significant explanatory power, accounting for 70% of the overall accuracy. A comprehensive analysis of our model reveals the importance of specific features in detecting hate speech. Our model's success stems from its ability to adapt to the challenges of hate speech detection, including dealing with the absence of prominent features. Furthermore, our model does not rely on any specific hyperparameters, complicating the replication of our results. Despite these obstacles, the features extracted by our model highlight the distinct ways in which offenders express hate speech. A subsequent survey of 13 researchers from diverse academic backgrounds further shed light on the different forms of hate speech and the potential applications of this research field. In summary, the research presented provides valuable insights into the various forms of hate speech and can be used to inform the development of automated hate speech detection tools. Ultimately, the extraction of key features has the potential to facilitate the understanding of the underlying semantics of hate speech. By applying this research to other fields, such as mental disease prediction, it may be possible to detect mental illness through the analysis of written text. Deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) have numerous applications in image processing tasks.  However, their extensions in multi-input multi-output (MIMO) formats struggle to surpass the performance of single-input single-output (SISO) frameworks. This limitation stems from DCNNs' inherent sequential processing nature that hinders simultaneous, inter-channel interaction among multiple input channels. To overcome this challenge, research has been conducted to develop more efficient MIMO-DCNNs through inter-channel feature exchange methods. This work aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of these feature exchange techniques and their implications on MIMO-DCNN development. As such, the study will conduct a systematic analysis of the design to identify trends and insights for MIMO-DCNN architecture design. This research will ultimately contribute towards developing more effective MIMO-DCNNs that can more efficiently utilize multi-channel inputs. Experimental results will be performed on the CIFAR10 dataset, with the results showing a better performance of MIMO-DCNNs with carefully designed feature exchange methods compared to a baseline DCNN model. Moreover, the research will reveal significant design influences of the number of MIMO layers and feature exchange channels on the model's performance. This, in turn, provides valuable guidelines for MIMO-DCNN architecture design. Ultimately, the research will verify the effectiveness of MIMO-DCNNs on ImageNet, with the accuracy achieving 85.46, a 1.34% improvement over the DCNN model. This research has the potential to contribute significantly towards reducing the gap between SISO and MIMO deep learning communities. Digital collections of historical manuscripts held within archives possess significant cultural and historical value, spanning thousands of years and diverse global origins. A variety of digital platforms, algorithms, and databases have emerged to facilitate access to these collections. However, numerous challenges arise in platform design, including data retrieval, as users often possess limited understanding of collection contents. This study examines the current digital infrastructure supporting cultural heritage manuscript collections, focusing on recent developments in data platforms, retrieval, and image-analysis tools. We also outline the range of tools currently available for creating, searching, and analyzing these collections. By synthesizing current research and experiences from the cultural heritage and adjacent domains, we identify key areas for improvement and propose future areas of exploration. Ultimately, we outline our objectives for developing a specialized search engine for digital manuscript collections: one that efficiently retrieves documents, extracts relevant semantic and visual features, and provides users with intuitive interfaces for collection exploration. A preliminary assessment of existing collections for XMiG-eu and relevant benchmark datasets is presented in the supplemental material. The benchmarking will guide further development of the search engine. A companion project, 'IntElligent eManuscript,' is also described in the appended document, with the ultimate goal of integrating these components into a unified search engine. The final section explores potential extensions beyond these objectives. The full paper, including project descriptions for 'IntElligent eManuscript' and the XMiG-eu search engine, is available in the supplemental for further examination.

Despite the effectiveness of standard numerical methods for solving the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, they have a significant drawback. These methods treat the quantum potential in a way that causes numerical noise to spread throughout the computational domain as the simulation progresses in time. This results in the loss of details at the microscopic scale and an inability to resolve initial conditions or features that are below a certain threshold. To overcome this issue, we suggest an unconventional approach based on a quadrature method that treats the quantum potential as a set of discrete coefficients. This method maps the quantum wave function to a set of microscopic points, allowing for local calculations of the quantum potential. This approach has the benefit of preserving fine-scale details without any diffusion or smearing of the results. We tested the method on a range of problems including nontrivial targets, Hamiltonian splitting, and quantum harmonic oscillators, and found that it is well-suited for simulating complex quantum systems. Additionally, we found that it is possible to achieve high accuracy with computational costs that are comparable to standard methods. Finally, we extended the method to allow it to be used on large-scale simulations by leveraging parallel processing capabilities. This extension opens up the possibility of applying this approach to realistic quantum systems that involve multiple degrees of freedom and are solved through sparse grid methods. One potential application of this method is the simulation of molecular hydrogen using the powers of ten parallel processing capability. This simulation involved the calculation of 2,160 billion coefficients over 2.5 billion time steps but despite not being able to achieve a fully converged solution, we were able to obtain a highly accurate solution that was within a small fraction of the total possible error. This success in the simulation opens up the possibility of applying this method to a wide range of realistic quantum systems. A $k$-directed hypergraph, defined as the hypergraph's partitioning of its vertices where each subset contains at most $k$ elements, is given. The notion of the maximum directed clique size in this type of hypergraph is then related to the Haar basis matrix's behavior. A determinant-based inequality is derived and further generalized for $k$-directed hypergraphs. By applying this inequality in specific instances, additional properties are revealed, such as the inequality's validity in hypergraphs where every vertex participates in at most two subsets and a connection between the maximum directed clique size and the second-largest eigenvalue of a particular adjacency matrix. Additionally, given a $k$-directed hypergraph, a quantity known as the $\mathcal P$-index is defined and related to the maximum directed clique size. As a result, conditions are established for the existence of maximum directed cliques in this type of hypergraph. Furthermore, a relationship between the $\mathcal P$-index and the maximum directed clique size in $k$-directed hypergraphs is demonstrated, along with its generalization and application to the analysis of power networks. A quantity known as the generalized spectral property is defined and related to several important indices of the power network. As a result, relationships between various important indices of the power network are established and demonstrated through practical analysis of a robust power grid consisting of eight nodes. Finally, limitations of the proposed approach are discussed and potential improvements or generalizations suggested. 

This research focuses on the study of the relationship between the Haar basis matrix and the maximum directed clique size in $k$-directed hypergraphs, which has practical applications to the analysis of power networks. A series of derived inequalities and essential properties are proposed. 2. Inequality and property applications involve the use of determinants and Haar basis matrices.
3. Generalized properties are achieved by applying a specific inequality in specific instances of $k$-directed hypergraphs.
4. Relationships between various important indices of the power network are established and demonstrated through practical analysis.
5. Our approach can be further generalized to the creation of the maximum directed clique.

To better understand the processes controlling tropical desert hydroclimate, research focuses on the spatial and temporal patterns of precipitation events. Analyzing numerical simulations, researchers found that heavy precipitation in the tropics was characterized by a recurring cycle. Initially, precipitation forms in localized areas, and as they move, they trigger secondary episodes of heavy rain. This pattern is indicative of a possible limit to precipitation intensity, known as the "peak irrigation by steady infiltration" (PISI) threshold. Exceeding PISI results in prolonged dry periods between episodes of heavy rain. PISI appears to impose constraints on deep systems, marked by a sudden shift from large-scale precipitation to more localized and persistent conditions. This mechanism is thought to contribute to the synchronization of precipitation events observed in tropical deserts. Furthermore, researchers discovered that very intense precipitation, occurring at rates greater than approximately 100 mm/hour, is largely confined to areas surrounded by mountains. As a result, very intense precipitation is relatively rare over flat regions, such as the Amazon basin. Quantitatively estimating PISI allows for a deeper understanding of how this mechanism influences precipitation patterns. When applied to a few examples, PISI reveals that desert regions, including the Atacama and the Sahara, are characterized by PISI values that could restrict precipitation intensity. However, deep systems may occasionally allow for higher precipitation intensity during rare events, such as mesoscale cyclogenesis, which is a potential factor contributing to the scarcity of consistent precipitation in these areas. On the other hand, PISI suggests that topological constraints are an additional mechanism limiting precipitation intensity. When exploring a variety of examples, researchers found that PISI typically falls within the range of a few days to a week. When applying the model to a few examples, PISI varies from 3 to 100 hours, with an average close to a week. Notably, PISI values greater than this average are associated with deep systems that reach low pressures of at least 950 millibars. This indicates that PISI values are influenced by the intensity of the low-pressure system. Consequently, researchers speculate that the average PISI could be restricted by the maximum pressure that can be achieved by a deep system. This, in turn, may impose a minimum timescale for precipitation events in tropical deserts. Such a minimum timescale could be significant, implying that tropical deserts may experience precipitation patterns influenced by a combination of factors, including both external (deep systems) and internal (PISI) factors.

A related random walk (also known as an autoregressive model) on a graph is defined by a set of equations where each vertex value at the next time step depends on the previous time step values of itself and its neighboring vertices. We investigate how the probability distribution of this random walk changes over time. For small instances of this random walk, we develop a general formula that captures the evolution of the distribution at any given time. Using this approach, we identify distinctive patterns in the distribution's evolution when the starting vertex is located in different areas of the graph. Furthermore, we show that our model can accurately predict the future state of real-world networks (such as Facebook's friend network and the Protein Interactions network) up to several time steps in advance by classifying the distribution's initial state into one of several pre-defined categories. Our model surpasses a relevant control method both in terms of accuracy and robustness. The developed model's features also demonstrate compatibility with the graph's structural components (such as clusters and connectivity groups) for various real-world networks. By combining the features corresponding to these structural elements, the model achieves improved accuracy and resilience. The proposed approach can potentially be applied to related random walk models in general, and we hope this method can be leveraged to classify distribution states in the future. We plan to enhance this model by training it on the graph's initial distribution rather than using a pre-defined classification system. Such a training method would make the model highly versatile, capable of being applied across domains. We intend to address this challenge in our future work. The model's code is available at https://github.com/jay-vee/Related-Random-Walk-Features. In formal specifications, definitions play a crucial role, yet frequently expire as their associated domains develop. This document presents an extension of the HOL type theory, specifically designed for definitions that incorporate temporal components, thereby allowing for an increase in the state domain's constraints over time. Furthermore, it is demonstrated how timed definitions' persistence reflects an intuitive understanding of their intended purpose. This is illustrated through an examination of several practical examples. The study further investigates the implications of incorporating timed definitions, highlighting differences in property verification and functionality across various scenarios. Ultimately, it is shown that while timed definitions and their standard counterparts often yield equivalent results, they can substantially differ in situations involving state changes or the utilization of non-deterministic operators. The presented approach has potential applications in various areas, such as real-time hardware design, embedded software development, and traditional (real-time) hardware design. The formalization has been implemented in a HOL Light theory extension. The associated verification tasks can be found on the Coq-ALP benchmark suite. This research represents an initial adaptation of the Coq-ALP benchmark suite to the HOL Ligth logic system. The primary objective of this project is to enable the use of formal verification for the design of highly reliable and predictably functioning real-time software systems.

Building upon recent breakthroughs in predicting shearing instantaneous statistical anisotropy, this study develops an approach to identify instantaneous boundary turbulence using a bottom-up approach involving two main procedures. Firstly, it employs an optimised coherent structure-based model to predict shear turbulence instantaneous statistics at the boundary of an imaginary surface layer before calculating a normalized difference with actual instantaneous statistics. Secondly, it compares this predicted statistics with actual statistics to determine instantaneous turbulence. This approach will be tested across varying friction velocity values and geostrophic shear rates to simulate boundary turbulence in both linear and non-linear shear instability conditions. Models used in this approach will be coherent structure-based models, include the Fovale model, were tested along with a model that takes into consideration the presence of very large coherent structures known as superstructures, called the SSFovale model, another model that takes into consideration the presence of finite sized very large coherent structures, called the MLCS model, and a model that doesn't take into consideration the presence of very large coherent structures but takes into consideration the interactions between very large coherent structures and the substructure, called the MLCS non-linear model. Several types of synthetic and real data were used to test the approach, with results showing that the MLCS non-linear model has the highest accuracy in predicting instantaneous turbulence. This new approach has the potential to significantly improve current understanding and predictions of instantaneous turbulence near surfaces of various media by addressing the long-standing problem of accurately identifying instantaneous turbulence using a coherent statistical model. This approach will be used in a upcoming project to investigate very large coherent structures in atmospheric data. These configurations feature a characteristic behaviour in regions of strong electric field, adhering to a set of equations that include the Euler-Lagrange equations and appropriate boundary conditions. Within this framework, we identify solutions to the Euler-Lagrange equations, demonstrating their stability through the establishment of an energy bound, valid for all time t. Furthermore, we illustrate the emergence of the traditional Skyrme model, comprising bogolon and Yang-Mills configurations, when electric field strengths become sufficiently weak. Our analysis also involves examining the influence of four-fermion coupling strength and Born-Infeld parameter on soliton properties within this modified Skyrme model. Lastly, we delve into the statistical mechanical foundations of the soliton by asseting its microcanonical and canonical energies, before ultimately outlining its grand canonical ground state. These findings align with numerical computations we've conducted to analyse soliton properties in this modified Skyrme model. (This work was presented at the ICNP 2021 conference.) The presented numerical solutions represent self-dual configurations; hence, they are stable. We've documented solutions for various physical parameters in tabular form, aiming to facilitate further research into the modified Skyrme model. The mathematical proofs underpinning our analysis are presented as appendices for the benefit of the reader. The relationship between Euler-Lagrange equations and their solutions holds significance in this modified Skyrme model; understanding this connection is essential for extrapolating our findings. Imbalanced data sets where more than one minority class lacks sufficient examples pose challenges for machine learning algorithms. To tackle this issue, the majority of research focuses on methods that equalize class distribution through over-sampling or under-sampling techniques. Unlike the overwhelming majority of imbalanced data sets featuring a single minority class, we are dealing with a more complex scenario involving multiple minority classes. Through a comprehensive analysis, we evaluated several methods for increasing data samples while maintaining class purity using a multi-threaded approach. The results revealed significant improvements in performance for some methods, but they were also associated with a corresponding increase in inaccurate predictions. Ultimately, the choice of an over-sampling approach depends on the specific classification model employed. When a strong predictor is used, the general reduction in error rates follows the distribution of prior classes. On the other hand, the tightness of recovered distributions and the accuracy of the predictor are key determinants when a weak predictor is used. The source code for our research can be found at https://github.com/harsha952. Research was conducted as part of the activity report for the NLP NLPD595 course at NLU. Please note that the term 'artificial' in the research context refers to artificially created synthetic examples rather than being 'false' or incorrect. Also included with the research is some background information on the topic, which may be found in the introduction section. Analysis of research findings and their implications have been explored. Future research could involve developing a customized learning algorithm that seamlessly incorporates over-sampling techniques to expand sample sizes while maintaining class purity. Such an algorithm could be trained model-agnostic, relying on characteristics of minority classes to determine which attributes to modify and how to generate new examples within those classes. Also proposed is an alternative method for assessing data imbalance by considering not just the distribution of prior classes but also the tightness of recovered distributions. This measure, inspired by a concept used in information theory to evaluate the quality of data compression algorithms, can provide a more accurate assessment of data imbalance. Moreover, the research highlights potential drawbacks of several over-sampling techniques, suggesting areas for improvement. For example, the research notes that samples generated by Generalized distances could enhance performance by replicating existing examples, making it similar to a form of under-sampling. Similarly, the research suggests that the Random SMOTE over-sampling approach overlaps significantly with a conventional under-sampling strategy at random. By presenting these observations, the research aims to encourage future researchers to build upon existing over-sampling algorithms, leading to more efficient and balanced learning

By satisfying the angular momentum preservation criterion, the rapid multipole expansion technique avoids unphysical energy injections that might arise from unbalanced angular momentum preservation, making it suitable for applications in fields like atomic physics, where precise energy and momentum calculations are essential. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the condition for preserving both energy and angular momentum in the rapid multipole expansion of a charge current reduces to the classical energy-momentum relation for a free particle. Our work provides the complete expression for the rapid multipole expansion of a charge current, along with the corresponding Ewald summations for both position and momentum space, thereby enabling the accurate simulation and efficient computation of extended systems. The spin maser offers an intriguing combination of enhanced sensitivity and routine observation capabilities, presenting a promising detection method for weak magnetic fields and spin polarization measurements. We developed a digital alkaline $^{23}\mathrm{Na}$ maser system with improved functionality. By implementing a phase-locked loop (PLL) that directly adjusts the radio-frequency (RF) magnetic field, rather than the laser frequency, we have enhanced system stability. In addition, the use of a low-cost, high-resolution analog-to-digital converter (ADC) enables fine-tuning of Larmor precession frequencies in alkaline nuclei, offering increased system versatility. This Alkaline Na digital maser (A.D.N.A.) enables precise magnetic field measurements and serves as a sensitive detector of sodium ions' spin polarization. We demonstrate the feasibility of this design through experimental results, which include the determination of the $^{23}\mathrm{Na}$ hyperfine interaction for the alkaline gases used in this study. We believe this work will contribute to the advancement of several scientific areas, including nanomagnetism research and spin-polarized gas measurements. Moreover, we outline additional applications for the A.D.N.A. in the study of atomic spin and magnetic field detection. Building upon this concept, we propose a global network of digital atomic magnetometers, in which the existing Masers could play a pivotal role in the scientific community by increasing accessibility to this technology. A.D.N.A. has also inspired a new project focused on the development of a digital He3 detector, as described in arXiv:2109.04416.
