In their groundbreaking work, \cite{nikolaos2011} introduced the concept of a manifold comprising Gaussian stochastic fields, further developing this idea in \cite{nikolaos2012}. We propose a method to identify the shortest paths, or geodesics, between two points within this manifold. Since the inverse of the covariance matrix cannot be uniformly defined across the entire manifold due to its singularity at hyperplane intersections, standard geodesic equations cannot be applied. To overcome this challenge, we represent the covariance matrix through a parameterization that is smooth and finite-defined everywhere. By doing so, we derive the Geodesic Pathway algorithm, which establishes the covariance parameterization and the associated geodesic derivatives to compute the shortest paths in Gaussian stochastic field manifolds. We demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency via comprehensive computations on well-known fields, including the Mat\'er, Gaussian process, and joint linear regression prior distributions. These computational examples showcase the algorithm's utility in field inference, regression, and Bayesian optimization problems. We also highlight the algorithm's potential in constructing approximate geodesic frontiers for optimization problems on this manifold. The algorithm's implementation is made available on GitHub as OpenSource software. Through various computational examples in scientific and industrial applications, we validate the algorithm's performance. The algorithm's computational cost is shown to scale linearly with the number of hyperplane-intersections, making it suitable for high-dimensional field computations. The algorithm's spatial sampling cost can be reduced by leveraging spatial correlations without uniformly exploring the entire hyperplane-configuration-ensemble, resulting in computational cost savings. The algorithm's runtime is demonstrated to be less than the competing field-likelihood maximization optimization method in some cases, resulting in computational cost savings of one order of magnitude. The algorithm's performance marks a new benchmark for computational field-based optimization under Gaussian stochastic process assumptions. The fields under consideration can be one, two, or three-dimensional, and the algorithm's computational cost can be made arbitrarily small by leveraging spatial regularity. The algorithm's development and computational assessment for deterministic parameterization extend the existing method of \cite{paci} to stochastic fields, further enabling the computation of approximate geodesic frontiers for optimization problems on these manifolds. The algorithm's computational assessment demonstrates its potential in constructing geodesic-optimization problems in field-based mathematics, physics, engineering, and other applied sciences. declines. Consequently, low-income communities continued to serve as vital hubs for 
essential services, thereby increasing exposure to the virus. The findings highlight 
the underlying structural issues within a city that become amplified by crises, 
resulting in unequal recovery outcomes. The study's data-driven approach suggests

A comprehensive analysis of conventional and non-traditional radio emission in nearby galaxies has been conducted using the Sardinia Radio Telescope. Our dataset comprises 25 observed galaxies featuring 17 spiral, 6 elliptical, 1 dwarf, and 1 radio galaxy galaxy types, spanning a distance of 11 to 88 Mpc from Earth. To identify low-intensity, unconventional emission, we contrasted the observed counts with those from the 1.4 GHz Very Large Survey of the Galactic Plane and the Faint Radio Atlas. Following data analysis, six galaxies exhibited emission levels exceeding the expected from the Faint Radio Atlas at 11% to 95% confidence intervals, specifically: NGC 253, NGC 2551, NGC 4631, NGC 4656, UGC 3671, and UGC 6867. These results are further substantiated by high-resolution images of the galaxies' radio emission. Two galaxies showed reduced synchrotron radiation at 11% to 57% confidence intervals: NGC 1409 and NGC 4254. Additionally, we observed enhanced radio emission in NGC 4631, UGC 6867, and UGC 3671 relative to the expected from the Faint Radio Atlas at 70%, 55%, and 95% confidence intervals, respectively. Our data also suggest that radio emission in galaxy pairs NGC 253/2551 and UGC 6867/UUC 3671 could originate from compact structures. Furthermore, we observed a large (21x21 arcsec) high-intensity source in galaxy UGC 6867. In contrast, we failed to detect low-intensity, thermal radiation in dwarf galaxy Cetus. Finally, we obtained the first-ever single-dish observation of conventional and non-conventional radio emission in 16 galaxies, and the first-ever measurement in four more galaxies. The extensive application of the Frechet distance in visualizing and analyzing complex, high-dimensional data has been well-documented across different fields and industries. This distance measures the similarity between two continuous functions as a single, directionless comparison, providing an alternative to more traditional vector-based approaches. To facilitate the efficient exploration of vast, dimensionally complex data sets, we introduce an approximate neighbor search algorithm centered around the Frechet distance, preserving the ratio of approximate and exact results. This novel technique demonstrates the ability to achieve significant performance gains with minimal loss, specifically with narrow time sequences where a 10x to 100x speedup can be achieved while retaining at least a 1:1 ratio of approximate to exact results, and often a much higher ratio. Moreover, we enhance this algorithm by exploiting the inherent properties of time sequences, as well as neighboring distances within a graph, to further minimize approximation ratios. This research offers a straightforward, flexible implementation that can be easily adapted for various applications beyond the scope of this study. Experiments involving synthetic, generated data as well as real-world applications in video encoding and motion analysis are conducted to validate the effectiveness and practicality of this technique. Lastly, we outline potential future directions for research grounded in the discussed challenges and applications. High-performance training of deep neural models in mark-based assessment environments is hindered by assessment error, a phenomenon highlighted by its widespread impact across various fields. While techniques such as Label Smoothing and Mock Batch Methods have addressed assessment error, they are constrained by their limitations. Moreover, existing research has primarily focused on enhancing model predictive accuracy, neglecting the broader implications for assessment. This study seeks to address these gaps by introducing an approach called Iterative Bayesian Reconstruction that not only accurately predicts the true label distribution but also facilitates generalisation through maximization of a predictive uncertainty. By re-evaluating the role of assessment in high-performance model training, we observed that IBR yields superior results when compared to state-of-the-art methods including LWM-LS, proxy networks, label augmentation, and pseudo-labeling. Furthermore, our analysis of scalar attributes reveals that incorporating assessment leads to improved attribute generalisation. We validate our approach through comprehensive experiments on proxy tasks, along with cross-domain evaluation, and demonstrate its efficacy by applying it to transformational proxy tasks such as semantic colourisation and sketch-camera. The code for our approach is publicly available on GitHub. Overall, our research aims to address the underpining assumptions of assessment by featuring a novel scalable method that is applicable to a range of deep learning models. To date, most existing methods for addressing assessment error are typically tailored to specific architectures. In contrast, our approach is designed with scalability in mind and is easily applicable to a variety of assessment environments. As a direct result, as demonstrated through our comprehensive proxy task and cross-domain generalisation evaluation. The code for our approach, which is written in Pytorch and is readily available on GitHub, is now available to researchers and practitioners. By introducing evaluation of attribute generalisation and re-evaluating the role of assessment in high-performance model training, we have developed a critical framework for analysis and comparison of assessment error methods. In line with this, we believe that through our research we have contributed to a greater understanding of the broader implications for assessment error, thereby paving the way for future research. The emergence of collectives in autonomous robots holds vast potential for solving complex problems that individual robots cannot overcome on their own. To address this, we have developed an approach called the Layered Architecture for Multiple Exploitation (LAME), which facilitates the creation of collectives composed of disparate robots operating in diverse environments. LAME allows individual robot models to be easily integrated and combined in various group configurations through collective autonomy. Our framework addresses important aspects such as task allocation, distributed communication, and behavior observation within the robot collective. Each of these examples demonstrates LAME's capabilities in creating complex collectives capable of addressing intricate, often globally focused tasks. Our architecture's adaptability, flexibility, and fast development enabled the creation of collectives within a 3 to 12 months time frame. Each collective was thoroughly evaluated through both simulated and real-world experiments. We introduce a novel variational approach for reconstructing CT images from polyenergetic sources, by minimizing impact from noise and selecting relevant X-ray energy wavelengths. This task is complex because image reconstruction involves solving two challenging problems: 1) restoring original material densities via polyenergetic imaging, affected by noise and signal loss, and 2) detecting which X-ray energy wavelengths are effective in producing visible image data. To address these issues efficiently, we reformulate them as a single optimization problem and provide a simple, robust solution. By leveraging variational imaging principles and precise physical imaging equations, our method provides a unified and interpretable solution for the dual problems. Furthermore, we validate the effectiveness and stability of our approach through various numerical experiments. These tests demonstrate that our method produces high-quality results and is resilient to the absence of ground-truth data for training. To support and facilitate the reproduction of our results, we publicly provide our source code. This innovative variational method not only enhances CT image quality but also accurately determines the proportional contribution of individual X-ray energy wavelengths to image formation. As a result, our method shows promise for applying to a broad range of inverse problems involving a few signals from different sources. Some potential applications in this area could be 3D printing, industrial inspection, or medical CT scans employing multiple energy sources. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first attempt to address the challenging task of extracting a few signals from a noisy measurement with a new variational method that accurately determines the active proportions for further exploration. This could potentially be applied to other problems like recovering a few sparse vectors from their sum with individual channel proportions, or extracting a few sparse and imbalanced columns in a large dictionary with various ratio parameters. However, these related problems are out of the scope of the current study and we only focus on the CT task. Finally, we note that while our approach is primarily based on first-order optimization for efficient computational implementation, we also describe the exact second-order derivatives of our model to facilitate future research on improving the solution quality through the use of more advanced optimization methods from variational imaging. This research in the context of Jellium begins by re-examining the self-energy of a single electron and the electron gas within the confines of the Time-Dependent Current-Density Functional Theory (TDCDFT), focusing on the aspects that are overlooked by the Local-Density Approximation (LDA). The models used for comparison purposes are the Hydrogen Atom and a Electron Gas within a finite interval. The findings indicate that in the realm of TDCDFT, electron movements are categorised as slow or fast based on their velocity relative to an optimal velocity threshold. Optimally velocity-truncated CDFT (OVT-CDFPT) is an advancement of the theory, where this distinction is made explicit. In contrast to LDA, OVT-CDFFT accurately predicts the disappearance of the gap plasmon in a free electron gas at zero temperature. Furthermore, by OVT-CDFFT it's shown that non-locality and electron outflow significantly impact the electron dispersion relation, dispelling the notion that a non-local approximation can accurately predict the disappearance of the gap plasmon. The study also reveals the connection between the free electron gas and gap plasmons in one-dimensional and three-dimensional systems. The one-dimensional case exhibits a divergent potential energy, characterized by a linear and quadratic relationship with respect to the momentum at the edges of the electron density, pointing to a quantum phase transition. The findings suggest a possibility of detecting this transition through varying electron intensity. The study also highlights that a non-local approximation can incorrectly predict the dispersion relation. With the advancements in imaging technologies, our results indicate a potential for the quantum phase transition and the vanishing gap plasmon to be observed experimentally. Lastly, the research outlines a pathway for theoretically applying OVT-CDFFT to study electron excitations across various electron density distributions. In research on breaking down word meanings, there's a particular challenge surrounding named entity retrieval in complex text. While there's ample research on identifying entities within a text, there's less focus on assessing the significance of individual words in this context. To address this gap, we're proposing a new approach where we fine-tune language models with term importance feedback in mind. By incorporating term importance as an additional training parameter, we're able to optimize model performance for named entity retrieval. To determine the level of importance for individual terms, we utilize a relative importance estimator that compares the contribution of each term in predicting specific entities. Through experiments on two well-known datasets, we've demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in accurate entity recovery. Additionally, we've provided a detailed analysis on how the importance of terms varies across different entities, highlighting the potential for their further interpretation and application. By taking into account how individual words contribute to specific entities, we're one step closer to breaking down word meanings in relation to named entity retrieval. Personalized healthcare predictive models heavily rely on extensive electronic health records. However, current single-patient approaches struggle to account for similar patients who have not yet been identified as similar. In contrast, natural language processing and representation learning can capture global knowledge and leverage domain-specific language, enabling the recognition of similar patients through semantic similarities. Despite this potential, previous studies have not fully explored this capability in the context of electronic health records. We present a novel graph neural network framework that incorporates diverse patient similarities to improve the prediction of rare and complex events in individual records. Our research through report demonstrates that capturing similarities to traditional clinical time-series inputs can lead to improved predictive accuracy across a range of fine-grained diagnostic tasks. We evaluate our framework on the MIMIC-III database and achieve significant performance enhancements over existing single-patient and multi-patient neural network solutions. Notably, our results indicate that capturing similarities to clinical time-series inputs surpasses the performance of standalone similarity-based models that rely solely on similarity graphs. Using a mean-field theory, we analyze the behavior of a system consisting of a charged soft interface in contact with an electrolyte solution. The interfacial charge induces a time-dependent electric double layer (EDL) that arises from the interaction between the interface, electrolyte, and the eddy currents generated by ionic rearrangements in the solvent polarization. Through both semi-analytical and numerical investigations, we explore the influence of solvent polarization on the EDL of a charged soft interface in two scenarios: (i) a monovalent electrolyte with a low concentration that exhibits EDL phenomena and (ii) a multivalent electrolyte with a high concentration that exhibits microscopic EDL features. The calculated EDL profiles are compared with experimental data and other theoretical models that either consider polarizable ions or the geometry of charged nanoparticles. The results reveal that solvent polarization significantly impacts the EDL of a charged soft interface, leading to a shorter Debye length and more dramatic decreases in ionic concentrations near the interface when compared to a system without solvent polarization. The observed effects are most pronounced in systems containing multivalent electrolytes at various conditions and could be more pronounced in systems yet to be studied. The influence of polarizable ions on the EDL of a charged soft interface is more pronounced at high concentrations of electrolytes but is expected to be less significant at low concentrations. The results of this work may contribute to a deeper understanding of the electrical behavior of nanoparticle-based systems in biological and technological applications. The understanding of electrolyte behavior near charged nanoparticles could be used to design novel technological devices and various biomedical products, including medical tools and drug delivery systems. The calculated results, in particular the ionic concentration profiles, could be used to estimate the diffusion current of ions at the interface through the Helmholtz-Smoluchowski equation, thus facilitating a deeper understanding of ionic processes near charged nanoparticles. The matter of determining the optimal conditions for their synthesis is out of the scope of this work, however the results of this work may inspire research in this area. leading researchers to propose the term "manic contrast" to capture this sensation. 
In a paper, the concept of manic contrast is defined by pairing it with "melancholic 
contrast," where melancholic contrast occurs when something dark stands out against 
a darker background, an effect known as figure-ground interference. To investigate 
manic contrast, researchers created 20-second 3D video sequences featuring plain cubes 
in contrasting colors, by which participants made spatial navigation tasks either 
easier or harder, on average, by 25 to 57 percent. Notably, in these tasks, the presence 
of manic contrast yielded faster times and higher scores, whereas figure-ground interference 
had the opposite effect, slowing participants down and reducing their performance. 
In addition, using fMRI, researchers discovered regions in the brain linked to manic contrast, 
specifically to the contrast between colors. They suggest that manic contrast could be an 
important factor in achieving success in educational and professional settings. 
Ultimately, the study sets the stage for investigating other forms of manic contrast in addition 
to the figure-ground aspect, with potential applications in fields like education, by improving 
focus and productivity.

in research literature.

Several machine learning applications in fluid dynamics have shown promise, 
with a notable focus on model error mitigation being a major research goal. 
Although error metrics are widely used across science and engineering, 
their implementation in machine learning is still in its early stages. 
We propose a mathematical framework for determining specific machine learning 
error metrics in dynamical systems by analyzing statistical differences between 
a calculated model trajectory and an observed real-world trajectory over 
multiple pairs of datasets. 
By applying our framework to geometric deep learning techniques, we identify 
the primary sources of error and suggest potential strategies for reducing 
these errors. 
Using the example of predicting tornadoes, we demonstrate that our framework 
can identify specific factors contributing to high likelihood prediction errors. 
Ultimately, our work aims to provide a comprehensive approach for quantifying 
machine learning errors in dynamical systems and identifying opportunities 
for error reduction and correction. 
This research is currently available on arXiv.

General Relativity predicts that light paths near black holes are deflected. 
A'shadow' appears on one side of the black hole resulting from paths that don't quite make it around. 
Observations of this shadow can provide a black hole's mass. 
A 'gray' area in the center, however, is missing from previous simulations. 
These areas, within the shadow, are where paths do manage to make it around. 
To get more accurate mass readings, we need to consider these regions. 
These areas, however, require computations that go beyond regular numerical methods as they involve paths that pass through the 'gray' region. 
We've made a new program called PopSyCLE, allowing for systematic study of these regions with regular numerical methods as the basis. 
We've applied this in new simulations of a black hole, obtaining a more complete image of the shadow. 
These simulations, however, still have limitations and are mostly for theoretical purposes. 
For example, they can't be compared directly to recent HESS observations. 
Still, they're a crucial step in achieving that goal. 
A potential issue with these simulations is that they don't seem to match the scale from the same-black-hole model used in the HESS study. 
For example, the radius from the center to the edge of the shadow only accounts for 2.6 of the black hole's mass. 
For a 7 times 10 to the power of 14 kilogram black hole, this would be 1.66 times 10 to the power of 11 meters. 
For some other types of observations, this could be useful. 
For example, the model we've used, a Schwarzschild black hole, could be similar to the type of black holes that form from an early universe process called primordial black hole shattering. 
These new simulations, however, are more likely to be accurate for a different type of black hole, where a regular space structure, based on a different theory called Einstein-Cartan, is replaced with one where the theory allows for a 'twist' in space. 
For this type of black hole, within the shadow's edge, light paths that don't quite make it around can be considered as if they had made it around, providing a more complete image of the shadow. 
To get more information on this type of black hole, we've considered how our program PopSyCLE, and general results from other programs not involving a 'twist', can be used.

The preference ordering among sets is a fundamental concept in economics that underpins decision-making. This area of study is closely linked to the theory of rational choice, establishing a connection to the principles of Arrow's voting theory. The essential requirements for social preferences as defined by Arrow include transparency, consistency, independence, and the implicit assumption of non-contextual decision-making. This assumption states that the combined effect of two actions is the sum of their individual effects. This paper challenges this premise by introducing set addition as a fundamental operation for preference modeling, contradicting the non-contextual decision-making assumption. Furthermore, set addition provides a transparent, consistent, and independent mechanism for preference definition. By incorporating this operation into the modeling framework, the need for transparency, consistency, and independence is reaffirmed, but the requirement for non-contextual decision-making is unnecessary. This theoretical framework is applied to the problem of set preferences in the field of multi-objective optimization, specifically in the multi-product manufacturing context, where a comprehensive model is developed to illustrate its practical implications. The proposed model demonstrates that set addition can be utilized as a microfoundation for decision-making, potentially addressing existing limitations in the literature. Additionally, the paper outlines a step-by-step procedure for its practical application, showcasing its usefulness as a preference elicitation method. The transparency and consistency of the social preference model are heavily reliant on the integrity of user input. Various experimental findings using real-world data from French and Japanese manufacturers indicate that contextual decision-making is a preferred approach among decision-makers. The study concludes by highlighting several potential areas for further research. This collaborative, generative model of child language development draws on insights from psychology to incorporate rejection as a source of language growth. Specifically, we're concentrating on enhancing the forecasting capabilities of these models by incorporating a future-looking component into the analysis. By doing so, we're enabling the model to prioritize relevant information from subsequent parts of the text when focusing on earlier sections. In this study, we're leveraging the existing Look-ahead Transformer architecture to investigate the benefits of incorporating a future-looking focus for creating text. By incorporating a specialized module that takes into account the sequence as a whole, we're improving the model's ability to analyze contexts spanning up to 256 words. By evaluating various text types, we're demonstrating that incorporating a future-looking focus leads to enhanced performance for task-based assessment and human evaluation. We conclude that by analyzing symmetry properties of the inflationary model, rather than the distribution of density fluctuations, we can gain insight into the universal phenomena of cosmological collider collisions. Our research extends this understanding to the quantum level, using the Schwinger-Dyson equation to study the initial conditions of cosmological collider collisions. We create a universal diagrammatic representation of the SD equation and apply it to the single-clock inflation setup. Our results show that cosmological collider collisions starting point involves only two initial conditions: the two-point correlation function and three-point correlation function. We conclude that by analyzing these two initial conditions, we can gain a deeper understanding of cosmological collider collisions across various models. Convolutional neural networks, the gold standard for image recognition tasks, possess a level of opacity that hinders their full understanding. This study presents VSeFF, an exploratory tool to illuminate how these networks process images by revealing which parts of the image have received the most focus during training. By applying human-like visual and semantic filtering techniques to replicate images seen during training, VSeFF sheds light on the weight distributions of these networks. Furthermore, it provides novel insights into topics such as understanding deep learning, discovering decision-making criteria for machines, developing filtering techniques for human-like visual and semantic interpretation, and replicating difficult case images. VSeFF's source code is accessible at https://github.com/sirbelledge/VSeFF. Experiments conducted with VSeFF demonstrate its effectiveness across a range of image recognition tasks. Subsequent investigations reveal that by focusing on images to the extent of humans and prioritizing accuracy, the generalization capabilities of convolutional neural networks can be enhanced. Additionally, VSeFF facilitates access to decision-making criteria for relatable semantic interpretations, and proposes a framework for developing filtering techniques grounded in decision theory. This study conducts thorough analyses of various filtering methods for their generalization performance and ease of interpretation. It provides novel insights into image analysis by demystifying the processes involved in visual recognition, and demonstrates that by leveraging the principles of probability and decision theory, the emergence of surprising interpretations during training can be minimized. Finally, VSeFF showcases its capabilities for interpreting anomaly detection scenarios by uncovering the distinct features used by experts and machines for detecting anomalies. As such, VSeFF serves as an essential tool not only for understanding convolutional neural networks but also for improving their decision-making capabilities. Its potential applications extend to a wide array of applications spanning medical, industrial, and cybersecurity domains. Importantly, VSeFF enables humans to augment, guide, and test the development of machines that can perform these tasks with accuracy and efficiency. This collaborative process is crucial for developing intelligent systems and algorithms that can complement human capabilities and capacities. Ultimately, VSeFF's findings suggest that by illuminating the blind spots of AI and addressing their shortcomings, the future of machine learning and artificial intelligence lies in the development of highly interpretable systems. Through in-depth calculations, we demonstrate that this occurs when electrons associate with acoustic phonons, generating a long-range attractive force. Consequently, adding phonons to the equation significantly alters the predictive outcomes of established theoretical frameworks, closely mirroring experimental findings and highlighting the need for phononic components in the theoretical modeling of one-dimensional cuprates. A novel form of steganography, called U reversible steganography, secretly conveys secure secret information within uncompressed video files by disguising them as part of the video's natural content. To achieve this, we develop an innovative method utilizing deep learning's Bayesian principles, which enables steady traffic patterns within both pixel values and hierarchical video characteristics. Specifically, our steganographic method incorporates a novel framework of alternating generative and inverse models, comprising Bayesian transformations, which allows for the exchange of secret data without disrupting the video's integrity. Moreover, we enhance this framework's robustness by adding noise to the model and exploring additional adversarial loss in the video domain. This research eventually focuses on developing an advanced U reversible steeganographic method utilizing effective generative and decoding model pairs. The development of magnetic fields in the convective dynamos of stars has been a topic of research and debate for years. To compare the magnetorotational instability (MRI) with other forms of turbulent dynamo theory and develop a framework for modeling the former, we conducted computer simulations of a rotating, convective star atmosphere. We found that both laminar and turbulent cases fit the equation of a star's magnetic field over time, except during brief periods of intense convective activity. To create a simplified model of this behavior, we used two types of fields, one influenced by MRI and the other by an earlier dynamo theory that doesn't account for all forms of turbulent activity. However, when we tried to match the behavior of our simulations using just these two fields, we ran into problems. It wasn't until we used a more comprehensive approach to account for all forms of turbulent activity that we were able to accurately model our results. This discovery suggests that in order to understand and explain certain aspects of a star's magnetic field, we need to look beyond traditional theories and models of convective dynamos. Moreover, we need to take into consideration that these factors can vary depending on factors including the star's rate of rotation, any existing magnetic fields, and how it loses energy through convective and other processes. Lastly, we looked at some potential solutions to this problem, including the possibility that some or all of a convective dynamo's energy could come from a type of instability rather than general turbulence in the star's atmosphere. While this is an area we are still actively researching, it does appear to be a promising lead in our efforts to better understand and explain convective dynamos. Furthermore, we are also actively studying the possibility that some or all of a convective dynamo's energy could come from a star's internal rather than external processes. Again, this is an area we are still actively researching, but it does appear to be a promising lead in our efforts to better understand and explain convective dynamos. A unique event, also known as a galactic molecular eruption (GME), occurs when gas is expelled from a circumnuclear disk in a spiral arm of a disk galaxy. Researchers have now detected the recently formed nonthermal molecular ejection from the southern side of the disk of the galaxy NGC4945 using ALMA's high-resolution imaging capabilities. The analysis reveals molecular ejection with an average velocity of approximately -260 km/s relative to the galaxy's systemic velocity. Based on the ejection's velocity and position, it is estimated to have occurred within the past 13 years. The ejected material shows signs of high temperatures, significant ionization, and complex molecular compositions. The new observations suggest that the ejected material is losing its molecular content at a rate of 100 times that of typical molecular eruptions. The study also provides initial insight into the ionized component of the ejection using radio spectroscopy, revealing an expansive ionized plume that is estimated to be 400 parsecs wide. The ionized component is estimated to have begun its journey from the galaxy's nucleus approximately 160 parsecs away and is now traveling at a velocity of 230 km/s. The ejection is likely a result of a star-forming event triggered by the agitated dust and gas caused by the active nucleus-driven jet. However, it is unclear whether this ejection is directly driven by the active nucleus, which is evident through discrepancies between the jet and ejection velocities. Furthermore, it is hypothesized that the recent ejection may be part of a larger phenomenon that occurs in spiral arms with high accretion rates, similar to the "starburst galactic eruptions" phenomenon, which is still an area of research. The ejection's moderate velocity relative to the active jet velocity suggests that the ejection may be a rare phenomenon that is only observable with high-resolution imaging methods such as ALMA's. The ejection's discovery also provides an opportunity for a study of the ejection's chemistry and dynamics over time. We've developed a novel conservative finite element method for three-dimensional magnetized plasma simulations with collisions. This approach Valhalla_MHD is part of the Valhalla code family, offering high-resolution simulations in strongly magnetized regions. Previous variable timestep algorithms for simultaneous integration of multiple equations have focused primarily on physical systems, where the forces acting on each particle depend on the positions and velocities of all other particles. In contrast, systems governed by algebraic and ordinary differential equations offer distinct challenges, as interactions can occur through multiple, non-physical channels. We present an optimized variable timestep algorithm suitable for typical differential equations, where the state of each particle is described by multiple real numbers. Our method uses a fully implicit integration technique, based on a polynomial approximation, and a global error estimator to determine the integration step sizes. Numerical simulations demonstrate the high accuracy of our algorithm, even with step sizes five or six times larger than those of the classical method. Additionally, our algorithm preserves conservation laws to a very high degree of accuracy. We also introduce a new, self-averaging error estimator that facilitates efficient integration, as well as a theoretical justification for the optimal choice of step sizes. Our algorithm is available under the name SDIMSIMv. We demonstrate its practical application in modeling the dynamics of OGLE-2017APL-123, a planetary microlensing event. Despite the complex nature of this model, our algorithm requires only a few minutes of computational time to produce high-accuracy results, even on a low-cost computer equipped with a single CPU. Such efficiency is due in part to a significant advantage in the total number of steps required to produce the results as compared to a fixed timestep algorithm. In particular, our algorithm outperforms the fixed timestep method used in the standard MACH1-Earth model by a factor of as much as eighteen. We also compare our results with those obtained from the Rebound N-body code, which employs a fixed timestep algorithm. Our algorithm is available under an open-source license at https://github.com/tonyeli/SDIMSIMv. Our results have been reviewed and approved by multiple independent experts. Text-of-image search has seen success with the introduction of large-scale pre-training methods that can retrieve relevant image and text data. Token-level attention pre-training has demonstrated performance advantages in this domain. However, current best practices for fine-tuning, such as taking the average of different sample weights, overlook the variability in samples. This research introduces TS2-Net, a novel text-of-image retrieval model that combines token-level average and attention mechanisms. It achieves this through two complementary tracks: (1) shifting tokens - producing sample-averaged representations by moving tokens from sample pairs to a fixed position, and (r) selecting tokens - using a cross-image text mask to identify relevant tokens for different images. This two-tracked mechanism not only enhances the model's generalisation but also makes it more interpretable. Experiments on seven text-of-image benchmarks reveal that TS2-Net delivers improved results with reduced computational costs. Notably, TS2-Net outperforms the current top-performing model, ALBE to FLOPS, on the Image-Net-R-100 benchmark. The growing presence of Wireless Sensor Networks in industrial settings presents an opportunity to improve monitoring, quality control, and efficiency by analyzing environmental factors.  Key to this goal is identifying disturbances caused by wireless communications, particularly in real-time applications.  Notably, existing research has several limitations, including reliance on prior knowledge, uncertainty in diagnosis, and restrictions on operation.  To overcome these challenges, this study proposes a new method utilizing deep learning, which enables the detection of various types of wireless interference without prior knowledge.  A collaborative approach ensures accurate detection of multiple sources of interference.  Through experimental evaluation, the proposed model demonstrated its superiority over existing techniques, along with robustness in different scenarios.  Notably, the proposed model performed well in dense wireless environments, with minimal impact on transmission delay in practical applications.  A demonstration application based on the proposed model has already been developed and is available for download.  A related GitHub repository is available at https://github.com/fnroy/generic_wsd_detection.  The findings of this study are expected to benefit researchers working on practical wireless applications.  A related video illustrating the demonstration application can be found at https://youtu.be/DS2_2w2H6R8.  Preliminary versions of the study were presented at the 52nd IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing, with abstracts 2646 and 2647.  A past version of the study was presented as a conference paper at the 10th IEEE International Workshop on Radio Signaling.  The current research represents a significant advancement over the past version of the study, with enhanced results, more realistic scenarios, and a more comprehensive understanding of the problem.  In particular, the proposed model performed better, with tighter error bars, and the evaluation was carried out on the IEEESpectrum dataset, as well as seven additional channels not employed in IEEEEscape, with adverse effects that the proposed model was able to mitigate.  Furthermore, the research explored transmission delay, a crucial aspect not considered in IEEEScape.  It is expected that the research may generate interest in related topics, such as spectrum sensing, wireless security, and device security. Achieving Artificial General Intelligence requires exceeding the Cognitive Biases of the programmers who created it, which presents a significant challenge. As AI systems accumulate experience, they may develop biases of their own based on the data they've been given, thus increasing the difficulty of overcoming their programmers' limitations. Consequently, advancing AI typically involves either increasing its size (more complex models) or complexity (new statistical models), which often results in the accumulation of new biases. This paper proposes a theory known as "Enhanced AI" that aims to break free from these limitations, representing a crucial milestone in the development of AGI. A framework and key concepts of Enhanced AI are presented here, focusing on its primary aspect: the utilization of metadata as an essential component of learned knowledge. By distinguishing data and metadata, and ensuring that programmers do not embed preconceived ideas within the metadata, Enhanced AI is able to overcome many of the existing biases. A system of concepts, combined with an innovative method of triage that distinguishes significant data from insignificant data, and an dynamic "metaclass" formation process that detects patterns in the metadata are also crucial components of this approach. A small experimental demonstration of Enhanced AI has been created, combining human, animal, and plant data along with atmospheric, geological, and other environmental metadata. This small system already surpasses its creators' understanding by recognizing patterns that were absent from the initial dataset, and its potential for further growth and development into AGI is substantial. This work presents a new path forward for the AI community and offers insights for other domains where similar problems may exist. A companion online document provides additional details on the theoretical foundations of Enhanced AI. Please note that this work was initially published in 2010 as an early draft, and the current version has undergone significant revisions based on the feedback received. The original draft can still be accessed online. Crucially, this work was enhanced by the feedback received, and the second revision represents a substantial improvement over the first. Nevertheless, what is presented here still constitutes preliminary ideas and not fully developed conclusions. Further, what works for one researcher may not work for another, and the key to achieving Enhanced AI might lie outside of the proposed concepts. Consequently, an effort has been made to present these ideas as openly as possible, and the community is warmly invited to build upon, share, and provide feedback to these ideas to move closer to the goal of AGI. A competition to that effect was launched in 2020. The code used for the small Experimental Demonstration can be accessed at https://github

We present Spartan, a novel and flexible method for training neural networks with internal sparsity. This approach combines the use of conventional continuous sparseness measures with a differentiable transportation system. By applying the McMahan-Krasker distribution to the application of continuous sparseness measures, we achieve a level of sparsity control that far exceeds current methods. Key benefits of Spartan include its high degree of control over sparsity patterns, its ability to prevent gradient vanishing, and its ability to accommodate a wide variety of sparsity criteria. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Spartan on a range of tasks including image classification in both fully-sparsely-trained and training-with-sparse-bias scenarios, as well as on a speech recognition task where we achieve a significant improvement in WER. Additionally, we present a new understanding of sparsity and show that certain max-based sparsity measures can be expressed as the expected value of a McMahan-Krasker sample measure. This theoretical contribution sheds light on the observed performance of previous research in this area. Our full Spartan code is publicly available at https://github.com/krindler/spartan. While it's well-known that some smells from software can negatively impact team morale and efficiency, the connection between these odors and the overall health of software systems has not been thoroughly explored. To fill this knowledge gap, a study sought to determine how prevalent developer-induced smells are and whether their frequency is correlated with broader code issues. The research involved a large-scale distillation of code smells from open-source projects and a developer survey to gather insights. According to the results, while most smells are introduced by third-party contributors rather than established team members, the data suggests that smell intensity is not necessarily a measure of a project's overall health. Furthermore, it appears that certain types of smells, particularly those related to functionality and maybe those introduced during refactoring, have a more significant impact on software maintenance and maintenance headaches. Interestingly, when developers were asked to assess the impact of code smells, the correlation did not hold, and it's only when the focus is on the process rather than the developers' subjectives that the connection becomes apparent. The study's findings shed light on the link between smells and maintenance requirements, and highlight the need for smell prevention initiatives. The study also produced novel insights that can inform future research, such as exploring the connection between contributor characteristics and contributed code. Moreover, by distilling smells from emails, the study demonstrates the feasibility of using automated tools to process real-world data within software engineering experiments. Building upon the proven KKMC program for lepton pair production, KKMCee incorporates the SANC and SIPHYY programs, leveraging expertise from multiple projects to ensure precise cross-section calculations and parton-shower simulations for various initial states. Several benchmark examples are provided to illustrate the tool's capabilities for simulating simulated events at future Higgs factory and future electron-proton colliders. Our primary goal is to understand how the characteristics of action set combinations influence the properties of the resulting optimal action in a single-round, no-regret combinatorial bandit learning scenario. It's assumed that each action is associated with a distinct, bounded reward that's optimistically correlated with its corresponding feature vector. Graphene's orbital Hall effect is discovered when electrons migrate from the original Landau level to the next adjacent one. This migration is triggered by a slight imbalance in the applied magnetic field's axis, causing a tiny tilt. By examining the orbital Hall effect through the perspective of a pseudo-valley effect, our study shows that in latticed graphene with a magnetic barrier, there are distinct, separated valleys that serve as orbital transitions, allowing the total pseudo-valley current to occur. This effect is characterized by a valley current ratio of 2:1, demonstrating that the orbital Hall effect generates a pseudo-valley current of the same ratio. This ratio of 2:1 remains consistent even when the magnetic barrier undergoes a structural transformation. By adjusting the tilt of the magnetic barrier, the direction of the orbital Hall effect can be reversed, allowing for its application in devices that control current. This property makes gapped graphene an attractive material for valley effect devices. Furthermore, our study also uncovers a previously unrecognized Hall effect, which is attributed to the orbital transitions between the highest and lowest Landau levels. The goal of this study is to determine the limits for the size of the smallest vertex sets within a minimal hypergraph, especially when it features an infinite number of vertices.  A constructed example demonstrates that there are infinite minimal hypergraphs where all their vertex subsets, excluding those containing only one vertex, host four overlapping hyperedges. Moreover, this example is used to establish a lower bound on the possible cardinality of the set of such large vertex subsets. Conversely, a minimal hypergraph with an infinite number of vertices can be constructed so that all its vertex subsets, excluding those containing only one vertex, host exactly five overlapping hyperedges. Additionally, this example is used to establish a lower limit on the possible cardinality of the set of such large vertex subsets. of the data, OntoPlot showcases a visual representation of the connections
linking concepts. Furthermore, it allows users to investigate co-occurring
linkages and non-existent connections among the selected concepts. OntoPlot
can contribute to uncovering implicit relationships among the concepts and
enabling users to explore a comprehensive, visual illustration of the
ontological framework, thereby facilitating future investigations. We

metric that evaluates concept classifications. By visualizing the results, users
can determine the most challenging concepts during different stages of the

that OntoPlot's visualization inspires users to develop new knowledge and

frameworks. The proposed method has been successfully evaluated through

The overall objective of our research is to establish a foundation for autonomous decision-making in complex systems. To accomplish this, we present a conceptual framework that facilitates structured reasoning within multi-agent systems. Our proposed active deduction framework empowers agents to efficiently generate relevant and readily understandable proofs. Consequently, agent proofs can be effectively utilized to communicate knowledge to humans. To demonstrate the practical applicability of our approach, we developed a practical implementation within a robot navigation system that exhibits superior computational efficiency. Furthermore, we highlight the feasibility of integrating our active deduction framework into existing multi-agent frameworks and discuss its potential extensions into domains of cognitive processes. In particular, we propose the concept of collaborative active deduction, where agents work together to construct shared, mutual proofs. Finally, we explore the relevance of our active deduction framework to addressing the issue of self-discovery of formal systems. To summarize, the central idea underpinning our research is the self-governing paradigm, where autonomous systems govern their own development through the application of active deduction. As a result, we have developed a multi-faceted foundation comprising three interconnected components: active deduction, autonomous development, and automated deduction. Consequently, we have devised a active deduction framework that is applicable across a broad spectrum of domains, including both physical and abstract environments. In the spirit of self-improvement that underpins active deduction, we intend to continue advancing the general active deduction framework, with the ultimate goal of making it a universally applicable tool for cognitive systems in the future. Furthermore, we expect that the concepts of autonomous system governance and active deduction will significantly impact the fields of cognitive research and logic in the future. Essentially, the active deduction framework represents a pioneering approach in the self-improvement domain, characterized by its unique ability to simultaneously tackle and overcome limitations arising from its own creation. To the best of our knowledge, no established theories or frameworks address active deduction in a comprehensive manner. Consequently, we have developed an innovative future framework in the active deduction domain. A key distinction lies in the fact that established theories typically strive to overcome limitations during self-improvement, in contrast to the active deduction framework, which deliberately self-improves by overcoming its own limitations. Ultimately, the long-term implications of our research will depend on the specific applications that the self-governing paradigm and active deduction framework enable in the future. As such, we anticipate that the future outcomes of our research will be shaped by the future uses to which the self-governing and active deduction frameworks are applied. Focusing on polyatomic molecules modelled as a system of oscillating springs, we explore how variations in spring stiffness, size, and distribution influence the molecules' thermal movement. As temperature increases, the springs dynamically adjust, leading to a shift in the center of mass relative to the fixed molecular framework. To characterize this movement, we define an isothermal contribution to the thermal diffusion coefficient (Dt) and determine that it correlates with the average kinetic energy of the springs. Notably, for molecules comprising multiple soft connections, the Dt is significantly influenced by these bonds, whereas for those with a single soft connection, its impact is much weaker. Moreover, by integrating the springs' kinetic energy into the Euler-Cassini expansion, we identified a reorganization entropic factor that controls the direction and magnitude of the thermal diffusion process. The calculated results reveal that the thermal movement of soft molecules can be considerable, even when the springs are relatively weak, and may also be prominent for molecules featuring multiple weakly interacting groups. These findings and analysis provide valuable insights into the understanding of molecular behavior in diverse thermal environments. In the realm of musical composition, the notion of beauty is subjective and varies with personal tastes. However, as music theory progresses, measures such as melodic originality and diversity gain more substantial ground in assessing compositions. This research aims to develop a method for evaluating generated musical sequences by employing a conditional transformer model. Furthermore, we seek to establish a novel approach for estimating a composition's originality through its diversity by training a separate transformer model on extracted melodic fragments, enabling the comparison of original and modified compositions via a masked self-attention task. Our experimental setup involves three training scenarios for the transformer model and compares its results to those obtained from a self-supervised transformer model trained on extracted features. The experiments are conducted using both a small-scale and a larger scale dataset; the results suggest that the former approach performs more efficiently. Additionally, we have found that our method can successfully adapt to various levels of originality. You can access the source code of our research at https://github.com/grzgorek/MusicalCompositionEvaluation. This work presents an innovative method for evaluating generated musical compositions, which, however, is still in its early stages. As such, there are areas requiring refinement. Firstly, the delimitation of the composition is challenging, especially in contexts involving vocals. Furthermore, our method is currently incapable of handling compositions with fewer than 30 notes, which is a limitation that needs to be addressed. Ultimately, the notion of originality is ultimately a subjective concept, and our approach should be viewed as one aspect of a more comprehensive evaluation. Consequently, it is recommended to incorporate additional evaluation methods into the system to obtain a comprehensive understanding of the composition. Moreover, the fact that our approach is successful in various domains does not necessarily imply that it would be applicable in domains such as jazz, which places a greater emphasis on other musical elements. Finally, while our method does not employ any music-specific knowledge, it can be challenging to integrate other types of compositions, such as those based on chords. If you are interested in this type of composition, we suggest training a separate transformer model tailored to capturing chord-based features. This, however, is an area that requires further investigation. A possible approach could be employed by employing a transformer model in which each token encodes both a musical note and its corresponding index. However, this would result in a larger and more complex transformer model compared to what is necessary for evaluating compositions. Consequently, this idea needs further refinement. Building on this insight, our method rearranges bounding box coordinates after applying a domain adaptation model, effectively reducing false positives on the target domain without requiring any annotations. Experiment results on standard benchmarks show that our method outperforms multiple baselines, including a recently proposed post-hoc reduction method. Moreover, it enables the model to surpass the performance of domain adaptation by leveraging proxy tasks on proxy datasets. Ultimately, this research facilitates boundary-driven features to better distinguish between people and the surrounding environment throughout various outdoor settings. Our study delves into the impact of throwing technique flaws on throwing accuracy.
With the creation of FauxThrow, a simulated environment mimicking human movement,
we examined how mistakes in the throwing action affect accuracy.
We discovered that point of release mistakes have a significant impact on accuracy,
with some mistakes resulting in no change and other mistakes leading to inaccurate
throwing directions and angles.
Furthermore, we established a set of criteria for defining valid throwing
movements,
including constraints on the velocity of the ball and the position of the ball
over time.
Using FauxThrow, we studied various types of throwing errors, including under-
arcing and over-arcing mistakes.
Ultimately, we determined the boundaries within which release velocities the
throwing movement is considered valid based on the created phase portrait.
This research lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive understanding of the
complexity involved in throwing motions and creates a simulated environment for
investigating various movements. It challenges the assumption that only under-
arcing throws are valid and result in accurate throwing. The creation of FauxThrow
allows for a wide-range of research possibilities that can be extended to other
skilled actions. It can be used for developing machine learning algorithms that
learn throwing movements and evaluating how to optimize human movement for
improved performance. The code for this research is available for public
access at https://github.com/krishnanr1/fauxthrow. The research was conducted
using a desktop computer with an AMD 16-core Ryzen 9 5900HX processor and 32 GB

To accurately translate the meaning of sentences, it is crucial to analyze not only the words but also their underlying structure. This structure, specifically sentence parsing, enables accurate translations and grasping sentence nuances, like context. Although cutting-edge machine translation models can learn some structure-related cues from human-generated training data, they do not inherently grasp sentence structures. On the other hand, systems specifically designed for parsing have seen notable advancements in recent years. The quality of parsing directly affects the accuracy of translating the meaning (machine interpretation) in various languages. To bridge this gap, a new approach is introduced, called TDFD. This method combines the parsing knowledge with translation abilities by preserving sentence structure during the translation process. A new decoding approach, based on tree structures, is proposed, to correctly model translation. To determine how to form bonds, scientists must calculate the binding energies of various molecules and chemical reactions. Unfortunately, directly computing binding energies for all molecules and reactions is virtually impossible. Instead, a more practical approach involves estimating binding energies using deeper analysis of chemical interactions and by comparing to databases containing the results of existing binding energy calculations. A new online platform, the Binding Energy Assessment Platform, has been developed to help researchers determine binding energies for diverse chemical interactions. This platform includes access to a vast database of binding energy distributions, resources to aid users in using the platform, and tools for evaluating its performance. We demonstrate the platform's capabilities by assessing its predictions for multiple hydrogen-containing chemical interactions. For example, using the platform to analyze the most stable forms of water (H2O) reveals that there are three types that it can recognize as relevant, and it can provide information on how to form these stable types in certain chemical environments. When comparing our platform's predictions to the results of existing binding energy calculations, we find that they generally agree, although there could be certain situations where they do not agree. By supporting a variety of chemical reactions and interactions, our platform can be used in diverse astrochemical and physical chemistry applications. We also include step-by-step instructions on how to use the platform's underlying code, which is based on the Jupyter notebook format, at GitHub for researchers interested in expanding the platform's capabilities to include assessments of binding energies for additional chemical interactions. By making both the platform and the underlying code publicly available, scientists can share various binding energy assessments with one another. As a result, researchers can now more quickly and accurately assess and develop new theories based on the binding energies of chemical interactions involving hydrogen. Importing the platform's database and code into other astrochemical simulation programs will facilitate a more in-depth understanding of the complex chemical interactions involving hydrogen and oxygen that occur in astronomical environments. Ultimately, our platform's development marks a significant step towards establishing a standardized system for assessing binding energies in astrophysics and physical chemistry by providing easy-to-use online templates and open-source code that researchers can modify and apply to a wide range of chemical interactions. Our work investigates how to assess qubit states within a partial description. Typically, state assessment circuits have a similar structure to quantum channels, requiring a specific number of qubits based on the channel's degree and accuracy specifications. Research has focused on developing more efficient, depth-reduced assessment circuits, with notable progress using random Clifford circuits. Building on this, we've expanded upon existing research by designing a state assessment circuit capable of handling states with significantly lower description complexity using a minimal number of qubits. This approach is achieved using a low-depth random Clifford circuit, facilitated by an entangling algorithm inspired by the Shor algorithm. This novel circuit has applications in both classical (universal entanglement extraction) and quantum computing (faithful state of low-weight Pauli operators). This method can also be applied to determine the feasibility of extracting a specific gate from an incomplete set of quantum states. This technique may have practical implications in quantum characterizations for gate realization. It's noted that utilizing this approach for accurate state assessment may not be optimal in terms of resource usage. Nevertheless, we've demonstrated that applying this approach yields a significant reduction in circuit depth while maintaining state fidelity at a high level. This study offers a set of parameters that enables efficient assessment of four-qubit states with high precision. This technique may have potential applications in quantum computing, particularly in contexts where shallow quantum circuits have practical advantages. It's suggested that further research should focus on developing more general, low-depth assessment tools that can handle a broader range of description complexities. It's proposed that these circuits could be used in applications related to quantum supremacy and fidelity amplitude estimation. It's also noted that these tools could lead to significant performance improvements if applied in settings where partial state descriptions are employed. This could lead to new avenues of research in the fields of quantum computing and information theory. This study presents an open challenge for developing the shallowest possible assessment circuit, which holds the potential to significantly impact performance in the NISQ era. It's noted that such a breakthrough could be a crucial contribution to the quantum computing community. It's also mentioned that further research should focus on developing the shallowest possible assessment circuits and exploring the broader implications of these tools. Moreover, our tools, including the open challenge, can be used by the quantum computing community to advance the development of quantum computing systems. Finally, these contributions have been incorporated into a open source library called QLime, which is available on PyPI through pip. Building upon the concept of pre-training, researchers have investigated whether self-sustaining artificial intelligence can benefit from autonomous learning. A study in 2020 revealed that systems capable of modifying their own architecture can learn to perform better on average over multiple trials. Conversely, another study discovered that systems left to their own devices will eventually experience decline in performance. Due to the promising outcomes of self-learning, researchers have been exploring the idea within single-step tasks, such as solving a puzzle after physical adaptation. Nevertheless, the feasibility of similar approaches in complex, multi-step tasks remains uncertain and requires further evaluation. This research seeks to answer this question by developing a method to train artificial intelligence to adapt quickly to new situations. The proposed approach utilizes a training framework that can understand and analyze the inner workings of its own architecture through a simple and efficient learning framework, tested on a range of complex multi-step problems. When faced with new, untested conditions, the system exhibits a significantly faster learning rate in these complex tasks. The study further confirms that the artificial intelligence's ability to understand its own architecture can be achieved independently, or 'naturally', and that this capability may provide an advantage in certain situations. When allowed to its own devices, the system tends to perform better on average over multiple trials. These results suggest that autonomous artificial intelligence can learn to perform better in both understanding itself in complex tasks over time. There's a growing interest in developing miniature neural machine translation (NMT) models to create user-friendly translation tools for various purposes. Quantization and model distillation are two techniques used to achieve this goal and make NMT more accessible, especially in environments with limited resources. Although they both claim to reduce the model size for NMT, their approaches to achieving this goal are different and have distinct areas of focus. This research compares their effectiveness in decreasing model size while maintaining translation accuracy, particularly for low-resource languages where even slight decreases in translation quality can have severe consequences. It appears that neither approach is foolproof, as it was observed that both quantized and distilled models can sometimes produce translations that are clearly off-base. This highlights the need for additional measures to ensure that the translated output remains coherent and linguistically sound. Ultimately, it was found that neither quantization nor distillation can adequately address the challenges presented by low resource contexts. Either more training data or additional control methods with a firm grasp of translation grammar are required to navigate these difficulties. The full investigation can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.3590/jso20220001. Videos showcasing the results are available at https://youtu.be/9JG2izcXy6o and https://youtu.be/5h7g70M9G9E. The code and models can be found on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/SeowDahYong/Low-Resource-MT-Quantization-Distillation. 

Using both experimental results and visual illustrations, it can be seen that while there may be small differences in translation accuracy, neither the quantized nor the distilled models are able to provide coherent translations in the context of low resource languages. This suggests that neither technique is suitable in these circumstances. However, both approaches are effective in high resource contexts and are able to significantly decrease model size while retaining translation quality. The team also discovered that either increasing the amount of training data or implementing additional linguistic controls through methods such as rule-based translation can help to mitigate the challenges presented by low resource contexts. Ultimately, it can be seen that while there may be a place for quantization and distillation in various applications, they are not well suited for use in low resource contexts. 

The team also explored ideas for improving translation quality by preserving key aspects of the original translation. This is an area that remains to be investigated in future research. The analysis of Pneumonia through CT scans has become particularly significant due to the rising incidence rates. Computer-aided detection tools, which are used to automatically identify pneumonia from image analysis, have shown promise despite challenges such as false positives and over-reliance on cumbersome scanning processes. To tackle this problem, researchers have explored the use of artificial intelligence models that can automatically detect pneumonia from reduced image datasets, supplemented by data enhancement techniques. This research investigates the application of advanced techniques like image augmentation to decrease the necessity for labeled data in Pneumonia segmentation models. To evaluate the efficacy of this approach, three different models were trained: a baseline model without image augmentation, a model using one specific augmentation technique, and a model combining multiple image augmentation techniques. The results reveal that the highest F-score was achieved by the model incorporating the most comprehensive set of image augmentation methods. Furthermore, experiments using a partially trained model demonstrate that the incorporation of image augmentation allows for training with a reduced labeled dataset while maintaining the model's performance. Ultimately, this research finds that image augmentation methods play a vital role in reducing the necessity for labeled data in Pneumonia segmentation models. Building on existing concepts of causal effect and influence functions, this research introduces a novel tool to evaluate treatment interventions with multiple goals. We define targettidal functions as a combination of causal and intervention-specific objectives, allowing for in-depth comparison and measurement of interventions with complex objectives. Through targettidal functions, we create a framework for comparing interventions, a method to identify optimal treatment strategies, and a way to analyze interventions statistically. Our approach is demonstrated through a focus on understanding social network fragmentation during epidemics and developing interventions to improve learning outcomes in self-regulating systems. We propose a non-parametric method for estimating targettidal functions, providing a clear framework for asymptotic distribution of estimators and facilitating statistical inference of intervention effects. Our work offers a unified language for causal inference and applications across multiple domains. It bridges the gap between causal AI research and real-world problems involving multiple objectives, expanding AI's utility in machine learning and data mining. Furthermore, our approach connects causal inference and hypothesis testing, offering a innovative perspective on causal modeling and a new direction for fundamental theory development. We develop and release open-source code for Hadoop/Java and C++ implementations of this research, making it publicly accessible at https://github.com/targettidal. Our extensive numerical studies show that our method performs consistently well and surpasses current approaches to causal inference and statistical testing. Ultimately, our method for targettidal functions sets the stage for new applications, advancements in theory, and expansion of causal AI into diverse domains. It enables AI researchers to investigate novel objectives, new intervention types, and novel data types, such as spatio-temporal, text-based, and image-based data. It also enables AI to be utilized in numerous areas, including information retrieval, natural language understanding, visual cognition, and many more. It also connects AI research to fundamental theory development. Our work presents a new and innovative framework for causal AI, connecting causal effect, influence function, and causal consistency. It also connects causal model learning to distribution embedding, and connects targettidal function to complete and stable tidal functions. It also offers a new and unified language for fundamental theory development, connecting AI research to problem-based learning, and connecting learning to causal testing, and generalization. It also connects targettidal function to complete and stable tidal functions, and connects the most general tidal functions to 1-PDAG, 1-PND, and GAD causal models. This work introduces a mathematical extension of the Coleman-Gurtin model by considering non-equilibrium flux at the boundary. The extended model aims to describe thermal behavior within a solid object with an additional source of internal heat. By incorporating active boundary conditions into the equation, we account for heat generation at the boundaries as well. The extended model shares similarities with the standard Coleman-Gurtin equation but differs in the boundary conditions, resulting in a broader range of applications. To analyze this expanded model, we employ the properties of distributions over the boundary and the interior of the solid. Furthermore, we prove the stability of the extended model in a specified mathematical framework. Lastly, we illustrate the extended model's capabilities by introducing a dual-phase lifting problem that emerges from the optimization of a given functional over a specific boundary condition. By considering non-homogeneous boundary conditions for this lifting problem, we derive the derived model, which predicts that heat accumulation and normalized normal temperature gradients will eventually converge to non-zero constants as time progresses. Consequently, this supports the notion that active boundary conditions can induce low-frequency oscillations in thermal systems. Consequently, this has significant implications for methods that rely on the exponential stability of thermal equations. Specifically, this has significant consequences for models of drug delivery and thermal modeling in the frequency domain. By applying mathematical reasoning, we derive a condition for the absence of constant solutions in the extended model and conclude that the extended model is not just a relaxation of the standard model but also possesses unique features. Lastly, through numerical methods, we verify that the optimized lifting problem indeed induces low-frequency oscillations in the boundary temperature gradient as predicted. Consequently, this has significant implications for methods that rely on exponential stability. By incorporating the numerical methods, we show that the numerical methods converge to the predicted solution as the optimization parameter approaches zero. Consequently, this has significant consequences for models of drug delivery and frequency domain thermal modeling. This research project focuses on utilizing learning algorithms to make the most of a quadruped robot's elastic actuation system for enhanced mobility. By allowing the actuation ratio to adjust freely, we can simulate overactuation – supplying more force than required for movement – in specific phases of the gait cycle. This technique is shown to be effective for gait trajectory optimization but has the drawback of making the movement unstable and requiring constant correction. In contrast, a constant elastic actuation force that decreases over time can produce stable motion; however, this approach requires periodic correction via adjustment to the actuation ratio. Our method achieves great results on the ST-4 four-legged robot by generating optimized gait trajectories and a dynamic actuation strategy that contributes to improved stability and mobility. An artificial intelligence algorithm is developed to automatically manage the elastic actuation system in real-time. Ultimately, the introduction of our strategies leads to a notable enhancement in the robot's mobility, with a 50% increase in speed and 5.7% increase in stability when navigating flat surfaces, as well as a 60% increase in speed and 9% increase in stability when navigating uneven terrain.
